member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiArchetype
member.summary: The nine behaviour scripts the AI system loads, and which uses which.

remarks.para: AIFunction_DefaultHandler (0x44E060) is the whole mechanism in one line: Script_Run(scripts[archetypeOf[ai->aiType]]), where archetypeOf is the twenty-nine-entry map at 0x53C94C.

The script order is the reverse of the string-address order, which is the trap here. The nine paths sit in .rdata as guard, patrol, civilian, priboi, ekk, anya, sniper, gunner, rpg — so index 0 looks like guard. It is not. The map's first seven entries are the identity (AITYPE_RPG is 0 and maps to script 0, AITYPE_GUNNER is 1 and maps to 1, and so on), which can only hold if script 0 is rpg. The remaining entries then agree perfectly: every PATROL type maps to 7 and every GUARD type to 8.

Two archetype scripts ship and are never loaded. common/ai/observer.qvm and common/ai/radioguard.qvm are in every installation, the engine names neither, and no retail .qvm anywhere mentions either name. They are dead content, like M6's SVOL model path and M9's .357 ammunition.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDetectionSchedule
member.summary: The three-level cost cascade the detection sweep runs behind: a phase gate on the whole sweep, then a rate-limited cone test per candidate, then a rate-limited ray behind that.

remarks.para: From 0x489750 (the sweep) and 0x4898D0 (the per-candidate test). The AI never looks at everyone every tick:

list.item: the sweep runs one tick in four, and the AI's own phase decides which — so AIs are staggered across the four ticks rather than all sweeping together;
the cone test runs at most once per sweeps;
the line-of-sight ray runs at most once per sweeps, and only while the target is already in a cone — so the expensive test is never paid for someone behind you.

remarks.para: Detection latency is therefore the product of the three, not any one of them. The sweep is also O(every human in the level) per AI: it walks the engine's global registry, with a fixed slot per index and no spatial index at all.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDetectionSchedule.PhaseCount

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDetectionSchedule.Sweep(OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDetectionSlot,System.Func{System.Boolean},System.Func{System.Boolean},System.Double)
member.summary: Runs one candidate through the cascade, as 0x4898D0 does.
member.param: The candidate's slot, updated in place.
Whether the target is inside a cone. Called only when the cone cooldown is spent.
Whether the line to the target is clear. Called only when the target is in a cone and the ray cooldown is spent.
The current distance, which is stored unconditionally on every sweep.

remarks.para: The cooldown arithmetic is worth stating exactly, because it is off by one from the obvious reading: a test sets its cooldown to interval + 1 and the same call then decrements it, leaving interval. The cooldown has to reach zero again before the next test, which takes interval further sweeps — so the effective period is interval + 1 sweeps, and an interval of zero tests on every sweep.

The asymmetry that matters: losing the cone clears the visible flag at once, but gaining it does not set it — the ray still has to run. So an AI loses sight of you instantly and re-acquires you no sooner than the ray period allows.

And the ray's cooldown is decremented only while the target is in a cone, so time spent out of the cone does not count towards the next ray. Stepping out of view and back in does not shorten the wait.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDetectionSlot
member.summary: One AI's tracking record for one other human — a 48-byte slot at a fixed index, not a dynamic entry.

remarks.para: The vision subsystem holds a 48-byte header followed by one slot per human, so slot i sits at vision + 48 × (i + 1) and the index is the human's position in the engine's global registry. A slot is linked onto the enemy or friendly list when it becomes relevant and unlinked when it stops, but the storage never moves.

Offsets, from 0x489500 (register) and 0x4898D0 (test): +8 a reference-counted task handle, +16 the cone-test cooldown, +20 the ray cooldown, +24 the tick it was first registered, +32 the distance as a double, +40 in-cone, +41 visible, +42 registered.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiDifficulty
member.summary: The three game difficulties, which together with the key every row of common/ai/settings.qsc.

remarks.para: The keys come out of the binary rather than out of the script: sub_406330(i) is &"GD_1"[16 * i], three names laid out sixteen bytes apart, and it is what the fallback path passes when it builds an item the script did not declare. GD_1, GD_2 and GD_3 are the game's easy, normal and hard, which the retail table agrees with from its own side: a guard's maximum health climbs 0.3 → 0.5 → 0.8 across the three and its hit probability at maximum range 0.1 → 0.3 → 0.5.
The difficulty in force is the player profile's, read once when a HumanAI is configured (sub_406F70 takes it from sub_406220()'s first field). There is no per-AI difficulty.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiEvent
member.summary: The twenty-four events an AI script dispatches on. An archetype script is one long if (AIFunction_GetCurrentEventType() == AIEVENT_…) chain, so this enum *is* the AI's interface.

remarks.para: The numbering is read from the registrar 0x44EEB0, which names all twenty-four in one run of literal Script_RegisterConstant(name, n) calls. Worth doing rather than reading the string table: the strings sit in .rdata in the reverse of this order, and M9 was caught out by exactly that — MISSION_TYPE_* is not in string order either.

The events divide into three kinds, though nothing in the engine labels them: lifecycle (, , ), state (, , , the two alarm events), and sensed — everything from down, which other systems post with a position so the script can ask for its distance and whether it came from behind.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiEyeSnapshot
member.summary: The eye snapshot at HumanAI+14896, and the cone test 0x489960 that reads it — which is the function the detection cascade actually calls.

remarks.para: Correction, from the live game. 0x4502F0 was first taken to be "the cone test" and the port transcribed it into . Hooking the retail executable through a whole mission-1 load that logged 22045 patrol events showed 0x4502F0 was never called once. The per-tick detection sweep (0x489750) builds this snapshot with 0x489960 and tests against it from 0x4898D0; 0x4502F0 is reachable only from the event-admission path. So detection has to be modelled on this type, not on that one.
Three things differ from 0x4502F0, and only two of them can ever show:

list.item: each cone carries one resolved length rather than a normal/alarm pair — so an AI whose alert latch flips mid-tick still sees with the range the snapshot was taken at (the original's one-tick lag);

the secondary cone is gated by a byte at +112 that 0x4502F0 has no equivalent of. The per-tick sets it to 1 for a soldier, but a level-1 SCamera reads back 0 with an all-zero secondary — so a security camera is a viewer with a primary cone and no peripheral vision, which is what the gate is for;

there is no "behind the eye" early-out. 0x4502F0 returns false immediately on local.y < 0; this function has no such test and computes both angles regardless. It cannot change an answer while every configured half-angle is under 90° — a point behind the eye gives an angle over 90° from forward and fails on the angle instead — and every retail cone is (the widest is the secondary's ±80°). Recorded because it is a real difference between the two functions, not because it is reachable.

remarks.para: The layout is pinned field for field by the offsets 0x489960 indexes: position at +0, the 3×3 at +24, primary {alpha, gamma, length} at +64/+72/+80, secondary at +88/+96/+104, and the gate byte at +112.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiNativeReturn
member.summary: What kind of value an AI native hands back to the script.
member.remarks: The registrar picks one of three wrappers, each passing a different tag to the common Script_RegisterNative (0x4BAAC0): 0x4B8890 passes 0, 0x4B88C0 passes 1 and 0x4B88F0 passes 2. The VM reads tags 0 and 1 identically — its rule is "3 is a string, 2 is a float, anything else is an integer" — so the split between and is the engine author documenting intent, not a type the interpreter enforces. It is kept because it separates the eighteen actions from the getters exactly.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolCommandKind
member.summary: The nine commands a patrol path is built from — the PATROLPATHCOMMAND_* constant family.

remarks.para: Registered by the tail of PatrolPath's own registrar (0x453550), which walks the pointer array at off_53E2A0 handing out i - 1 — so the first constant is = −1, not zero. The array is in descending string-address order, the same layout as AIEVENT_*, so it has to be read as an array rather than off the string table.

A command is a PatrolPathCommand task (40 bytes, 0x4533B0) whose two Int32 script parameters sit at +32 and +36 — the kind and its operand, which is exactly what the accessors sub_453540 and sub_485320 read. Retail level data declares them "Command" and "Command Parameter".
Two walkers consume these and neither implements all nine. The human walker (0x48E920) has arms for 0–5 and 7; CarAI's (0x425DE0) has 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 8. See for what that costs.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolCommandKind.None
member.summary: No command — the value a PatrolPathCommand carries when nothing was authored.
member.remarks: −1 rather than 0, because the registrar's loop starts its counter at −1. It appears in retail data as the operand of an , never as a kind.

member.summary: Marks where the looping body of the path begins. Never executed — the cursor consumes it.
member.remarks: This is the kind whose name mattered most. It has no arm in either walker's switch, which an earlier pass read as "a kind that cannot be executed"; in fact the commands run to the end of the list and then wrap back to the command after this one, so everything before it is a run-once prologue. Retail data says so in words — the label on level 1's is "End script, only runs commands after this one."

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolRoute
member.summary: A running patrol — the 28-byte cursor 0x4537E0 initialises, and the walk over a path's commands.

remarks.para: A patrolling AI does not index its path by step number. It keeps a cursor holding the current command, where the loop starts, the last two movement commands, the gait, the crouch flag and a delay deadline. For a human this lives inside HumanAI at +5372 + 28n (patrols nest — the per-tick reads the last pushed, and +5396 is the count); for CarAI it is a plain member at +48. The same 28 bytes either way.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolRoute.Start(OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolPath,System.Int32)
member.summary: Starts a patrol at a command index — 0x4537E0.
member.param: The path to walk.
The command to start on; the original's third argument, always 0 so far.
member.returns: The cursor, or when the path has no command at that index.
member.remarks: The scan to (0x453880) records the most recent movement command and the most recent on the way, so a patrol entered part-way through still knows where its loop starts and where it was last heading. If the command it lands on is an it steps past it at once — which is what stops a path that opens with one (as level 1's does) from hanging on it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolRoute.Advance
member.summary: Advances to the next command — sub_453760.
member.returns: when the cursor moved; when the patrol stopped, in which case the current command is left as it was.

remarks.para: The command list runs to its end and then wraps back to the command after the . Two s in a row are fatal in the original ("END command following END command"); here they stop the patrol rather than halting the process, which is the one deliberate divergence in this class.

The wrap happens once. is both the wrap target and the already-wrapped marker, and the guard that reads it is tested before it is written — so on the second time the list runs out, the peek returns the recorded , the guard matches, and the cursor stops where it is. A patrol therefore runs its prologue, runs its loop body once more, and then repeats its final command. This is read behaviour, not an interpretation.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolRoute.Peek
member.summary: Looks at where the cursor would go next without moving it — sub_453730.
member.returns: The command index, or .
member.remarks: Three sources in order: the next command in the list; failing that the recorded ; failing that the path's first command. In the original the first test is next != 0 && *next != 0, where the second half is not "the next command has a successor" but "the next pointer is not the list's end marker" — the engine terminates a child list with a pointer to a slot holding zero, so *p == 0 is how it recognises the end. Mistaking that for a successor test reads as the last command being unreachable.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiPatrolRoute.Begin(System.Int32)
member.summary: Applies the current command's own effect on the cursor's state.
member.param: The engine tick counter, which a delay's deadline is measured against.
member.returns: when the command finishes on the tick it starts.
member.remarks: Only the state the cursor owns is here — the gait, the crouch flag and the delay deadline. The movement, animation and turning a command drives belong to the AI, because the walker reaches out to the body for those.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiScriptApi
member.summary: The complete vocabulary an AI behaviour script is written against: fifty-five natives and four families of constant, transcribed from the registrars rather than from the string table.

remarks.para: Two registrars between them publish the lot. 0x44CCA0 registers the natives — eighteen AIAction_* and thirty-seven AIFunction_*, each with its argument count and one of three return tags. 0x44EEB0 registers the constants: the twenty-four values, the two , the twenty-nine values (by walking a string table), the two values, and two bare distances.

This table is the authoritative vocabulary, separate from the native bodies and the event pump (HumanAI's per-tick, 0x44F410). Keeping it independent lets every retail AI script be checked against it: 884 shipped .qvm files, and every AI name any of them mentions has to be in here.

member.remarks: HUMANAI_DETECTIONEVENT_GUNSHOT_RANGE, registered as the literal 122880 — 30 metres on the 4096-units-per-metre scale. M9 read the same number off the weapon module's own constant (0x1E000 at 0x44EFF3), so this is the second independent sighting of it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.PatrolPathTask
member.summary: A patrol path — the original's PatrolPath, whose steps are its child tasks.

remarks.para: Registered at 0x453550 with an instance size of 52 and no script parameters at all (Task_DeclareParameters("PatrolPath");). That is not an oversight: a path's identity is its task id, which the post-load handler 0x453680 reads with Task_GetId and stores at +40 before linking the task onto a global list at 0x5BDA70. AIAction_Patrol's first argument is that id, and sub_453840 is the walk of that list looking for it.

The private list exists because the engine has no reverse index from a type to its instances — the id table maps id to task for every type at once, and a patrol id has to resolve to a PatrolPath specifically.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.HumanAiTask
member.summary: A soldier's brain — the original's HumanAI, a 16080-byte child of its body.

remarks.para: Its two script parameters answer the question the milestone plan was written assuming had no answer: the AI type is an ordinary parameter, carrying the AITYPE_* constant's name as a string. Level data reads Task_New(1506, "HumanAI", "", "AITYPE_PATROL_AK", 1), and the resolved number lands at HumanAI+15672, from where a type-to-archetype map picks one of the nine archetype scripts.
The graph id beside it selects which graph<n>.dat the AI walks — the id of the AIGraph task that loaded it, which is why level 1 ships a graph4019 beside its graph1.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiType
member.summary: The twenty-nine soldier archetypes a level can spawn. Each names a behaviour script and a row of common/ai/settings.qsc, which is keyed by (AIType, Difficulty).

remarks.para: Registered by a table walk — 0x44EEB0 iterates the string-pointer array at 0x53C9C0..0x53CA34 handing out 0, 1, 2, … in order. So the numbering is the table's order, and the table's order is not the string-address order, not alphabetical, and not what you would guess: is 0 and the named characters come before the generic guards.

The faction prefix has no behavioural effect. All twenty-nine collapse onto nine scripts through the map at 0x53C94C (see ), and every PATROL variant — plain, SECURITY, MAFIA and SPETNAZ alike — resolves to patrol, every GUARD variant to guard. AITYPE_MAFIA_GUARD_AK and AITYPE_GUARD_AK run byte-identical behaviour; what differs between them is the settings row and the model, not the script.
The weapon in the name is likewise not read by the script — it is part of the settings key.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiViewCone
member.summary: One of an AI's two view cones — an elliptical cone with a vertical half-angle, a horizontal half-angle and two lengths, the longer of which applies once the AI is alerted.
member.param: The vertical half-angle in radians. AIFunction_SetViewAlpha writes it.
The horizontal half-angle in radians. AIFunction_SetViewGamma writes it.
The range in engine units while unalerted.
The range in engine units once alerted.

remarks.para: is the vertical angle and the horizontal, which is the opposite of what the names suggest and of what an earlier reading recorded. Three independent arguments agree on it:

list.item: 0x4502F0 compares against an angle measured with the local X component zeroed, and against one with Z zeroed.

The eye orientation is built by 0x4B38E0 — the Real32x9 Euler composer pinned as Rz(γ)·Ry(β)·Rx(α) — and 0x464BD0 passes zero for the middle angle. So the frame is yaw about world Z over pitch about X, whose columns work out to X = right (always horizontal), Y = forward (which the local.y < 0 early-out independently confirms) and Z = up. Zeroing X therefore leaves the vertical plane and zeroing Z the horizontal one.
The constructor's secondary cone is wider in than the primary and barely half as long — peripheral vision, which is wider horizontally.

remarks.para: AIFunction_SetViewLength takes metres and stores × 4096; the angle setters take degrees and store × 0.017453292, the same single-precision constant the weapon zoom is built on. Both length setters also raise the alarm length to match if the normal length is set above it, so an alarmed AI can never see less far than a calm one.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiViewCone.DefaultPrimary
member.summary: The primary cone 0x44F060 starts an AI with — ±45° vertically, ±50° horizontally, 26 m, with no extra reach when alerted.

remarks.para: Correction. These were previously recorded as ±57.29° and ±59.55°. 57.29° is exactly one radian, which is the tell: the earlier pass had picked up values that were not these fields. The constructor's own dwords say otherwise — +160 is 0x3FE921FB60000000, which is π/4 to the bit, and +168 is 0x3FEBECDE60000000 = 50.0°.
Confirmed twice over: the raw store in the constructor, and the live game, where the eye snapshot of every level 1 guard reads back 45° / 50° before its script overrides them.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiViewCone.DefaultSecondary
member.summary: The secondary cone 0x44F060 starts an AI with — ±45° vertically, ±80° horizontally, 10 m. Peripheral vision, and no shipped script ever changes it.

remarks.para: Correction. Previously recorded as ±63° at 12.5 m. The constructor stores +200 as 0x3FF6571860000000 = 1.396264 rad = 80.0° and +208 as 0x40E4000000000000 = 40960 units = 10 m.

This one matters more than it looks. No script touches the secondary cone — verified again over every shipped .qvm, none of which contains a SetSecondary at all — so every AI in the game peers through exactly this cone, and it is considerably wider than the ±63° previously recorded. A guard notices someone beside it at a much greater angle than the old figure implied.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiVision
member.summary: An AI's pair of view cones, and the test that decides whether a point is inside either.

remarks.para: Read before . Hooking the retail executable settled that 0x4502F0 — which transcribes — is never called by the detection sweep. What the sweep runs is the cone test on the per-tick eye snapshot, . This type holds the parameters both share and takes the snapshot; is kept because 0x4502F0 is a real function on the event-admission path, not because detection uses it.

From 0x4502F0. Both cones are always tested and the results are OR'd — which corrects an earlier reading's "cone selection switches on the alert latch". The latch does not select a cone; it selects each cone's range. So an AI sees through a long narrow cone or a short wide one, and being alerted lengthens both.
The parameters live at HumanAI+160..+223 as two blocks of four doubles — {alpha, gamma, length, alarmLength} — which is why the per-tick snapshot copies exactly that span.

member.remarks: The per-tick sets this to 1 unconditionally for a soldier, so it is on for every AI in the game. The one live observation of it being 0 is a level-1 SCamera, whose secondary cone is all zeroes — a security camera has a primary cone and no peripheral vision. Only the snapshot test () consults it; 0x4502F0 has no equivalent.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiVision.Capture(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Takes the per-tick eye snapshot — 0x489750's copy into HumanAI+14896, whose cone test is what the detection cascade actually runs.
member.param: The eye's world position, in engine units.
The eye's orientation, columns X right / Y forward / Z up.
The alert latch, which picks each cone's length once, here rather than on every test.

member.remarks: The snapshot is taken before the alert latch is recomputed, so the cones used on a tick are the ones last tick's state selected — a one-tick lag that is in the original.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiVision.IsVisible(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Tests whether a world point is visible from an eye, ignoring occlusion.
member.param: The eye's world position.
The eye's orientation, whose columns are the local axes in world space: X right, Y forward, Z up.
The world point.
The AI's alert latch, which picks each cone's range.
member.returns: when the point lies in either cone.

remarks.para: This is geometry only. The original's caller is the event-admission filter, which has already decided there is something to look at; nothing here casts a ray, so a wall does not block it.
Note the mixed comparisons, reproduced as-is: the range is <= while both angles are <. A point exactly on the cone's rim is out; a point at exactly maximum range is in.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiVision.AngleFromForward(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: The vertical half-angle from the forward axis to a direction, with X dropped.
member.param: The local forward component.
The local up component.
member.returns: The signed angle in radians, positive when is.

remarks.para: 0x4148F0. It zeroes the local X in place — which is why its caller re-copies the vector before every call — normalises what is left, takes the arc cosine of the forward component and signs the result by the remaining one. A degenerate vector yields zero.

The horizontal twin 0x414950 is the same function with Z dropped instead of X, and it signs the result the other way round (negative when its off-axis component is positive). Both callers take the absolute value immediately, so the disagreement never shows; this one helper serves both, and the asymmetry is recorded rather than reproduced.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AiVisionPhases
member.summary: Which of the four sweep ticks each detection record a level loads takes -- the round-robin counter dword_5C8B08 that 0x4896C0 hands out, one value per record, as each one initialises.

remarks.para: One counter serves every kind of record, and the order is the level's: the camera lenses as they are built (0x4415C0), then a post-load walk of the whole task tree, dormant containers included -- each HumanAI as its init (0x4505D0) runs, each Car and Heli before its children (0x42F530, 0x432950), each AIStationaryGunHolder after them (0x46E7F0 post-loads its children first). A plain StationaryGun has no record of its own -- mission 4's gun 775 took none. A GuardGenerator's children are templates and are not post-loaded; a clone takes the next value when it is made.

Probed on mission 4 (hook on 0x4896C0): 48 records on tick 0, cutscene HumanAIs and both helicopters among them, so Harrison's squad 400..405 took phases 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1 and guard 411 phase 3. The port had numbered soldiers by their own load order alone and vehicles on a counter of their own, which put 411 on phase 2 and squad member 404 on phase 2 -- and 404 saw guard 411 a sweep before retail's did.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AlarmSpeakerRegistry
member.summary: All placed sirens in one mission and whether each is sounding.

remarks.para: The retail task (0x4397C0, 504 bytes) is a speaker with a lamp: its update (0x43A270) evaluates its own level expression each tick and, while it holds, spawns a looping sound child at its own position — destroying that child the moment the expression clears. That is why every siren in a level starts on the same tick and stops together, and why each one is heard from where it hangs. A destroyed speaker (+417) silences itself for good. Rich world contacts use to preserve the struck task's identity; radius damage and legacy contacts use .

The expression machinery is the same one AiAlarmControlRegistry evaluates the controls through, over the same live level variables — so a speaker whose expression names AlarmControl_5.isAlarm follows that control exactly as retail's does.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AlarmSpeakerRegistry.CameraDestroyThreshold
member.summary: The damage that breaks a security camera's lens.
member.remarks: 0x4415C0 writes 0.5 into the lens's +264; its hit handlers (0x4422B0 for a round, 0x4422F0 for a blast) add to +260 and flag the explosion once the sum reaches it. Retail's rounds carry 0.2 in Mission 1, so a camera takes three.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.AlarmSpeakerRegistry.SirenDestroyThreshold
member.summary: The damage that blows a siren up.
member.remarks: A siren is an ExplodeObject (0x449360, parent 0x481340). Its constructor (0x4492A0) hands 0x481360 1.0 for +496, which the object's setup (0x481C40) copies into its threshold +492; sirens declare no explosion parameters to change it. A round (0x481E60) and a blast (0x481EA0, the blast flag +564 left set by 0x481780) add to +488, and the siren goes off, with no delay, once the sum reaches it: five of Mission 1's rounds.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.GuardGeneratorTask
member.summary: A retail GuardGenerator: one authored soldier template with a bounded spawn count.
member.remarks: IGI1 registers this type at 0x487BE0. Its update at 0x487EE0 evaluates the Generate guards expression, creates at most Max spawns copies of the one authored child, and exports isOn, isSpawned, and nSpawns. The native clone helper (0x488000/0x488040) recursively rebuilds the authored subtree; the managed runtime keeps the typed authored task as the template while creating a fresh live brain/view for every instance.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.ISoldierBodies.Arm(OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedMission,OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponTypeRegistry)
member.summary: Puts each soldier's own weapon model in its hand.
member.param: The mission whose packs hold the weapon models.
The weapon table, which maps a WEAPON_ID_* to the model that draws it.
member.returns: How many soldiers ended up holding something.

remarks.para: Three reads join up here. What a soldier carries is authored, as ordinary Gun child tasks of the HumanSoldier carrying a WEAPON_ID_* — the same mechanism that arms the player — and the first of them is the one in hand, because everything that asks a human what it is holding takes slot 0 of the list at Human+1220 (see PlayerLoadout.WeaponsOf). Which model comes from that id's row of the weapon table, whose GunModel field is what the world draws it with. And where it hangs is , bone 22, which 0x4600C0's third-person arm reads out of the body's own palette at +2928/+2940.

Correction to the milestone's own framing. The weapon is not resolved from the soldier's AIType. The AK in AITYPE_PATROL_AK is part of the settings.qsc key (AIType, Difficulty), and a level-1 guard whose type says AK routinely carries an MP5SD — because its own child task says so. Nothing in the engine maps a type to a model.

member.summary: Loads the player's third-person body — the model the level's HumanPlayer declares, on skeleton 0's set, standing in clip 2 — so the death camera has a body to reveal.
member.param: The mission whose packs hold the model.
The player's model, from the HumanPlayer task's Model parameter.
Skeleton 0's animation set (000.iff), the same one the player walks on.
Where the level places the player, in engine units.
The heading the player starts facing.
member.returns: when the model does not resolve or does not upload.
member.remarks: The body is built from a synthetic HumanSoldierTask because that is all SoldierView needs — skeleton, stand clip, position and heading — and the player's constructor (0x410370) builds exactly that on Human+104 (see HumanPlayerBody). It is kept out of _groups so nothing else draws or ticks it; only the death path does.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.ISoldierBodies.StandPlayerBodyAt(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Single)
member.summary: Stands the player's body at a place and draws it, outside death and outside climbing.
member.param: Where the body stands, in engine units — the level's own spawn.
Which way it faces, as the spawn's gamma.

remarks.para: A third reason to draw the body, and deliberately a separate flag rather than a reuse of either existing one. The mission-entry shot dives onto the character standing at their spawn and seats the view inside their head, so it needs the body visible for a second — but it must not touch _playerBodyActive, which is the death latch and also drives the fall's per-tick re-skin and the knock-back, nor the climbing latch, which the ladder code clears on its own schedule.

It has to place and re-skin, not merely make visible. LoadPlayerBody uploads the model's REST mesh and leaves the body unplaced — the death path places and poses it, the climbing path places and poses it, and until one of them runs there is no pose in the vertex buffer at all. Drawing it in that state put enormous black shards across the middle of the descent, which is exactly what an unskinned rig looks like when its vertices are still at the origin.
Cleared by and by Release, so a mission that ends mid-shot does not leave a body standing in the next one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.VehicleGunTurret
member.summary: One gun a vehicle model carries, turning toward what its vehicle sees and deciding to fire.

remarks.para: A port of AIStationaryGun's run handler (0x46F390). Each tick the gun asks its vehicle for the first target the vehicle currently sees (message 0x489630), turns its elevation (+444) and traverse (+448) toward it at the authored rates, and holds the trigger only while both are within five degrees of the target and the target is beyond the authored minimum range. A target that drops out of sight is still aimed at for 90 ticks (+468), after which the gun swings back to its rest pose.

Angles are measured in the vehicle's frame, as 0x414950 measures them: traverse is the heading from local +Y with +X negative, elevation is signed by local Z. The gun's own limits clamp the pose after it turns (0x46F9D0); the aim it compares against for firing is the unclamped one, so a target outside the arc is never fired on.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Ai.VehicleVision
member.summary: A firing vehicle's eye: the detection record a Car keeps at +2704 and a Heli at +2240, which its guns and its CarAI read.

remarks.para: It is the same record every AI viewer uses (0x4896C0), run by the same sweep (0x489750): one tick in four on the record's phase, the cone test every second sweep and the sight ray every third while the target is in the cone (0x4898D0, intervals 4/4 and 8/4). What a vehicle sees is therefore last sweep's answer, not a fresh look every tick.

The cone comes from the vehicle's authored "ViewCone" parameters as 0x42F530/0x432950 store them: alpha and gamma in radians and not halved -- 0x489960 compares each absolute angle against the whole value -- and the length in metres times 4096. There is no secondary cone (+112 = 0).

The phase comes from the global round-robin counter 0x5C8B08, advanced by every record's initialisation. On mission 7 the four camera lenses take 0 to 3 at construction and the vehicles then take theirs in tree order at post-load (Heli 356 → 0, Car 355 → 1, 354 → 2, 357 → 3, 361 → 0, Heli 353 → 1, Car 352 → 2, 351 → 3), probed.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Config.ConfigScript
member.summary: Reads config.qvm, which is where the game keeps every setting it remembers.

remarks.para: The save file is a compiled script. Its entire body is calls into sixteen GO* natives the engine registers, one group per profile, and running it is loading the configuration — there is no separate parser and no binary record on disk.

The shape, from a retail file: GOStart(n) and GOContentControlPW(s) once, then for each profile GOPlayer(name) followed by that profile's settings and its twenty-seven GOInRemap(action, device, key) bindings. GOPlayer is the delimiter: every setting after one belongs to it.

Bindings are stored by name — MoveLeft, INPUTPORT_DEVICE_KEYBOARD, KEY_LEFT — rather than by number, so they survive a change to the engine's key numbering. The names arrive as script constants, which is why the loader registers each one it has not seen and records the name rather than the value.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Config.ConfigScriptWriter
member.summary: Writes a configuration back out as a compiled script, in the format the original saves.

remarks.para: Saving settings means emitting bytecode, because the save file is a script — see . The body is one call per setting, in the order a retail file uses, and the header's five sections are laid out exactly as the reader requires: each butts up against the next and the code section ends at the end of the file.
A call is emitted in the shape the original's compiler produces:
remarks.code: PUSHIIB <function> ; 2 bytes CALL argc=n ; 5 + 4n, each argument an absolute code offset BRA +len ; 5 bytes, jumps over the argument blocks <argument block> ; the value, then BRK POP ; discards the result
remarks.para: The argument blocks sit between the branch and its target rather than anywhere else in the file, which is what makes the offsets in the CALL and the displacement in the BRA agree.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Config.PlayerProfile
member.summary: One player's saved settings and progress.

remarks.para: The original keeps these in a fixed array of sixteen 1380-byte records (Config_GetActiveProfile, 0x406220, is base + 1380 * activeIndex), and every option is per-profile — graphics, sound and input included. Two players on one machine do not share a resolution.

The field layout below is the record's, for anyone checking against the binary. It is modelled as properties rather than a byte blob because nothing outside the save file depends on the packing, and config.qvm — which is the save file — is keyed by name, not by offset.

member.remarks: The port keeps the retail action set but uses a conflict-free modern movement layout. They must live in the model rather than the Controls screen: a profile created before that page is opened still has to serialize to a complete configuration and provide usable input to the game.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Config.PlayerProfile.RetailDefaultBindings
member.summary: The bindings the original's own fresh profile starts with.
member.remarks: The 27 rows Config_ResetToDefaults (0x405300) copies from 0x536410, read from the binary: DirectInput codes 0xCB, 0xCD, 0xC8 and 0xD0 are the arrow keys, jump is Numpad 0, activate the right Shift, walk/run W. The retail config.qvm an installation ships lists exactly these. Kept to recognise a profile nobody ever rebound, which is what is for; nothing is given them any more.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Config.PlayerProfileInputBindings.WheelNoiseFloorNotches
member.summary: The smallest wheel motion that counts as a notch, in scroll units. Discrete mice report whole notches; precision trackpads report fractions, including feather-touch noise from resting fingers. Below this floor motion is ignored rather than fired as input.
member.remarks: A wheel notch is a momentary edge with no held state, so a bound action reads on every frame that scrolls past the floor in its direction — one frame per scrolled frame, which is what makes scroll-to-switch-weapons track the gesture. The same edge semantics apply to sustained actions: scrolling continuously holds them, while a single notch nudges them for exactly one frame.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Config.TaskTypeConstants
member.summary: The TASKTYPE_* constants a configuration script names, given ids in the script namespace and remembered by id so a definition's task type can be read back by name.

remarks.para: The weapon, magic-object and animation-trigger tables each name task types by these constants, and all three share the one process-wide namespace, which outlives every table: a mission restart, a level change, or simply the table loaded second finds a constant already there. Such a constant keeps its id, and that id is adopted into this table's own map. Skipping it instead left the map without the name -- every task type the table read back came out empty, which is what made the optical weapons lose their zoom after a restart (issue #79) -- and numbering afresh from one gave two names the same id.
A constant new to the namespace takes the next id after the highest this table has seen.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars
member.summary: The gameplay layer's console variables.

remarks.para: Declared next to the code that reads them, the way the renderer and the audio seam declare their own. The g_ prefix is the one the settings screen already builds its Gameplay page from, so the rows here appear in the menu, the console and settings.cfg without any of the three being told.

Nothing declared here may change what the simulation does, with one named exception. These gate presentation only — what is drawn, not what is recorded — so the determinism contract and the vanilla regression gate both stand whatever they are set to. Anything that would alter observable game logic belongs with the faithfulness work instead.

The exception is and its family: tactical ballistics is a gameplay change — a round takes time to arrive and drops on the way — and it says so rather than pretending to be a look. It is defensible here because it defaults off, no profile turns it on (vanilla forces it off, enhanced leaves it alone), and the regression gate never runs with it set. A player who types g_ballistics 1 is explicitly asking for a game the original is not.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.Preset
member.summary: Which named profile the gameplay-presentation settings correspond to.
member.remarks: Setting this writes the profile's values over the variables it names, which is how -vanilla reaches the gameplay layer: the flag emits g_preset vanilla as a start-up statement, exactly as it emits gfx_preset vanilla and snd_preset vanilla.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.Ragdoll
member.summary: Whether the dead are simulated rather than playing a canned death animation.

remarks.para: Off, a body dies exactly as it does in the original: one of the death clips the hit zone and the killing weapon name, played out with the nine-ray travel limiter behind it. On, that clip still runs — it is what the simulation moves the corpse by, and none of that changes — but what is drawn is a physically simulated body, seeded from the round's own direction and the weapon's momentum.
Applies to guards and to the player alike; both die through the same rig.
Off by default, and no profile turns it on: the canned deaths are the game as shipped, and the simulation is something a player asks for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.RealisticDrops
member.summary: Whether a dropped weapon falls as a real rigid body or the way the original drops it.

remarks.para: Off in the Vanilla preset, which drops a gun exactly as GunPickup does (0x46C980/0x46CEA0): laid on its side, falling straight down onto the surface under it and bouncing at half speed until it settles.

On in every other preset: the gun leaves the hand with the body's motion and the round's knock, and falls as a rigid body with its real mass, the inertia of its own mesh and contacts against the real world triangles -- tumbling, bouncing, sliding off slopes and lying across ledges.

Where the gun ends up decides where the player picks it up, so this is a second exception to the rule above, alongside . It is safe for the same reason: the Vanilla preset forces it off, and the regression gate runs Vanilla.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.SteadyTurns
member.summary: Whether I.G.I. 2's player's ground speed turns with him, or drifts on as retail's does.
member.remarks: Retail keeps the speed pointing where it pointed when the player turns, and clears the part left pointing sideways only at the strafe step a tick, so a turn at a run slides him sideways like a car. On, the speed turns with him, as Project I.G.I.'s player's does. A third exception to the rule above: where the player goes is game logic. The Vanilla preset forces it off, as with .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.RagdollForce
member.summary: How hard a round throws a body it kills.

remarks.para: One multiplier over the whole impulse model, so the feel of the feature is a single number the player can turn. See RagdollImpulse for why the exaggeration underneath it is deliberate. Zero makes bodies simply fall.

One and a half, measured: a rifle round carries a body about 1.6 m, a shotgun about 3, a pistol about half. At 1 the knock is real but easy to miss, because a guard is standing on the floor when he is shot and the contact takes most of it back straight away.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.RagdollGravity
member.summary: What fraction of real gravity a corpse falls at.

remarks.para: Seven tenths. The one number in the ragdoll that is a look rather than a measurement, and it is a variable rather than a constant for exactly that reason. The solver already falls at the original's own 9.8 m/s² — see Gravity, which deliberately picks that over the 18.6 the player jumps under — so this is not correcting anything.

Real gravity simply reads fast on a corpse: the camera is close, the fall is a metre and a half, and there is none of the anticipation that sells the speed of a jump. Dropping a ragdoll under one g is what most games do about it. 1 is honest physics; below about 0.5 bodies start to float.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.RagdollSubsteps
member.summary: How many solver substeps each ragdoll takes per game tick.

remarks.para: Position-based dynamics converges with substeps far better than with iterations, so this is the dial that trades cost for stiffness — and it is the only convergence knob that matters, because each substep runs a single solver sweep. It is also the whole cost of the feature: every constraint in the body is projected this many times a tick.

Eight, measured. Sixteen costs three times as much and buys nothing that can be seen — at both counts every body settles, and the joint drift left at rest is around a centimetre either way. Below about six the drift starts to show on impact.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.Ballistics
member.summary: Whether a round is a simulated projectile rather than the original's instant ray.

remarks.para: The one gameplay-mutating variable in this container; see the container remarks for why it is allowed to be. Off, every round resolves the tick it is fired, exactly as retail does. On, the player's rounds fly at their weapon's real muzzle velocity, drop under gravity and slow by calibre drag () — you lead a moving target — and both sides' fire draws a visible streak.
Off by default in every profile. vanilla forces it off; enhanced does not touch it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.BallisticsDrag
member.summary: How much air a round flies through.
member.remarks: One multiplier over every profile's drag constant, so the feel is a single number: zero is a vacuum where only gravity bends the shot, one is the calibre model as computed.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.BallisticsGravity
member.summary: What fraction of real gravity a round drops under.
member.remarks: The rounds fall at the engine's own 9.8 m/s² — the same constant the ragdoll picked over the player's 18.6, and for the same reason: a bullet is an object, not a jump. This scales it for players who want a flatter or more exaggerated arc.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.BallisticsMinimumFlight
member.summary: The least time a ballistic round flies in open air, in seconds.
member.remarks: The weapon table's effective ranges were authored for the hit-scan path and are short for a flying round — an MP5's 80 m is a fifth of a second. The round's range is raised to at least this many seconds of flight, so far targets are reachable; a wall or a body still stops it the moment it is met.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.BallisticsAiTracers
member.summary: Whether the AI's fire draws ballistic streaks too.
member.remarks: Visual only, and only read while is on: a guard's round is still resolved by its own combat code in its own tick, and the streak flies the line that resolution already chose. Incoming fire becomes something you can see and duck.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.BallisticsImpactSounds
member.summary: Whether bullet impacts are heard as well as seen.
member.remarks: The sounds are the material table's own six per row — dirt for terrain, the struck row for objects, the Flesh row for a body — picked and rate-limited exactly as the retail shot loop does (BulletImpactSounds). It applies to hit-scan fire and to the optional ballistic path.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.ThirdPerson
member.summary: Whether the player is drawn from behind rather than through their own eyes.

remarks.para: Presentation only, and deliberately so: the eye the shot is fired from, the ear the world is heard through and everything the simulation records stay exactly where the first-person view put them. Only the point the frame is rasterised from moves, and the character the original always carried — the body describes, the one the death camera reveals — is drawn instead of the arms.

Not archived, on purpose. A default key is bound to it (DefaultBinds), and the one rule that table has is that a key the game binds for itself must not decide what the game starts as tomorrow. A view the player flipped to while looking at a jump is not a setting they saved.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.ThirdPersonDistance
member.summary: How far behind the head the third-person eye settles, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.ThirdPersonShoulder
member.summary: How far to the player's right the third-person eye sits, in metres.
member.remarks: The shoulder offset is what keeps the character out of the middle of the frame. It costs a truthful centred crosshair — the round still leaves the eye, which is no longer on the camera's own axis — which is why the remaster HUD projects the aim point rather than drawing a cross at the centre of the screen. Zero puts the camera exactly on the eye's sight line, where the two coincide again.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.ThirdPersonHeight
member.summary: How far above the eye the third-person camera sits, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.ThirdPersonBlend
member.summary: How long the move between the two views takes, in seconds.
member.remarks: The whole point of the feature having a number at all: the camera travels the arc between the eye and the shoulder over this long, with zero velocity and zero acceleration at both ends, so neither entering nor leaving the view is a cut. Zero is the cut, for anyone who wants one.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.GameplayCVars.#cctor
member.summary: Wires the profile variable to the values it stands for.
member.remarks: A static constructor rather than a registry, the same way AudioCVars does it and for the same reason: the preset registry lives in the renderer, which this layer does not drive. The profile is not recomputed when one of its variables is changed by hand — it says what was asked for, and a player who then turns one thing off is not silently switched to "custom" mid-session.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Hosting.MissionLevelBuild
member.summary: A mission being brought up by the host: the loaded mission, its tree and how it arrived, and what each of the host's mission systems leaves for the ones after it.

remarks.para: Both titles pass through these systems: they build the picture, the sound and the I.G.I. rig, and a title that brings its own player stands it in . What a system leaves is set as it finishes, so a later one that reads it finds it set; see for the order.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Hosting.MissionSystemNames
member.summary: The mission systems, in the order a mission is brought up.

remarks.para: The order is load-bearing: the AI's ray cast closes over the terrain the first system sets, the interactions exist before the brains are animated, and the weapon rosters load before humanplayer.qvm runs. A mod inserts its own system by these names.

The game brings its own steps (the cutscenes, objectives, vehicles, interactions, cameras, nav graphs, brains and walk) and sets them before the host's; a ...View system is the host's half of a step, handing what the game's left to the picture.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.LanguageCVars
member.summary: The language the games' text is read in.

remarks.para: Both games ship each language as a folder of archives, language/<name>/, and every archive names its strings after its own language: German's missions.res holds LOCAL:german/Mission 1 Name. So the folder and the name a key is asked for go together, and swapping two folders by hand leaves the menus asking one language for another's keys -- the RM: Mission 1 Name the mission list showed. The original picks both from its configuration; here it is this variable.
A change takes effect at once: the host swaps one language's archives for the other's between frames, and everything that shows text looks its keys up as it draws.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Level.LevelRun
member.summary: One tick of a level's task tree: every task reached is run, by the work bound to it, by its own , or by the title's rule for a task of no class of its own.

remarks.para: The original's update walk is the same in both games: Task_Update runs a task's run handler, and a container's handler runs its children in order. What differs between titles is only what the many task types with no class of their own do -- I.G.I. walks their children unless they are Static or Idle; I.G.I. 2's level and dynamic containers count the tick and run their deferred work -- which is .

A task is run by the first of: the work bound to it (), which is how a system that owns a task drives it; its own ; . Children are run in order, each sibling read before its predecessor runs, so a task may delete itself as it runs.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.BackgroundFxTask
member.summary: The slow green vector overlay that turns behind every menu screen.

remarks.para: An eighteenth task type — BackgroundFX (0x419760, 36 bytes) — that no script declares. The manager creates one at +10208, and MenuScreen_Render (0x421C20) draws it between the logo and the background.

The whole state is one float: a frame counter, incremented by BackgroundFX_Update (0x419800) and nothing else. Every position in the effect is a function of it, so it needs no per-shape state and never has to be reset.

It is drawn twice per frame, at t and at t + 1 (BackgroundFX_Render, 0x419820). Two passes one frame apart at alpha 0.075 each is what gives the lines their soft doubled edge; drawing it once at 0.15 would not look the same.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.ControlsMenuTask
member.summary: The controls list's behaviour: a row per action, clicked to take the next key or button held.

remarks.para: Transcribed from the ControlsMenu class (0x4230A0). It is made at 360 by 200 (0x4232B0), which its frame lines up, and shows of its rows from , which the slider beside it scrolls.

Its update (0x4234E0) hit-tests its own rectangle. A click picks the row under the pointer, shows the prompt in its key column and lets the manager's pointer and keys go (0x418FC0). Each tick after, Escape held cancels; otherwise the first key or button in the table () that is held is the row's, and a row that had it takes the row's old one instead. Either way the queued input is thrown away (0x48A8C0) and the manager takes input again (0x418FD0).
The rows are read from the profile as the screen takes its data in (0x423DB0) and written back as it commits (0x423EB0), through the manager's .

member.summary: The controls-configuration screen's key-binding list.
member.remarks: The one menu type mainmenu.qvm spawns without a Task_DeclareParameters block: it takes no parameters, so the editor emits nothing for it and the engine is expected to know it — the same arrangement as the structural types. It exports nOffset, which the controls screen reads back through ControlsMenu_ConvertFloatFromOffset(ControlsMenu_954.nOffset).

member.summary: Everything the menu manager needs from the shell around it: this tick's input, a way to measure and draw a screen, and somewhere to send a sound or a decision to leave.

remarks.para: The manager task owns the menu's per-tick logic, because that is where the original puts it — MenuManager_Update (0x418080) is the class's update method and runs off the task tree's walk. Anything platform-shaped that it needs comes through here, which keeps OpenIGI.Game free of a window, a device or a font.

member.summary: The single-line text field: the only control the player types into, and the only one that is modal.

remarks.para: From InputBox_Construct (0x41D290) and InputBox_Update (0x41D450). The instance is 424 bytes; the text buffer at +84 is forty, so a value is truncated at thirty-nine characters however long String Length says.

It takes the keyboard. Choosing a field — by click or by enter — grabs input from the manager, and from then until enter or escape the field drains the raw event queue itself and every other control sees nothing. That is why the field can use left, right, home, end and backspace for editing without the menu navigating away underneath it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.ListBoxTask
member.summary: The horizontal spinner: an arrow at each end and one item's label between them.

remarks.para: Transcribed from ListBox_Update (0x41EC70) and ListBox_Render (0x41ED70). It is not a drop-down: left and right cycle through the items and only the current one is on screen, which is why it fits on a line beside a label like a slider does.

Two values are kept, and confusing them would break the graphics screen. is the position in the list and wraps at both ends; is the id stored in the item, which is what the script reads — Config_FillScreenResolutionListBox( ListBox_951.nActiveID) passes the device's id, not its position.

The items themselves come from Collect Items Script, which calls a Config_* native to fill the list. Those natives do not exist yet, so a retail list box loads empty and draws its box and arrows and nothing between them — which is the truthful result, not a placeholder.

The flags are not cosmetic: a list box is placed by its frame's line-up, and the graphics screen's frames are HorizontalFillOut, which assigns the horizontal position and leaves the vertical one to the child's own centring. Without them every list box on that screen sits at the top of the display.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuBorderLayout
member.summary: Works out where each piece of a frame's eight-piece border goes.

remarks.para: Transcribed from MenuFrame_Render (0x4226D0) and its two edge helpers, 0x4227A0 horizontal and 0x4229A0 vertical. The arithmetic lives here rather than in a renderer so it can be checked without a graphics device — the retail main menu turns out to use no frame borders at all, so nothing in the shipped data exercises it.
The eight sprites form a clockwise ring from the top-left, named <sprite>_1 through _8: see .

Nothing is stretched. The edges tile at their native size an integer number of times, so a frame whose width is not a whole number of tiles leaves a gap before the far corner rather than scaling to fit. The bottom edge and the right edge are pulled back by their own size so they sit inside the rectangle, and the vertical runs span only what is left between the horizontal edges.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuBoxTasks
member.summary: The six remaining control types' constructors, data wiring and content.

remarks.para: Grouped because what they have in common is what matters: every one of their constructors sets both centre flags, and several fix a default size the script never mentions. That is not a detail — a control placed by a HorizontalFillOut frame takes its vertical position from its own centring, so an untranscribed constructor leaves it at the top of the display. It cost a debugging session on ListBox before it was understood, and it is the reason these were read constructor-first.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.ScrollListBoxTask
member.summary: A scrolling list whose contents come from an expression.
A scrolling list whose contents come from an expression.
The vertical list: several entries visible at once, with the selection moving through them.

remarks.para: Shares its item model with — both are filled by a Collect Items Script and both report the selected entry's id as nActiveID — but this one shows the whole list and scrolls, where a list box shows one entry between two arrows.

Behaviour transcribed from ScrollListBox_Update (0x41BDD0). Two things there are easy to miss and are what make the control usable: clicking a row selects that row rather than activating it, and clicking the row that is already selected a second time within half the double-click interval is what runs its action. That is how the original starts a mission from the Select Mission screen.

remarks.para: From DialogWindow_DrawBox (0x419D30), which the popup's render (0x419CB0) calls after its controls. The rectangle is the popup's own X-Pos, Y-Pos, Width and Height, and the rule sits below its top.

Unlike a screen's panel every edge, the rule's included, is pulled into the box's centre by the fade: c + (edge - c) * alpha. At alpha 0 the box is a point and at alpha 1 its full size, so the popup grows as it fades in.
It is drawn as the screen's panel is, in the same greens, over a black backing at , which is what sets the popup apart from the screen beneath it.

The authored vertical position.
The back-buffer width in pixels.
The back-buffer height in pixels.
The magnification the menu is drawn at; see .
member.returns: The screen position in pixels.

remarks.para: The original computes (screenWidth >> 1) + x - 320 and (screenHeight >> 1) + y - 240. So the menu is centred at its authored size, not scaled: at 1024×768 the text stays 640×480-sized in the middle of the screen rather than growing.

Divergence. On a display several times that size, faithful is unreadable — so the offset from the centre is magnified by a whole number (). At this is exactly the original's arithmetic, and the caller has to magnify the art by the same amount or the layout and the sprites will disagree.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuNavigator
member.summary: The menu manager's state machine: its screen stack, its popup, its fades, and the states its natives set.

remarks.para: Both games' managers run it. Project I.G.I.'s is MenuManager_Update (0x418080) with the natives its constructor (0x417260) registers; I.G.I. 2's is MenuManager_RunHandler with the same natives (menumanager.c). What differs is in .

The navigation natives all do the same three things: set the pending screen, set the state to return to once the fade completes, and drop into . The screen does not change until the fade reaches zero. What separates them is what they do to the stack:

item.description: Push saves the current screen and returns with .
Pop restores the saved one and returns with , so the screen returned to keeps what its controls held rather than taking its data in again.
Request replaces the current screen and touches the stack not at all, so a screen reached by request cannot be popped back out of.

remarks.para: A popup is opened without a fade out: MenuManager_ActivatePopupScreen enters directly, and the popup fades in over the screen. Closing it fades the popup out to .

remarks.para: Correction. The argument was read here as "reset the screen's data" and ignored. It is the opposite: MenuManager_PopScreen opens with if (Arg_GetInt(args, 0)) MenuManager_SaveScreenData(manager), so it decides whether the controls are written back through their Set Data Scripts. It is the OK-versus-Cancel distinction, and dropping it made every options screen commit.

Both games decrement the depth unconditionally and would read below the base of the stack; refusing is the one place this diverges, and it cannot change behaviour on data that balances its pushes and pops.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuPointer
member.summary: The pointer state a menu hit-test reads: a position in authored coordinates and three button signals.

remarks.para: The manager keeps this block at +10188 and refreshes it each tick in state 2 of MenuManager_Update (0x418080). The three flags are derived there from the button and its previous value: down, the pressed edge, and the released edge.

The position is converted out of screen space on the way in — x += 320 - (screenWidth >> 1) — which is the exact inverse of the centring the items are drawn with, so the hit-test works in authored 640×480 coordinates whatever the back buffer is.

member.param: The panel's left edge in authored pixels.

The panel's right edge.

The fade, 0 to 1.

remarks.para: From MenuScreen_DrawPanel (0x421CD0). The rectangle is the screen's own Frame x0/y0/x1/y1 parameters, each plus one — so the panel is data, and every screen has its own.

The horizontal edges are interpolated out of the centre of the authored 640 by the manager's fade alpha: 320 + (edge - 320) * alpha. At alpha 0 the panel is a vertical line down the middle of the display and at alpha 1 it is its full width, so it opens outwards as a screen fades in and closes as it fades out. That is the animation, and it is why the panel cannot be drawn from the parameters alone.
The vertical edges do not animate.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuSelection
member.summary: The manager's selected item: the one thing the arrow keys move and the pointer follows.

remarks.para: Transcribed from Menu_SetSelected (0x4186E0), Menu_SelectItem (0x418FE0) and the key handling in Menu_HandleKeys (0x418580). The manager keeps a flat array of the screen's selectable items at +60, its length at +188, the selected index at +192 and the selected item at +56.

The point worth naming: the mouse and the keyboard drive the same selection. Hovering an item calls the same setter the arrow keys do and plays the same menu_high sound, so there is never a keyboard highlight in one place and a mouse highlight in another. Exactly one item carries the highlight flag at +77, which is what MenuText_Render tests before drawing an entry lit and putting a glow behind it.

member.summary: A slider bound to a value through get/set expressions.
The slider's per-tick behaviour and its value model.

remarks.para: Transcribed from SlideBar_Update (0x41FA10), SlideBar_LoadData (0x41FF30), SlideBar_SaveData (0x420020), SlideBar_GetIndex (0x420290) and SlideBar_SetIndex (0x4202D0).

The carret position is a double in [0, 1] and everything else is derived from it. The three scripts have distinct jobs and are not interchangeable: Get Data Script seeds the value when the screen is entered, Modify Data Script runs on every change — it is the live preview, which is why the music slider's is Game_SetMusicVolume(this.vValue) — and Set Data Script runs only on the way out, which is where Config_SoundOptionsSetMusicVolume(this.vValue) sits.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.ToggleBoxTask
member.summary: An on/off switch bound through get/set expressions.
The two-state switch's per-tick behaviour.

remarks.para: Transcribed from ToggleBox_Update (0x41E020). The control is two half-width windows side by side — the left half is on and the right half is off, which is the opposite way round from what the names suggest and is worth stating plainly. The original splits its own rectangle with w >> 1 for the left half and w - (w >> 1) for the right, so an odd width gives the extra pixel to the right half.

Left and right therefore set the state rather than flipping it, and pressing left on a switch that is already on does nothing at all — not even a sound. That is what makes a still-posted command harmless: the control never clears +80, and only a genuine change is announced.

member.summary: Registers the menu task types and the constants their scripts name.

remarks.para: The original spreads this over fifteen registrars — MenuManager at 0x4170A0, MenuScreen at 0x421750, MenuText at 0x420CC0 and so on. Each declares its class, binds its methods and builds a property block; only the property blocks matter to a reimplementation, and those are declared by the script rather than the engine.

Parameter order is wire order. Every list here was transcribed from the Task_DeclareParameters calls in retail mainmenu.qvm, which is the authority on what the data contains: Task_New parses positionally, so one wrong entry shifts every field after it and silently swallows the following child tasks. MenuTaskRegistrationTests checks the lists against the script itself rather than against this file.

remarks.para: Transcribed from MenuItem_HitTest (0x4248A0). Two details are worth naming because they are what make the buttons feel right and are easy to simplify away:

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Menus.MenuWindowTask.Arrange
member.summary: Arranges this window's children, then recurses into them.

remarks.para: Transcribed from MenuWindow_LineUp (0x4244B0). Three passes: measure every child and total their sizes, compute a start cursor and a step from the line-up mode, then walk the children again placing each and advancing the cursor. Finally recurse, so a frame inside a frame lays out after its parent has positioned it.
All of the arithmetic is integer, and the divisions truncate toward zero, so the leftover pixels of an uneven split land at the end rather than being distributed.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.ConvexHull
member.summary: A closed convex hull over a point cloud, with its faces and uniform-density mass properties.

remarks.para: Built incrementally: an initial tetrahedron, then every remaining point either falls inside or replaces the faces it can see with a fan to their horizon. The point clouds this serves are a weapon's rendered vertices — a few thousand at most, hulled once per drop — so the plain O(n·F) visibility scan is quicker to trust than a conflict-list quickhull and fast enough.

The faces are what make it a mesh collider rather than a cloud of probe points: they let a world edge or corner that cuts into the gun find the face it entered by, which a vertex test alone never sees.

member.summary: Advances mesh collision, gravity and angular motion for one game tick.
member.remarks: The ground query behind is a full terrain-octree descent plus a collision ray. One tick asks it up to three hundred times — every contact vertex, every resolution pass, every substep — from positions millimetres apart, and a tumbling gun kept that up for seconds after every kill. The memo collapses those to one descent per ten- centimetre cell per tick, which is finer than any surface the queries can distinguish.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.DroppedGunMeshBody.MemoizedWorld(OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollWorld)
member.summary: Wraps a world so its ground query answers repeats from .
member.remarks: Built once per source world and reused: the shell hands the same to every step, so this allocates on the first step and never again. The memo itself is cleared per step by the caller. Positions are keyed at — points that share a cell can differ by centimetres, which is below the resolution of the terrain descent and flat within any floor a gun can rest on; a gun overhanging a ledge edge may read the ledge's height a few centimetres past it, which for a dropped prop is invisible.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RetailGunDrop
member.summary: A gun falling the way the original's GunPickup falls: straight down, bouncing at half speed.

remarks.para: GunPickup_Create (0x46C980) lays the gun on its side -- it keeps only the hand's heading from the 0x4B3C50 decomposition and sets the other two angles to 0 and 90 degrees -- and traces from half a metre above the drop point to fifty metres below it. The gun comes to rest ten centimetres (409.6 units) above whatever that trace meets, or at the drop height when it meets nothing.

GunPickup's tick (0x46CEA0) then moves only Z. Below the rest height it is put back on it and its speed reversed and halved, with one of weapondrop_01/_02. It keeps moving while above the rest height or faster than 409.6 units a tick, and otherwise stops.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollPose
member.summary: Reading orientations back out of the matrices the bone palette stores.
member.remarks: All that is left of what used to be a whole pose-reconstruction stage. When every bone was a single particle the solver knew where a bone was but not which way it faced, and the facing had to be recovered by fitting a rotation to where the bone's children had ended up — a least-squares problem, solved per bone per frame, that could only ever approximate the simulation it was reading. A rigid body carries its own orientation, so the drawn pose is now a direct read and the fitting is gone. This is what remains: the conversion between the two ways the port stores a rotation.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollPose.QuaternionOf(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f)
member.summary: Reads a rotation matrix back out as the quaternion the bone palette stores.
member.param: The rotation, in the M · v convention.
member.returns: The quaternion, such that returns the same rotation.
member.remarks: The inverse of , and it has to be exactly that and not the inverse of — the two differ by a transpose, which is the trap BonePose carries its own warning about. The largest-diagonal branch is the standard numerically stable form; taking the trace branch alone loses all precision at a half turn.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver
member.summary: The pure mathematics a ragdoll is solved with: rigid-body integration, the swing-twist split, and the one-dimensional angle limit every joint constraint is built out of.

remarks.para: Extended position-based dynamics, after Müller, Macklin, Chentanez, Jeschke and Kim (2020), Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with Extended Position Based Dynamics. The shape of it: take many small substeps and solve each constraint once per substep, rather than few large steps with many iterations. Constraint stiffness then follows from the substep size instead of from an iteration count, which is why a ragdoll built this way holds together without tuning.
Everything here is a free function over values. What holds the arrays and does the stepping is RagdollBody; this is the part worth testing on its own.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver.ParallelEpsilon
member.summary: How near two directions must be before the turn between them counts as nothing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver.Advance(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double)
member.summary: Advances an orientation by an angular velocity.
member.param: The current orientation.
The angular velocity, in radians per unit of .
How long to advance for.
member.returns: The new orientation, normalized.
member.remarks: q += ½ h (ω ⊗ q), then normalize — the standard first-order quaternion update, with the angular velocity as a pure quaternion on the left, because ω is in world space and q takes body space to world.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver.Recover(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,System.Double)
member.summary: Recovers the angular velocity a substep's orientation change implies.
member.param: Where the body was pointing.
Where it is pointing now.
How long the substep was.
member.returns: The angular velocity, in radians per unit of .
member.remarks: ω = 2 (q q_prev⁻¹).xyz / h, with the sign taken from the scalar part. The sign matters and is easy to miss: a quaternion and its negation are the same orientation but opposite halves of a turn, so reading the vector part without checking w makes a body that rotated a little past a half turn appear to have spun almost the whole way back.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver.SwingTwist(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Splits a rotation into a twist about an axis and the swing that carries the axis.
member.param: The rotation to split.
The twist axis, in the same frame as the rotation, unit length.
member.returns: The swing and the twist, whose product in that order is the rotation.
member.remarks: q = swing · twist, with the twist's vector part parallel to the axis and the swing's perpendicular to it. Splitting the two is what lets a joint limit them differently, which every real joint does: an elbow swings through most of a half-circle and barely twists at all.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollSolver.LimitAngle(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single,System.Single,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f@)
member.summary: The rotation vector that brings a violated angle limit back inside its range.
member.param: The axis the angle is measured about, unit length.
Where the angle is measured from, perpendicular to the axis, unit length.
Where it is measured to, perpendicular to the axis, unit length.
The lowest the angle may be, in radians.
The highest, in radians.
Receives the correction as an axis scaled by its angle.
member.returns: when the angle is already inside its range.

remarks.para: The limitAngle routine of the XPBD rigid-body paper. The angle comes from the signed sine rather than from a dot product, because a sine keeps its sign and a cosine does not — and the from · to < 0 test is what extends it past a quarter turn, which every real joint range needs.
The correction it returns turns to exactly the limit it crossed, never further: a limit is a wall, not a spring, and a joint pushed back past its limit oscillates.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollWorld.GroundSearchAboveInUnits
member.summary: How far above a point the ground search starts, in engine units.

remarks.para: It has to be above the point at all, because the port's ground query only ever looks downwards and reports nothing when the surface is above where the search began. Start it at the bone and a body that has got even slightly under a floor can never find that floor again, so it drops out of the world — and a bone moving fast enough to end a substep below the surface is exactly how it gets under there.

But it must be only just above, and that is not a tuning preference. The query returns the highest surface below where it starts. Begin the search two metres up and, in any room, what it finds is the ceiling — which it then reports as the ground, whereupon the contact dutifully pushes the bone up to it and the corpse flies into the roof. Outdoors there is nothing overhead so the same code behaves perfectly, which is precisely how a bug like this survives being tested in a field.
Forty centimetres: further than a bone can sink in a tick at any speed it falls, and well under the height of anything a body could be standing beneath.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RigidBodyKernels
member.summary: The rigid-body steps both games compiled to the same arithmetic, written once over the precision each ran at.

remarks.para: Project I.G.I.'s rigid body (0x4EC6A0 and the helpers under 0x4FC0E0) and I.G.I. 2's (Physics_Update, igi2 0x5A9580, and its helpers) are one engine module. These steps match term for term in both builds' disassembly; each is transcribed with the first game's store points, which change nothing at the sequel's 24-bit precision ().

What the two compilers ordered differently stays with each game: the length estimate (0x4B2A10 against Real32x3_FastLen, igi2 0x561820), the angular velocity and the quaternion step of the integrator, and the contact response.
