member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RigidMeshBody
member.summary: A free rigid body whose collider is the convex hull of a rendered mesh, simulated against the real world triangles around it.

remarks.para: Real mass and real inertia. The body carries the object's actual mass and the full inertia tensor of its hull, integrated about its centre of mass. Rotation is integrated from angular momentum, not angular velocity, so a long gun tumbling in the air behaves as a real one does -- stable about its long and short axes, wobbling about the middle one.

Mesh collision. Once per tick the world hands over every solid triangle the body could reach. Each substep then finds two kinds of contact against them: a hull vertex at or below a triangle's surface (the stock or muzzle landing on a floor), and a world edge cutting into the hull (a ledge or step corner the gun lies across). Contacts carry the real surface normal, so a gun on a slope slides down the slope, not straight down.

The solver resolves every contact of a step together by sequential impulses with Coulomb friction and velocity-threshold restitution. Contacts are speculative -- a vertex about to reach a surface this substep is caught before it passes through -- so a fast drop cannot tunnel. Penetration left over is removed by a separate pseudo-velocity pass that moves the body without adding energy, which is what lets it come to rest instead of buzzing on the floor.
Cost. One triangle gather per tick over the swept box, a few dozen hull vertices and faces, and nothing at all once the body sleeps.
Units are the engine's: 4096 per metre, and time in 30 Hz ticks.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.FlashlightRig
member.summary: The player's flashlight as a thing held in a hand: whether it is on, and where it points.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original has no flashlight. This is the half of the remaster's that is not rendering, kept apart from the host so it can be tested: the switch, how the light comes and goes, and the aim.

The light is an LED torch's, and it does not fade like a slider being dragged, any more than the level's lamps do (). Nothing changes until the switch's latch snaps over, a beat after the press and on the click's snap (). The driver then soft-starts it in about ten milliseconds, with a small overshoot that settles over a fifth of a second. Now and then a worn contact chatters first -- a blip or two before it catches -- rolled per switch-on, so it is never the same twice and never every time. Switching off, most of the light is gone in a few milliseconds and a dim glow bleeds away over a third of a second as the driver's capacitor drains.

The curves are functions of the time since the switch, and each frame shows the curve's average over the frame rather than its value at the frame's end, as a camera's exposure would: a blip thirty milliseconds long is seen the same at thirty frames a second as at two hundred and forty, instead of being caught or missed by where the frames happen to fall.

The aim is what makes a torch read as held rather than bolted to the screen. It trails the view by a short exponential lag -- no spring, so it never overshoots and wobbles back -- and walking sways it on a figure of eight, one loop a stride, the way a light carried at the chest rides the body's gait. A turn of more than in one update is not a turn but a cut, and the aim is taken as given.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanAttachPoints
member.summary: The bones a human hangs things off, read out of the palette offsets its own handlers index.

remarks.para: The Gun class allocates five message ids (0x477E30), and Human registers a handler for each (0x45E450). Four of them answer "where is this attachment", and every one is a constant offset into a bone matrix palette:
remarks.code: 0x4600C0 first person *(view->palette + 420) position 420 = 132*3 + 24 bone 3 *(view->palette + 432) rotation 432 = 132*3 + 36 third person *(human->palette + 2928) 2928 = 132*22 + 24 bone 22 *(human->palette + 2940) 2940 = 132*22 + 36 0x4601A0 *(view->palette + 6888) 6888 = 132*52 + 24 bone 52 0x460210 *(view->palette + 7284) 7284 = 132*55 + 24 bone 55
remarks.para: The last two are what makes a reload animate. A weapon's magazine and its moving part are objects of their own, and their render handlers replace their transform with bone 52's and bone 55's on every frame, so they follow the view rig's clip instead of riding the gun body.

The arithmetic is the evidence. 132 is the palette stride the skinning path indexes with, and +24 and +36 are the world position and the world 3×3 inside a record — so every one of the four offsets factors exactly, with no remainder, into a bone index and a known field. Two of the three view-rig indices also land inside the 56-bone skeleton and outside the 33-bone one, which is an independent check that the first-person handlers really do read the view's palette and not the body's.

Each handler adds the object's own double position at +32 to the bone's position and copies the bone's rotation whole, so an attachment is the bone's world transform in the object's space, offset by the object's world position — no per-weapon offset anywhere.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanBodyInput
member.summary: What one tick of a human body machine reads.

remarks.para: Each Human class's signal handler (0x45CCF0 for a soldier, 0x454BA0 for a female soldier, 0x456CF0 for an RPG soldier) packs the machine's flag word from two sources: the input frame at Human+432, which the AI or the player writes, and a handful of bits the engine sets itself. The classes differ in which frame slots they pack and what those bits mean; this type carries the raw material and leaves the packing to each class.

The frame slots an AI writes are the ones its type resolves its logical channels to (off_54151C), so the same "take the firing pose" request lands on slot 27 for a guard and on slot 23 for Anya — and each body reads it from where its own handler looks.

member.param: The input frame written this tick — Human+432.
Bit 0x1: the current state's clip finished a cycle this tick.
Bit 0x4: the body has ground under it.
Bit 0x10000: a hit passed the class's flinch rule this tick.
Bit 0x20000: the damage that killed the body landed.
Bit 0x80: forward locomotion. The port's AI moves its bodies directly rather than through frame slot 4, so it reports the fact here.
Bit 0x40000: the run byte at Human+3328.

Frame slot 26 on its own: the AI's combat movements (RePosition, Follow, LookForTarget) hold it on every tick they run, whether or not the walker wrote forward. Held without forward, the tense run stands the body up.

Frame slot 4 on its own: the patrol walker's forward, which takes a standing body into its gait (state 3 with the run byte, the walk; 2 without it) and keeps it there -- no tense run, which is a combat movement's.
The zone the hit that raised struck — Human+744, which names the flinch clip. -1 when nothing was hit.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanBodyMachine
member.summary: A human class's body state machine — the machine every Human class builds at Human+748.

remarks.para: The engine's machine (0x4EC190, ticked by 0x4EC1E0) is the same for every class: a flag word the class's signal handler packs, the current and previous state, and one entry function per state that sets the state up and installs its per-tick. A transition makes the previous state the current one, enters the new state and runs its entry at once, so at most one transition is taken per tick. What differs between classes is the state set, their entries and per-ticks, and the table of clips at Human+824 — which is what a derived class supplies.

Two entries are the same shape in every class and live here. The flinch state plays the struck zone's limb clip — the row Human+744 names in the class's hit-zone table, +4 into it — and the scripted-animation state plays the clip the AI wrote to its class's request slot, consuming the request as it enters so only a fresh -1 can end it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanBodyStateMachine
member.summary: The player's body state machine for standing, moving, crouching, jumping and falling: states 0 to 29 of the 49 in gBodyStates (0x5385B4), each state's per-tick and what its entry does.

remarks.para: StateMachine_Update (0x4EC1E0) builds the input word and runs the state's per-tick. A per-tick that moves on calls the target's entry, and the entry only installs the target's own per-tick (0x408770 and its siblings): so a tick makes at most one transition, and a diagonal pressed from a standstill is reached a tick after the straight move that leads to it. The tests below are the per-ticks' own, in their order — lists the same targets, extracted from the code.
The states the other systems own — the uses, the ladder, the wire, the zipline, lean, the computer, hit and death — are left to them: from any of those this machine reads the body as state 0 would.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanBodyStateTable
member.summary: What clip each state of a human class's body machine plays — the table a class installs at Human+824.

remarks.para: Every Human class builds its state machine at Human+748 over its own pointer table and installs its own {animation, mode} table at Human+824; each state's entry function then calls 0x489E70(human, stateId, blend), which indexes it. The classes do not share state numbering: a soldier has 38 states, a female soldier 13 and an RPG soldier 15, and the same id means a different posture in each. A clip id is always read through the body's own table.
Animation id 0 means "this state names its own clip", not animation 0 — clip ids start at 2. Death, scripted-animation and flinch states carry it.

member.summary: How a hit becomes damage, and how damage becomes death.

remarks.para: From the human's hit handler (0x45F930), which is what the bullet resolution dispatches with the shot's Damage Factor. The whole model is four lines:

The counter runs upward. A human stores accumulated damage and a maximum, not a remaining-health value — the HUD draws 1 − total/maximum to turn it back into a bar (0x460400). Nothing subtracts, so healing has to reduce the accumulator rather than add to a pool.

remarks.para: Only a hit that already mapped to is refined; anything that named a limb keeps its zone. The test is a comparison of magnitudes, so a round arriving more from the front or back than from the side takes a directional zone and a glancing one does not.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanDamageFlash
member.summary: The red wash the screen takes when the player is hit — the four corner alphas sub_411300 decays every tick and HumanPlayer_DrawDamageFlash paints as a full-screen quad.

remarks.para: The original keeps four floats on the player (human+3532 in I.G.I. 1, the same block I.G.I. 2 names this[800..803]), one per screen corner, and does exactly two things with them. Each tick sub_411300 walks the four and subtracts 0.022222223 — one forty-fifth — from any that is non-zero, clamping at zero, so a corner set to full fades out over forty-five ticks, a second and a half at thirty hertz. And each frame the draw (I.G.I. 2's HumanPlayer_DrawDamageFlash, 0x4bb770) paints a screen-filling red quad — RGB (255, 0, 0) — whose four vertex alphas are those four floats, so the wash is brightest at the corner the damage came from and fades corner-first.

Both halves were read in I.G.I. 1. The damage handler (0x412440) draws one value from the engine random stream, maps it to [0.4, 0.8), transforms the incoming round into view space, and writes it straight into the four corners. The dominant view axis selects an edge; its opposite edge receives half the alpha. A zero direction, which explosions use, writes all four equally. This is deliberately an assignment rather than an accumulation: each hit replaces the previous flash, exactly as the executable does.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanDamageFlash.FadePerTick

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanGroundQuery
member.summary: The ground query — what a human is standing on, how far below it is, and how far it is willing to drop to stay attached.

remarks.para: From 0x462390, the second of the movement integrator's three passes. It casts downwards from a point above the feet, and if the ground it finds is within the caller's step-down budget it snaps the human onto it and raises the on-ground flag. Beyond that budget the human is declared airborne instead.
The budget is the interesting part: it is not a constant, and the caller (0x4614B0) picks it from the human's current state. See .

member.summary: Picks the step-down budget for a human's current state.
member.param: Whether the on-ground flag (bit 2) is set.
Whether the slope slide is active this tick.
member.returns: The furthest the human may drop and still be considered standing.

remarks.para: Three values, chosen in that order — sliding wins over merely being grounded: 0 in the air, 0.5 m on the ground, 2 m while sliding.

The grounded value is what stops a human falling off every kerb: walking over a 0.3 m drop keeps the feet planted rather than starting a fall. The sliding value is four times larger, which is what keeps a human glued to a steep slope instead of bouncing down it in a series of little falls — the one case where the ground is moving away underneath you fastest.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHealth
member.summary: One human's accumulated damage, and whether it has killed them.

remarks.para: The original counts damage taken rather than health remaining: a human dies when the total reaches , which is 1.0 for everybody. So a weapon's Damage Factor and a zone's multiplier are both fractions of a whole person, and the arithmetic is a plain sum with nothing scaling it by range or by what the round has already been through.
The lethal multiplier is what makes a head shot a head shot: zone 15's row carries = 100, so any weapon at all reaches 1.0 in one hit.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitTest
member.summary: Casts a round at a human and works out which zone it struck.

remarks.para: The zone rules here are the original's, out of : the torso default, the front and rear refinement by which way the round arrived, and the 614.4-unit proximity test against bone 4 that makes a head shot a head shot. Every constant is read — the body's radius and height are 's cylinder, which the original uses for human-versus- human collision.

The zone comes from a bone. sub_489C60 reads an index off the hit record and maps it through , and that index is a bone index — the bone the skinned vertex under the ray's triangle names. This resolves it by finding the bone segment closest to the round's line in the posed skeleton the soldier is already drawn with, which agrees with the original wherever the nearest bone is the one whose skin the round went through.

Divergence, and a bounded one. The gate is still 's upright collision cylinder rather than the mesh, so whether a round hits at all is decided by a capsule and only where it hit is decided by the rig. A human given no pose falls back to , which is what the port did everywhere before this.

member.param: Where the round starts, in world units.
Where it stops.
The human's feet, in world units.

member.remarks: The original (BoneDynCubeObj_TraceLinesHandler) skins every collision vertex by its one bone into the current pose, ray-triangle-traces the round against the deformed mesh, and takes the bone of the struck triangle as the hit part; sub_489C60 maps that bone to a zone, refines the trunk by direction, and promotes a front hit within 15 cm of bone 4 to the lethal head zone. This reproduces all of it, so a round scores at the exact limb it passed through rather than at the nearest bone to a fat cylinder.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitTest.NearestCrossing(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d[],OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefCollisionMesh,OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitTest.MeshCrossing@)
member.summary: The nearest face of a skinned body the segment crosses, and which way it crosses it.

remarks.para: A round that goes through a body is cast again from just inside it (0x47B750 steps 20.48 units past each contact), so the segment may START inside the body, and its first crossing is then the way out. Which side a face is cannot be read off its winding — a body mesh's is not established — so the line is reached back to outside the body's every vertex, where its first crossing must be an entry, and every crossing facing the way that one does is an entry too ('s rule, made independent of where the segment starts).
The struck triangle's bone is its first vertex's, unless the other two name a different one together — the original's rule when a face spans a joint, as 0x5655A0 reads it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitTest.NearestBone(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BonePose)
member.summary: Finds the bone whose segment passes closest to a round's line.
member.param: Where the round starts, in world units.
Its travel, origin to end.
The human's own position, which the pose is relative to.
The posed skeleton.
member.returns: The bone index, or -1 when the skeleton has no bones to consider.

remarks.para: A bone's flesh lies between itself and its children, not between itself and its parent: the skin over a thigh is weighted to the thigh bone at the hip, not to the knee below it. So each bone is measured as the set of segments running out to its children, and a leaf is measured as a point.

The weapon chain is skipped as a candidate — bones 20 to 22 run out in front of the chest and carry no skin, so a round cannot go through them and letting one win would score a chest hit as a limb. Its root is still reachable as a child segment of the spine, which is where the six models that bind anything to it put their vertices.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitZoneTable
member.summary: The per-class hit-zone tables, and what they say about how much a hit hurts.

remarks.para: 0x489C30 is what fills a human's damage state, and every derived class calls it from its constructor with a table of its own: HumanPlayer passes 0x5389F8, the soldiers 0x53F1D0. It sets the maximum health to , stores the table pointer, and then 0x489E30 copies one multiplier per zone into the human's own array — seventeen iterations, which is the third independent confirmation of the zone count.

Maximum health is 1.0, so a zone multiplier is literally the fraction of a life one point of damage factor takes. A Glock's 0.25 into a torso worth 1.0 is a quarter of a human, which is why it takes four.

The player's multipliers are script data, not compiled constants. DefineHumanPlayer (0x410070) writes humanplayer.qvm's arguments 9–25 over the player's table and 26–42 over a second one. The values compiled into the executable are a stale initialiser the script overwrites — reading them instead of the script gives the player a headshot multiplier it does not have.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitZoneTable.MaximumHealth
member.summary: Every human's maximum health.
member.remarks: Literally 1.0, set by 0x489C30 for every class alike. Humans do not differ in toughness — they differ only in their zone multipliers, and in retail those are identical too.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitZoneTable.LethalMultiplier
member.summary: The multiplier that makes a zone a one-hit kill.
member.remarks: 100.0 against a maximum of 1.0, so any weapon in the game with a damage factor above 0.01 kills instantly there. Both of the zones carrying it are head-and-neck ones — and only on the soldier table; the player's head is worth 1.0.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanHitZoneTable.Player
member.summary: The player's table, at 0x5389F8, with the multipliers the script writes.

remarks.para: The player has no headshot bonus. Its head and neck are worth 1.0, the same as its torso — so nothing one-shots the player through the head, which is the opposite of what the executable's stale initialiser (100.0 there) suggests.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanLocomotionAnimator
member.summary: Plays a human's locomotion animation and hands back the ground it covered this tick.

remarks.para: This is what replaces a walking-speed constant. A locomotion state names an animation (), the animation carries a root-motion translation track (its last key sits one frame step past the duration precisely so a looping cycle yields the whole cycle's travel), and the difference between two samples of that track is how far the body moved.

So the speed of a walk is a property of its animation. Sampling the retail set bears that out: state 1's clip travels +Y, state 4's −Y, state 7's +X and state 8's −X — forward, back, right and left — which is how 's four movement bits were named.

member.remarks: One authoring frame — , 160 — per simulation tick. That is what makes a clip's duration in frames its duration in ticks.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanLocomotionGraph
member.summary: The locomotion state machine's transition graph — which states each state can move to, in the order its per-tick function tests them.

remarks.para: Extracted from all 49 per-tick functions rather than read one at a time: every transition compiles to the same shape, mov [sm+0Ch], currentState; mov [sm+10h], N; call states[N], so the immediates written to +10h are the targets and their order in the code is the test order.
Order is priority. Almost every state begins with the same three — lose the ground, then the two death flags — and the movement states then test the run/walk toggle, the jump edge and the directions.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanLocomotionStates
member.summary: The table binding each of the 49 locomotion states to an animation.

remarks.para: Every state's entry function has the same three lines: clear the crouch flag, call 0x489E70(human, stateId, 0.15f), and install the state's per-tick function. That middle call is the whole binding — it indexes Human+824 by the state id and pulls out an { animationId, mode } pair.

The table is at 0x538870 and runs to 0x5389F8 — exactly 49 × 8 bytes, ending precisely where the 17-row tables from DefineHumanPlayerGeneral begin (). That boundary is what pins the entry size and the count.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanLocomotionStates.ForDirection(OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotionState)
member.summary: The state a set of movement flags puts a running or walking human into.
member.param: The motion flags for this tick.
member.returns: The locomotion state, or when nothing is held.

remarks.para: There are eight directions, not four. State 0's own per-tick only reaches the four cardinals, because from a standstill you can only start in one; the diagonals are reached from the movement states — state 1's per-tick (0x408C80) tests forward and right and moves to state 2. Selecting straight from the flags reaches the same state in one step.

The layout was read off the animations rather than assumed: states 1 to 8 travel +Y, +X+Y, −X+Y, −Y, +X−Y, −X−Y, +X and −X. The walk set is exactly eight higher — 9 to 16 travel the same eight ways, more slowly. Crouch states are separate: 19 is stationary and 20 to 27 move.

member.summary: Reports whether a state drives itself instead of playing a clip from the set.
member.param: The locomotion state id.
member.returns: when the state's animation id is zero.
member.remarks: The seven consecutive states 30..36, plus 46 and 47, carry animation id 0. Those are exactly the states whose entry functions name a clip by string instead — picklock_loop at 30, typecomp_loop at 32, wire_slide_1 at 40's neighbours and player_death_ at 47 — so a zero here means "this state does its own thing", not "this state is unused".

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion
member.summary: How a human moves: gravity and air control while airborne, and root motion while animating.

remarks.para: Both halves come out of the player's per-tick, 0x4109A0, and the airborne integrator it calls, 0x408460. Between them they are the whole of how a body's position changes — there is no walking-speed constant anywhere, because walking is not driven by one.

And they are added, not chosen between: the move-and-collide at 0x4614B0 opens by summing the velocity at +1636 with the root-motion delta at +1312. So a jump carries its take-off velocity and whatever the airborne animation covers.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.GravityPerTick
member.summary: Gravity, in world units per tick squared.

remarks.para: 84.741692, from the airborne integrator 0x408460 — about 18.6 m/s², which is nearly twice Earth's. That is deliberate and it is what stops the jump feeling floaty: a 1024-unit take-off reaches its apex in twelve ticks rather than twenty-three.

Correction. An earlier pass took 44.600887 for gravity because it sits in an integrator that looks like the airborne one. It is not: 0x40DBF0 is the ladder-slide state's per-tick — its entry plays the wire_slide_1 sound — and that constant, along with the 0.99 drag beside it, belongs to state 40. See .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.LadderSlideGravityPerTick
member.summary: The ladder slide's own gravity, which is not the airborne one.
member.remarks: 44.600887 — exactly 9.8 m/s². Kept named so the next reader does not mistake it for gravity again, since it is the more ordinary-looking of the two.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.LadderSlideDragPerTick
member.summary: The ladder slide's per-tick damping, applied to all three axes.
member.remarks: 0.99000001, and on the vertical it is applied after its gravity. The airborne integrator has no damping at all — a falling body simply accelerates.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.Integrate(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Advances an airborne velocity by one tick.
member.param: The current velocity, in world units per tick.
member.returns: The velocity after gravity.
member.remarks: Gravity only: no damping, and no terminal velocity. A long fall keeps accelerating, which is what 0x408460 does.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.IntegrateLadderSlide(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Advances a ladder slide's velocity by one tick.
member.param: The current velocity.
member.returns: The velocity after the slide's own gravity and damping.
member.remarks: 0x40DBF0. The order matters: its gravity is subtracted from the vertical first and the damping applied to the result, which is what gives the slide a terminal speed the ordinary fall does not have.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.AirControl(System.Single,System.Single,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f@,System.Single)
member.summary: The air control one tick adds to an airborne velocity.
member.param: Forward intent, −1, 0 or 1 — the movement slots, not an analogue axis.
Sideways intent, likewise.
The body's facing.
— argument 3 of humanplayer.qvm, which is what the integrator scales each axis by.
member.returns: The velocity change to add.
member.remarks: You can steer in mid-air after all, a little: 0x408460 reads the same four movement slots the ground states do and adds along each held one, in the body's own frame, every airborne tick. It accumulates rather than replacing, so it nudges a jump rather than turning it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.DefaultDeltaTranslationScale
member.summary: The factor an animation's delta translation is scaled by before it moves the body.
member.remarks: Argument 0 of humanplayer.qvm; 1.75 in retail. It is applied only while the human's gate at +1324 is clear — see .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotion.ApplyRootMotion(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f@,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Turns an animation's own delta translation into a world-space step.
member.param: The animation's delta translation for this tick, in the body's own frame.
The body's orientation.
The scale from .
Whether the human's +1324 gate is set, which leaves the delta unscaled.
member.returns: The step to move the body by, in world units.

remarks.para: This is how a human walks. There is no speed constant: the animation carries the translation, the scale stretches it, and the body's own basis turns it into a world direction. A walk cycle that covers less ground is a slower walk, and changing the animation changes the speed.
The scale is applied before the rotation, which matters only in that the two do not commute with the gate — a suppressed tick rotates the raw delta rather than a scaled one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanMotionState
member.summary: The bits of the locomotion state machine's flag word (Human+756) that the state functions branch on.

remarks.para: Only the bits actually tested by a state function are named here. They are read from the branches themselves rather than from any table, so each one is as certain as the transition it drives — and where a bit's meaning is inferred rather than read, the member says so.

The four movement flags are the action mask's own bits shifted up five. The binding table () gives MoveLeft 0x1, MoveRight 0x2, MoveUp 0x4 and MoveDown 0x8; here they are 0x20, 0x40, 0x80 and 0x100, in the same order.

Which is which was settled by the animations rather than by the names: state 0's per-tick (0x4087B0) sends 0x80 to state 1, 0x100 to state 4, 0x40 to state 7 and 0x20 to state 8, and sampling those states' root-motion tracks shows them travelling +Y, −Y, +X and −X — forward, backward, right and left.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanPlayerBody
member.summary: What the player's third-person body is made of — the rig Human+104 that the first-person view never shows but the death camera pulls back to reveal.

remarks.para: The player is not only the arms. Its constructor (0x410370) builds a full body BoneObject at Human+104 and plays animation 2 on it (sub_489EA0(player, 2, 0, 0.0) forwards to sub_4D61D0(Human+104, 0, 2, 0, 0.0)), exactly as a standing soldier does. Unlike a soldier the HumanPlayer task declares no Bone Heirachy — the skeleton is not a level-data decision — so the body uses skeleton 0 (anims/000.iff), and its mesh is the ordinary Model the level's HumanPlayer declares (spawn.Model), resolved by name in the chained Human handler like any other character's.

So the body is drawable with the same machinery a soldier's is — a SoldierView over the 000.iff set, standing in clip 2 — and the death state (0x40E560) plays a fall clip from the player's hit-zone table (201/202/215/112/204) on it, which are ids in this same set.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanPlayerParameters
member.summary: The 43 values DefineHumanPlayerGeneral publishes, converted into the units the engine runs in.

remarks.para: The native (0x410070) scales six of its arguments as it stores them, and the scales are what give the arguments their meaning: speeds are authored in km/h, distances in metres and durations in seconds, and all three become engine units per tick, engine units, and ticks. The conversions are read instruction by instruction — the original reuses one x87 stack slot across them, which makes them look cumulative, and they are not.
Only the arguments whose consumer has been identified are named. The rest keep their index, because naming them would be a guess; see .

remarks.para: Correction to the M8 reading, which had this landing at +3336. The constructor (0x410370) first runs sub_489C30 (which sets max health to the universal 1.0) and then overwrites Human+600 with this argument: mov edx, flt_56E204; mov [ebp+258h], edx at 0x4104C6/0x4104E1 — 0x258 is 600. So the player is worth three soldiers.
Confirmed live: a probe on the player's hit handler (0x412440) read max=3.000 off the running retail game, dying at nine 0.30-factor AK hits on Hard — the accumulator reaching exactly 3.0.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanPlayerParameters.ElectricFenceDose
member.summary: Gets argument 8 — the dose one powered electric-fence contact adds to the player's damage accumulator (retail 0.5).
member.remarks: The only reader is the HumanPlayer fence-contact handler 0x412F80, which the powered-fence callback 0x43FF70 reaches through the entity event table. It multiplies this value by the human's damage scale and adds the result straight to Human+596, bypassing the generic hit path and its difficulty scaling.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSeparation
member.summary: Human-versus-human collision — the third and simplest of the three passes the movement integrator runs.

remarks.para: From 0x462BA0. It is not a push-out: for every other human close enough, if the move would end up nearer than it started, the move is rejected outright and the human stays where it was. Bodies therefore block each other without ever being displaced, which is why two guards in a doorway jam rather than squeeze past.
The test is a cylinder, not a sphere: vertical separation is compared against and the horizontal distance against .

member.summary: The half-height of the cylinder, in engine units — 1.8 m.

member.summary: The radius of the cylinder, in engine units — 0.55 m.

member.param: Where the mover is now.
Where it wants to be.
The other human's position.
member.returns: when the move is allowed, or when the other human blocks it.
member.remarks: Only the horizontal distance decides "closer": the original recomputes the 2D length at the start position and compares it against the one at the end.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSeparation.Resolve(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d})

member.remarks: The original walks the whole list and lets each blocker overwrite the end position in turn, so one refusal is enough — later humans are tested against the already-refused position.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanShot
member.summary: Offers a round to whatever humans are in the world.
member.param: Where the round starts, in world units.
Where it stops.
The weapon's Damage Factor, which the round carries.
The firing weapon's category. It decides how a body that this round kills falls: 0x45D3C0 records a shotgun kill as a and everything else as a .

How far from , in world units, the world lets the round reach: the distance to the nearest surface the caller's own trace met, or when it met none. A human at or beyond it is behind that surface and is never struck.

Whether the guards have already been offered this round's near miss. Retail offers it once per round, over the whole range, before the march (0x47B690); a march that casts again past a surface or a body passes for every cast after its first.
The nearest crossing of a human's skin, when there is one. An exit () is the round leaving a body it went into, and is reported without damage.
member.returns: when the round meets nobody short of .

remarks.para: A delegate for the same reason is one: it lets the firing path be tested against humans placed by hand rather than only against a loaded level, and it keeps the player from having to know how the world stores its soldiers. The implementation is expected to apply the damage — the caller only needs to know where the round stopped.

The stop is passed in rather than applied by the caller afterwards because the damage happens during the call. 0x47B750 traces each pass once (sub_4CC2A0) and dispatches the gunshot handler (0x47BA54; the human's is 0x45F930) on that trace's nearest contact alone, so a wall in front of a guard takes the round and the guard is untouched. The whole segment is still the round's for hearing: the near-miss handler 0x4606F0 runs from 0x47B690 before the march, over each round's full remaining range (0x47B290), so a guard behind the wall still hears it go by.
A human on the shooter's own side is not there at all: the trace's evaluate (0x45E3E0) rejects it, and the narrow test is never run (0x4D76E6), so the round goes on to whatever is behind.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSlopeSlide
member.summary: The slide a slope imposes on a human standing on it.

remarks.para: From the free-movement integrator (0x4614B0). The ground normal gives a slope angle, and four bands decide how hard the human is pushed down it. The two steep bands set the accumulator outright — a cliff face gives you no say — while the two shallow ones add to it, so a gentle slope builds up drift over several ticks instead of snapping.

The four speeds are hard-coded constants. The two shallow ones are exactly 1.5 and 0.5 km/h through the same 37.9259 units-per-tick factor uses — and the shallowest is bit-for-bit the value general argument 3 converts to. The two steep ones are round numbers of units rather than of km/h: 948 and 1137 work out at 25.00 and 29.98 km/h.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSlopeSlide.SlopeDegrees(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Converts a ground normal to the slope angle the bands are compared against.
member.param: The ground normal; need not be unit length.
member.returns: The angle in degrees, 0 for flat ground and 90 for a vertical face.
member.remarks: The original is 90 - asin(normal.z) * 57.295776, using a helper (0x4B27D0) that clamps its argument to [-1, 1] before the asin — so a denormalised normal cannot produce a NaN. It is asin, not acos: flat ground has to come out at zero degrees, and the two differ by exactly the sign of the whole scale.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierBodyMachine
member.summary: A soldier's body machine — off_53EC10's thirty-eight states, packed by 0x45CCF0.

remarks.para: Every state is transcribed from its entry and per-tick. The per-ticks share a prefix: off the ground ( clear) leaves for , then a flinch pulse for , then a kill for the death state the posture calls for — 32 standing, 33 kneeling, 34 prone. The transitional states (rolls, kneel and prone changes) test the ground and the kill but no flinch, and prone ones flinch into the prone flinch, 31.

The combat cycle is 0 → 11 → 10 → 6: the fire pose (slot 27) racks the weapon, the rack holds until its clip ends, the trigger (slot 6) fires from ready, and the fire holds until its clip ends with the trigger released, returning to ready while the pose holds or recovering (12) to standing. Only 6, 18, 22 and 27 forward the trigger to the weapon.

I.G.I. 2's symbols name what I.G.I. 1 strips: HumanSoldier_StateSignalHandler is 0x45CCF0, state 0 is RunStateStand, and 17 is the tense forward run. I.G.I. 2 split firing into an upper-body layer; I.G.I. 1 folds it into this one machine, which is what this follows.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierClass
member.summary: What distinguishes one AI-driven Human class from another — HumanSoldier, HumanSoldierFemale, HumanSoldierRPG and HumanSoldierPistol.

remarks.para: The original registers the three as siblings under Human (0x45CAB0, 0x454970, 0x456AD0), each with its own handler set. The handlers are the same code shape over different data: the create defaults, the stand fallback, the hit-zone table, the body machine and its clip table, and the death rule. The port runs one soldier pipeline and asks the soldier's class for that data, rather than carrying three copies of the pipeline.
HumanSoldierPistol (0x459880) is a fourth sibling. No shipped level declares it, but a mod may, and the original carries it complete.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierFemaleBodyMachine
member.summary: A female soldier's body machine — off_53E400's thirteen states, packed by 0x454BA0.

remarks.para: Every per-tick first leaves for off the ground, then for on a flinch, then for on a kill — the prefix models. What follows is each per-tick's own list, in the order it tests.

The weapon has one path: drawing it (frame slot 23, 0x200000 — where the Anya/Ekk channel row puts the firing pose) raises it (6) into the aim (5); the trigger fires (3); releasing it returns to the aim while the weapon stays drawn, and lowers it (7) otherwise. The reload (4) completes on its clip and returns to the aim or to standing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierRpgBodyMachine
member.summary: An RPG soldier's body machine — off_53E6A8's fifteen states, packed by 0x456CF0.

remarks.para: Most per-ticks first leave for off the ground, then for , then for — the prefix models. The shoulder raise and lower (0x4560F0, 0x4561A0) test no flinch, and the flinch reuses the lower's per-tick.

A held trigger from standing or moving is a hip shot (4 → 3 → 0). The aim bit — frame slot 21, where the RPG channel row puts the kneel the combat arm holds — raises the launcher to the shoulder (5 → 7), and from there the trigger fires aimed (10 → 8 → 7) and a reload request reloads (9 → 7). A reload asked for away from the shoulder raises it first. The per-ticks also accept bit 0x10 as the aim, which 0x456CF0 never sets and nothing in the port raises.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates
member.summary: What clip each of a soldier's thirty-eight locomotion states plays — the table at 0x53ED10.

remarks.para: HumanSoldier's constructor (0x45CC50) builds a state machine at Human+748 over the pointer table off_53EC10 and installs this table at Human+824 — the same pair of fields the player has, with the player's own tables at 0x538870. Every state entry function then calls 0x489E70(human, stateId, 0.15f), which indexes it.
Animation id 0 means "this state names its own clip" (), and it is what the three death states carry ().

These ids are a soldier's, not the player's. The same number in the player's animation set is a different clip: playing the weapon table's ids on a soldier's rig made guards fall flat on the floor, get up and do it again. A body clip for a soldier comes from here.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.BlendSeconds
member.summary: The blend time a soldier's state entry passes, in seconds.
member.remarks: Zero, measured. Forty-four state lookups against this table in a live retail mission all passed 0.000; the player's table 0x538870 is looked up with 0.200 and sometimes 0.000. A static reading gives 0.15f for the player — whatever that literal is, it is not what reaches this argument, and a soldier blends nothing.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.FiringState
member.summary: The state a soldier fires from — and the only state it can fire from.

remarks.para: Measured first, then read. A live capture showed a fighting guard sitting here on every tick its burst counter was draining; 0x45B060, the state's per-tick, then said why. It is the only one of the four combat states that touches the weapon, and what it does is set the byte at Human+1233 to 1 whenever the float at Human+456 is non-zero — Human+456 is input-frame slot 6 (the newest frame lives at +432) and Human+1233 is what the weapon tick hands the gun. So the chain that starts with the AI writing HumanAI+15500 ends here, and a soldier holding the Fire slot up in any other state fires nothing at all.
A firing soldier is crouched. State 6 is the only one of the four that sets Human+829. It is not the AI's kneel — that is state 19.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.GrenadeThrowState
member.summary: The standing grenade-throw state, animation 58.
member.remarks: Measured in mission1-parity.log: 0x48DBF0 wrote logical channel 8 to input slot 29 while the body was in state 0; the signal builder immediately selected state 8 and animation 58. The state held after the child callback completed and returned to standing only when the clip ended.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.CloseCombatState
member.summary: The standing close-combat state, animation 70.
member.remarks: Measured in the same retail capture: 0x48DBB0 wrote logical channel 9 to input slot 30, selecting state 9 and animation 70. Like the grenade state, it owns the body until its clip ends.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.ReloadState
member.summary: The state a soldier's body is in once its burst is spent.

remarks.para: The combat cycle is 0 → 12 → 10 → 6, and 12 is the only way back to 0 — its per-tick 0x45B820 leaves for state 0 and nothing else. So a guard between bursts is here, not standing. The live capture agreed: state 12 on the tick the burst counter reached zero, and state 0 only once the target was out of sight.
Reading a spent burst as standing put a tick of the idle clip between every two bursts, and because bursts are back to back that was a visible flicker.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.RunState
member.summary: The state a soldier runs in — what the move-and-fight arm's Follow puts it in.

remarks.para: Measured by hooking "Combat - Follow" (0x48C860) in the running game: a chasing guard sits in locomotion state 17 (its diagonal twin is 18), at 4.0–5.0 m/s — about three and a half times the 1.28 m/s patrol walk. Through the table (0x53ED10) that reads as animation 48 (state 18 is 52), whose own root motion carries the run; the walk it was drawn with instead is why a chasing guard looked like it was strolling.
Which of 17/18 is straight-ahead versus diagonal is not yet pinned — both were seen at the same speed — so 17 is taken as the forward run and the distinction is recorded as open.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierStates.RunFiringState
member.summary: The tense forward-run state which forwards a held trigger to the weapon.
member.remarks: IGI 1 state 17's per-tick (0x457FC0) enters this state on signal 0x200. Its own per-tick (0x45AB00) calls the weapon-forwarding helper while slot 6 is non-zero and returns to state 17 when the trigger is released. Animation 52 is therefore run-and-fire, not a diagonal locomotion variant.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView
member.summary: The HumanView a human carries at +1260 — the first-person rig, and what the held weapon actually hangs off.

remarks.para: The original registers this as a task class of its own: HumanView, 808 bytes (0x464260). Every Human creates one in its constructor (0x45EB30) and 0x464660 initialises it with skeleton 5 and the model 005_01_1 — both literals in the executable. That is the 56-bone set, the only one of the six that is not the 33-bone body rig, and 005_01_1 is one of exactly two shipped models whose bone indices reach past 32.

It is not a camera with a gun pasted in front of it. The eye is a transform on this object (+224 position, +248 orientation, both filled by 0x464BD0 from the human's aim angles and a wall probe), and the weapon is a model on a bone of this object's skeleton. That is why the port needed a bone runtime before it could draw a knife.
Two things about the transform are worth stating because they are what make the attachment come out of the data rather than out of a tuned number:

list.item: 0x4D38C0 builds the palette with a zero root position and the object's own 3×3 as the rotation above the root, so the pose is in the object's space and is added at use — which is exactly what 0x4600C0 does.

The palette is rebuilt lazily: 0x464BD0 raises a dirty byte at +218 when it writes the orientation, and 0x465700 — called first thing in the render handler — rebuilds and clears it. reproduces that, so posing twice in a frame costs one evaluation.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.Position
member.summary: Gets the object's world position, in engine units — the original's +32, and not the eye.

remarks.para: 0x464BD0 commits it as eye + orientation · rootMotion + bob (through 0x4C6940), and the root-motion term is the one that makes a first-person weapon look right. Each weapon's standing clip carries a translation track holding that weapon's own hold offset — the knife's is (233, −837, −751), 6 cm right, 20 cm back and 18 cm down — so the rig, and everything hung off it, sits below and behind the eye rather than in the middle of the screen. The track also oscillates by 17.5 units over its cycle, which is the idle breathing.
The final term is : a 0.5 m forward probe pulls the rig back when it meets a wall, taking the arms and held weapon with it while the eye remains fixed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.RootMotion

member.remarks: 0x464BD0 composes it from the eye orientation and the weapon sway, and marks the palette dirty on every write. Setting it here does the same.

member.remarks: The camera takes this, not the human's own position (0x45FCD0 via 0x465800). It is not derived from the skeleton: 0x464BD0 computes it from the human's position (0x465820 adds the standing or crouched eye height to Human+32), applies the lean offsets, and then pushes it out of walls with a multi-ray cast. Everything else on this object, included, hangs off it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.EyeOrientation

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.WallPullbackInUnits
member.summary: Gets how far collision has pulled the first-person rig back from the eye.
member.remarks: This is HumanView+804. It is zero with 0.5 m of clear space and otherwise non-positive, so the arms and weapon move opposite the eye's sight vector without shifting the camera.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.TanX
member.summary: Gets or sets the horizontal field-of-view half-tangent — the original's +484.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.ViewModelTanX
member.summary: Gets or sets the view model's own field-of-view half-tangent — the original's +488, tan(30°).
member.remarks: Not a zoom. 0x45FCD0 copies it to HumanCamera+220, 0x482700 publishes that as dword_B81700, and 0x49F700 feeds it through the standard view-block build (sub_497D70's own algebra, inlined) while drawing a bone model with no LOD chain — which the first-person rig is. The world renders with = tan(45°), so the arms and the held weapon are drawn tan 45° / tan 30° ≈ 1.732× magnified about the screen centre — which is what holds them low in the frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.PlayWeaponAnimation(System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Single)
member.summary: Plays a weapon animation on the whole rig.
member.param: The animation id out of the weapon's own record.
Whether the clip repeats.

How long to cross-fade from the clip already playing into this one. Zero snaps; the standing and moving actions ease over the weapon table's default 0.4 s, which is what keeps a weapon from teleporting back to its idle pose after a shot, a reload, or an injection.
member.returns: The clip, or when skeleton 5's set does not define that id.
member.remarks: 0x489F20 is one line — BoneObj_Play(human->view->boneObj, bone 0, id, loop, blend) — and bone 0 is what makes it drive the whole rig. The blend argument was dropped in an earlier port; forwarding it is what restores the eased return to the stand pose. This is where a weapon's full-body animation ids go; its UpperBody* ids go to bone 1 of the human's own skeleton-0 rig (0x489ED0), which is why the two halves resolve in different sets.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.IsPosed
member.summary: Gets whether a weapon clip has ever been played on the rig, so it has a pose to draw.

remarks.para: Retail has no posture for a rig without one. 0x4D2F80 zeroes every bone node, and the palette build (0x465700 → 0x4D38C0 → 0x4D3A90 → 0x4D3F50) reads the pose through bone 0's source slot (node+128), which only 0x4D61D0 fills — so the arms are never evaluated, let alone drawn, before 0x4137E0 has played something on them. The port's bone object instead falls back to identity rotations, which is the rig's raw bind posture: a bare hand.

That is what the start of a mission would show. The player spawns empty-handed, and the first weapon arrives through an ordinary change (0x40F760 from 0x4109A0's first tick, then 0x40F230/0x40F280): eleven ticks of lowering with nothing in hand, and so no clip, before the swap plays the stand pose and raises it. Nothing ever clears bone 0 afterwards — 0x4137E0's action 0 releases bone 1 of the body, not this rig — so once posed it stays posed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.ClipEnded
member.summary: Gets whether bone 0's clip reached its end on the last tick — the node flag 0x100.

remarks.para: This one bit is the whole clock of the weapon state machine. sub_4D4B60 clears it at the top of every advance and re-raises it when the clip crosses its end, so on a looping clip it marks the wrap tick and on a one-shot clip it latches — the clock is clamped at the duration and every following advance meets the same condition again.
0x410700 reads it into the machine's flag 0x1 and 0x489F50 reads it directly as "the animation has finished", which is how a reload knows when to move the rounds.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.ClipProgress
member.summary: Gets the normalized progress of the active whole-rig weapon clip.
member.remarks: The weapon state machine consumes the medipack at the same time as the first-person syringe animation advances. Reading the clip before preserves the native update order: the health accumulator sees the frame that was visibly displayed during the previous tick, rather than jumping to the end of the injection on its first update.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanView.CrossedEvent(System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets whether the first-person rig crossed an authored event on its last tick.
member.param: The event id stored in the active weapon animation.
member.returns: when the active whole-rig clip crossed the event this tick.
member.remarks: Weapon reload sounds are authored as events in this clip rather than as fields on the weapon record. Exposing the clip's interval test here keeps callers from reaching through the view object's animation implementation just to dispatch those events.

member.summary: Gets the magazine attachment — bone 52, from 0x4601A0.
member.remarks: The native handler reads palette offset +6888. A weapon's TASKTYPE_GUNCLIP and TASKTYPE_CABARREL children hang here, and so does the dual-Uzi's TASKTYPE_GUNX2 child, which is why the two Uzis occupy opposite hands rather than sharing bone 3. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanViewSway
member.summary: The two angles the first-person rig is turned by relative to the eye, and the ease that drives them.

remarks.para: This is the weapon-change animation, and it is not a clip. Swapping weapons plays no animation of its own: 0x40F230 asks these two angles to travel to −35° and −20°, which tips the whole rig down and aside until it is off the bottom of the screen; the model is exchanged the moment they arrive; and 0x40F280 sends them back to zero. The same lowering is shared by peeking, throwing and placing.

The four fields are the original's HumanView+460 and +472 (current), +464 and +476 (target) and +468 and +480 (rate). 0x464770 sets a target and a rate, 0x4647A0 snaps both ends together, 0x4647D0 reports arrival, and 0x464BD0 steps them once a tick.

Both angles arrive together. 35° / 0.0581776 and 20° / 0.0332444 are both 10.5 ticks, so the pair is one motion rather than two — the rates were chosen to make it so, and a port that picked its own would tip the weapon crooked on the way down.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanWallProbe
member.summary: The world-collision sweep: three probe rays along the direction of travel, and the rules that turn a hit into a slide.

remarks.para: From 0x461A70, the first of the movement integrator's three passes. Each iteration casts three rays from the start position along the direction of travel, at three heights above the feet, with length |delta| + . The nearest hit that counts as a wall is resolved by projecting the destination onto the wall plane and pushing it out, and then the whole sweep runs again — up to times.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanWallSweep
member.summary: Slides a human along the walls in its way — 0x461A70, transcribed.

remarks.para: Called from the move-and-collide (0x4614B0) with the body's start and its intended destination, and it hands back the destination it could actually reach. Three rays go out at the heights names, and the loop repeats — up to ten times — because sliding off one wall can put you into another.

A wall is a surface within about 5.7° of vertical — |normal.z| < 0.1. Anything flatter is the ground query's business, not this one's. And a wall's normal has its Z flattened to zero and the remainder renormalised before it is used, so a body slides horizontally along a leaning wall and is never pushed up or down it. That one detail is most of what stops the original's player climbing scenery.

The same cast also handles the two airborne cases that are not walls: the low probe snaps a falling human to an almost perfectly upward-facing object surface, and the high probe keeps a jump below an overhang. Those use the raw hit from their respective probes; neither is a substitute for the normal wall slide.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanWallSweep.SkinInUnits
member.summary: How far a body is held off a wall it slid against, in world units.
member.remarks: 10.24 — two and a half millimetres. It is added to the ray's length so a wall is seen slightly before it is reached, and again along the normal after a slide so the body ends up clear of the surface rather than exactly on it.

remarks.para: 0x410700 rebuilds this every tick from the human's current input frame and one word of the first-person rig. The locomotion prologue 0x4105C0 maps the same slots onto the same bits, which is what makes the mapping checkable rather than assumed.
The mask 0xFFF7001C is what survives a rebuild: the ground and death bits, and everything above . Every other bit is cleared and re-derived.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanWeaponGraph
member.summary: Which states each weapon state can move to, in the order its per-tick tests them.

remarks.para: Extracted the same mechanical way as : every transition in this code compiles to the identical five-instruction shape, so the immediates written to the machine's current-state field are the targets, and their order in the function is the order the branches test them.

The shape is worth stating because it is the opposite of the locomotion machine's. This one is a star: branches thirteen ways and every other state returns to it and to almost nothing else. That is why the weapon side reads cleanly and the locomotion side needed a mechanical extraction to be trusted at all.

member.remarks: Thirteen — the length of off_538678, fixed by where the next table begins.

member.remarks: None. Arguments 5 and 6 are 0 and NULL, against the locomotion machine's two four-step double-taps — so no weapon action is a gesture.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanWeaponState
member.summary: The thirteen states of the weapon-action machine at Human+3320.

remarks.para: The second of the two machines HumanPlayer's constructor registers through 0x4EC190; the first is the 49-state locomotion machine (). Its function table is off_538678 and its prologue 0x410700, and it registers no triggers — there are no double-tap gestures on the weapon side.

Thirteen, not more. The table runs from 0x538678 to 0x5386AB and then meets the locomotion machine's trigger step arrays at 0x5386B0, exactly as the locomotion table's own boundary fixed its count. Entry 13 onward decode as {polarity, tolerance, mask} step records rather than as code addresses.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.ITitleAudio
member.summary: The host's mixer, as a title's own player sounds through it.

remarks.para: A title whose sounds are defined by its own natives brings its own table and the directories its banks are in; the host mounts those and resolves every name through that table instead of its own. What is played is still the host's voice: the title only says which definition, and where.
Nothing the title decides may depend on what comes back. Whether a sound exists is the title's own table's answer, so a game with no audio device runs exactly as one with.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.ITitleGameplay
member.summary: A title that brings its own player rather than walking the host's.

remarks.para: The host's walking rig is Project I.G.I.'s, built over that game's body, weapons and HUD. A title whose player is a different machine — I.G.I. 2's HumanPlayer, with its own states, collision and view — supplies it here, and the host steps it and looks through its eyes. A title that has none returns from the composition root and keeps the host's own player.
A fifth lookup in the composition root for the reason the other four are: the reference graph forbids putting it on , and only that root may name a title.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.MapComputerGate
member.summary: Whether a level lets its player read the map computer's map.

remarks.para: HumanPlayerInput's update (0x45DCF0) stores (__int64) of its "Mapcomputer on expression" (0x4F16E0, a floating-point evaluation) as the flag every computer page reads (0x46C0B0), and 1 when the slot holds no expression (0x4F16C0). The computer opens either way: with the flag clear 0x46BB10 gives it no mapcomputer model and opens its objectives page (mode 2 of 0x46AFB0), and neither text page offers a MAP link (0x468920, 0x468E90).
Most levels leave the slot empty. Missions 7 and 14 write 0; mission 8 waits for GenericPickup_860.isPickedUp; mission 13 reads !AreaActivate_3999.nActive.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.MouseLookSettings
member.summary: How far a mouse movement turns the view, and which way its vertical axis runs — the look half of , resolved once into the numbers the cameras actually multiply by.

remarks.para: The rate is per mouse count, not per screen pixel. The window locks the pointer with GLFW's raw motion mode (SilkGameWindow.ApplyCursorMode), so what arrives is the sensor's own counts with the desktop's pointer ballistics bypassed. One count is therefore the smallest aim adjustment the player can physically make, and is the size of that step.

Why the rate is not the one this project shipped with. The look used to be a hardcoded 0.0035 rad/count — 0.2 degrees, so about 1800 counts for a full turn, which is a 5.7 cm 360 on an 800 DPI mouse. At the engine's ninety-degree horizontal field of view () that makes the smallest possible crosshair movement roughly three pixels on a 1080p display, and there is no way to aim between them. It reads as small movements being dropped: below one count nothing happens at all, and at one count the view jumps further than the thing being aimed at is wide.

— the retail 0-to-1 slider, which round-tripped through the save file but which nothing in the look path read — now chooses the rate geometrically between and , so equal slider steps are equal ratios rather than equal absolute rates and the low end stays usable. The top of the slider is exactly the old hardcoded value, so nothing that liked the previous feel has lost it; the retail default of 0.4 lands near a 34 cm full turn at 800 DPI, which is where modern shooters sit.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.MouseLookSettings.#ctor(System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: How far a mouse movement turns the view, and which way its vertical axis runs — the look half of , resolved once into the numbers the cameras actually multiply by.

remarks.para: The rate is per mouse count, not per screen pixel. The window locks the pointer with GLFW's raw motion mode (SilkGameWindow.ApplyCursorMode), so what arrives is the sensor's own counts with the desktop's pointer ballistics bypassed. One count is therefore the smallest aim adjustment the player can physically make, and is the size of that step.

Why the rate is not the one this project shipped with. The look used to be a hardcoded 0.0035 rad/count — 0.2 degrees, so about 1800 counts for a full turn, which is a 5.7 cm 360 on an 800 DPI mouse. At the engine's ninety-degree horizontal field of view () that makes the smallest possible crosshair movement roughly three pixels on a 1080p display, and there is no way to aim between them. It reads as small movements being dropped: below one count nothing happens at all, and at one count the view jumps further than the thing being aimed at is wide.

— the retail 0-to-1 slider, which round-tripped through the save file but which nothing in the look path read — now chooses the rate geometrically between and , so equal slider steps are equal ratios rather than equal absolute rates and the low end stays usable. The top of the slider is exactly the old hardcoded value, so nothing that liked the previous feel has lost it; the retail default of 0.4 lands near a 34 cm full turn at 800 DPI, which is where modern shooters sit.

member.summary: How much to slow the look while an optic has narrowed the field of view, so aiming stays as controllable zoomed in as it is unzoomed.
member.param: The view's current horizontal half-FOV tangent.
member.returns: A multiplier in (0, 1]: 1 unzoomed, and the zoom ratio while scoped.
member.remarks: Divergence, deliberate. Retail turns the head at one rate whatever the Dragunov's scope is doing, so a single mouse count that was a fine correction unzoomed sweeps the crosshair across a whole magnified field at the tightest zoom — the aim gets harder the more you zoom in. Scaling the look by the same factor the field of view narrowed by ( over the unzoomed ) holds the on-screen crosshair speed constant across the whole zoom range, which is what a modern scope does. Unzoomed the ratio is 1 and the look is untouched, so ordinary play is unchanged.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerAction
member.summary: The actions a key can be bound to, and the bit each sets in the input mask.

remarks.para: Read from the binding table at 0x536558 — 27 records of 36 bytes, each a name and its mask, which 0x402FF0 walks. This had been unresolved: the action slots were numbered rather than named because the table that names them had not been found.

It cross-checks the one independent identification. Jump was named from locomotion state zero's per-tick, which tests it by name and moves to the state that plays jump_1; the table gives Jump the same 0x1000. Two unrelated routes to the same bit.
The movement pair is MoveUp and MoveDown rather than forward and back — named for the screen rather than the world, as the era's key-binding dialogs were.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody
member.summary: A player standing in the world: root-motion movement, gravity, and the terrain under its feet.

remarks.para: The tick order is the original's, from 0x4109A0: turn, then take the animation's delta translation and rotate it into world space (), then move and settle against the ground.

What is faithful and what is not. Gravity, the air control, the root-motion scale and rotation, the tick rate, the eye height, the ground query, the wall sweep and the slope slide are all read from the game — the tunables from , which is the script's own. What is not is the broad phase: walks a flat list of placed objects rather than the octree 0x4C6940 commits into. It finds the same surfaces. walks states 0 to 29 of the original's graph; the others belong to the systems that own them (ladder, wire, uses, death).

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.StandingEyeHeight
member.summary: How high the eye sits above the feet while standing, in world units — 1.637 m.
member.remarks: The view update (sub_464BD0) takes its eye from sub_465820: the Human's origin (+32) raised 0.69 m standing / 0.35 m crouched — the same point the AI marks the player at. Measured on mission 2's spawn: the origin stands 3877.2 units above the ground under the player (Human+1704), so the eye is 6703.4 units up, and every player round leaves from exactly there. The 1.8 m this used to be (the wall probe's top sample) put every shot 16 cm high.

member.remarks: Crouched the origin drops to 1753.8 units above the ground and the eye rides 0.35 m (1433.6) over it, measured the same way. The 1.3 m this used to be (the wall probe's crouched top sample) was half a metre high.

member.summary: Gets how much air control one tick adds, in units per tick.

remarks.para: — argument 3, 0.5 km/h, about 19 units a tick. The airborne integrator adds this along each held movement axis every tick.

It accumulates into the velocity rather than replacing it, so it is an acceleration: a jump can be leaned into over its two dozen ticks, by something over a metre, but it cannot be turned. This is why the original lets you keep pressing keys mid-air without the jump becoming steerable.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.InheritedVelocity
member.summary: Gets or sets the velocity a jump inherits from whatever the body was standing on.

remarks.para: Human+1832. The jump entry adds it to the take-off velocity on all three axes, and 0x4632D0 zeroes it in the same breath as it clears the on-ground bit — so it is consumed, not carried. Nothing else in the airborne path reads it.

It is zero for a player standing on terrain, which is why the jump behaves the same with and without it today. What fills it in is unresolved; a moving surface or an explosion's shove is the shape of thing it must be for. It is exposed so that when the writer is found there is somewhere for the value to go, rather than the term being quietly dropped.

member.summary: Gets or sets the terrain's ray cast, which the wall sweep meets as well as the placed objects.
member.remarks: 0x461A70's rays are Coll_LinesEx over the whole world, the ground included: a slope steeper than the wall limit stops a body as a wall does, rather than being climbed and then slid off.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.SlopeSlide
member.summary: Gets the slope slide the body has accumulated, in units per tick.
member.remarks: 's four bands, damped by 0.9 a tick. Zero on anything under 45°, which is most ground.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.HitShove
member.summary: Gets the shove taken from gunfire and blasts, in units per tick.

remarks.para: Its own accumulator, not the slope's. 0x4614B0 damps and adds two separate triples into the same move — the slope slide at Human+1660, and this one at Human+1648. They cannot share storage, because the slide is rewritten from scratch every tick: the bands over 60° assign it outright and anything under 45° — which is most ground a player stands on — zeroes it. A shove folded in there would be erased on the tick after it landed instead of decaying over the twenty-odd ticks 0.9 a tick buys it.
Nothing rebuilds this one; it is only ever added to, damped, and cleared outright by the events that zero all six velocity words — the landing at 0x40BE40 and the ladder mount at 0x4113E0.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.HitShoveUnitsPerTick
member.summary: The horizontal shove one connecting round gives the player, in units per tick.
member.remarks: 189.62962 — exactly 5 km/h on the 37.9259 units-per-tick-per-km/h grid. The player's hit handler (0x412440) normalises the round's travel direction and adds x·189.62962 and y·189.62962 into Human+1648/+1652, which decays by 0.9 a tick on its own.

member.remarks: State 41 leaves on the clip's end bit for state 29 (0x40DD00), whose entry (0x40BDB0) puts the last root step into the horizontal velocity and nothing into the vertical. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.FacingBasis(System.Single)
member.summary: The body's orientation about the vertical, as the root-motion rotation uses it.

remarks.para: Only yaw turns the body: the pitch is the view's alone, so looking down does not walk a player into the floor.

The columns are the view's own axes, because the root-motion multiply reads the matrix by rows. gives right as (cos, −sin, 0) and forward as (sin, cos, 0); putting those in as columns is what makes a delta of (strafe, forward, 0) come out along the axes the player is looking down. Building it the other way up transposes it, and the player then walks at right angles to the view — which is exactly the bug this comment exists to stop recurring.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.Settle(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d@,OpenIGI.Game.World.IGroundHeightField,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Puts the body on the ground, or leaves it falling.

remarks.para: The step-down budget is the human's own: nothing while airborne, and while walking, which is what lets a body follow a slope down without leaving the surface at every bump.

Terrain and objects, in one query. The original's downward ground cast (0x4CBE40) sweeps the placed models (0x4CDB20) and the terrain octree (0x4CB050) in the same call, and keeps whichever surface sits nearest the probe — terrain overwrites an object hit only when it is the closer of the two. For a downward probe that is simply the higher of the two surfaces. Without the object half a body walks through a crate, a ramp or a building floor and stands on the terrain beneath it, which is the collision bug this restores.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerBody.PlacementSearchUnits
member.summary: How far a placement search looks below its start, in world units.
member.remarks: Half a kilometre. Placement is not the runtime ground query and does not share its four-metre reach: dropping a player into a level starts from wherever the caller was looking, which may be tens of metres up. The search walks down in whole probe lengths and takes the first ground it meets, so it lands on the highest surface below the start rather than the lowest.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerInputFrame
member.summary: One tick of player input: the 40 floats HumanPlayerInput samples, records and replays.

remarks.para: The original samples this in 0x45E060 and posts it to the parent task, which keeps the newest at HumanPlayer+432 and the one before it at +272 (see ). The frame is bytes and the record/playback buffers hold 9000 of them, so a demo is capped at five minutes at 30 Hz.

Every slot is a , including the booleans — and a boolean slot holds the masked bit value rather than 1, because the original stores mask & bit. Nothing may compare a slot against 1; is the only correct test.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerInputSlot
member.summary: The slots of a , in the order 0x45E060 fills them.

remarks.para: Most slots are one bit of the engine's action bitmask (dword_BC210C), and the bit each slot carries is recorded below because the sampler writes them out of bit order. Joining that to the binding table at 0x536558 — 27 records of { char name[32]; u32 mask; }, read in — names every one of them.

The join is checked, not assumed. Three consumers agree with it independently: locomotion state 0 tests the four movement bits in an order that matches the directions measured off the animations; 0x411000 reads slots 23–31 as a nine-way weapon-category selector; and 0x40E9C0 raises the binoculars on slot 34. was named from a consumer before the table was found and the table agrees.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerInputState
member.summary: The player's pair of input frames — the newest and the one before it — and the edge tests over them.

remarks.para: HumanPlayer's handler for the input message (0x410960) is three lines: copy current to previous, copy the incoming frame to current, then run the update. The pair lives at +432 (current) and +272 (previous), and every edge-triggered action in the update is current != 0 && previous == 0.
The copy is skipped entirely while is set (HumanPlayer+592), which holds both frames still rather than clearing them — so an action already held stays held and no edge fires until input resumes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerSpawn
member.summary: Finds where a level starts its player.

remarks.para: The original does not compute a spawn: the level script places one. Every mission's objects.qvm declares a HumanPlayer task with Position, Gamma, Model and Team, and builds it with Task_New like any other object. So finding the spawn is finding that task in the loaded tree — no heuristic, and the same answer the game itself uses.
A level may place more than one; the original takes the first, and so does this.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanTask.IsDead
member.summary: Gets or sets whether this character has died — the original's Human+3317.
member.remarks: A permanent latch, not a health test: the byte is cleared only by the Human reset (0x45ECD0) and set to 1 by every death path there is (0x408447, 0x45551C, 0x45574F, 0x4573DB, 0x45A376, 0x45D51D, …). The host owns it, the same way the original's death handlers own the byte.

remarks.para: One export for every character, on the class they share. The original installs its ExportVars/UnexportVars pair on Human itself (sub_45E450 registers sub_460850/sub_4608D0), and neither HumanPlayer (sub_40FE30) nor HumanSoldier (sub_45CAB0) registers an exporter of its own — both pass sub_460BE0(), the Human type word, as their parent. So the player and every soldier are exported by the same code, and a subclass added later is exported without being asked about.

sub_460850 binds exactly these two: isDead to the byte at Human+3317 and eTeam to the int at Human+252. Both are bound writable because the original binds the raw storage — a script assigning to either changes the character.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanSoldierTask
member.summary: An AI-driven character — the original's HumanSoldier.

remarks.para: Registered at 0x45CAB0, 3408 bytes. Its two extra parameters are the ones the player's list lacks: Bone Heirachy is the skeleton id (default 1, at +3320) and Stand Animation the clip it stands in (default −1, at +3324; −1 or an id the set lacks falls back to 2). The init handler 0x456E50 reads both and hands the skeleton to the bone object, which is what settles that a model does not name its own skeleton — and the mesh comes from the ordinary Model parameter, resolved by name in the chained Human handler 0x45F890.

The siblings share this task. HumanSoldierFemale (Level 14) and HumanSoldierRPG (Level 10) are separate classes in the original, registered beside this one under Human, but every level declares them with the same six parameters and their handlers are this class's over different data. and carry that data as their .
Its hit events are 's: 0x45CAB0 links WeaponHit to 0x45D3C0 and ExplosionHit to 0x45A3D0, over Human's WeaponCollisionEvaluate (0x45E3E0).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerTaskTypes
member.summary: Registers the player task types.

remarks.para: The original registers each in its own function — Human at 0x45E450, HumanPlayer at 0x40FE30, HumanPlayerInput at 0x45DB70. What those functions declare is the class and its message handlers; the parameter lists come from the level script, exactly as the menu types' do, and every level's objects.qvm declares the same ones.

Parameter order is wire order. The lists on the task classes were transcribed from the Task_DeclareParameters calls in retail level data, and Task_New parses positionally — one wrong entry shifts every field after it and silently swallows the following child tasks. RetailPlayerTaskTests checks them against the script rather than against this file.
