member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerWeapons
member.summary: The player's weapons: the state machine at Human+3320, the gun it talks to, and the cycle it switches through.

remarks.para: Three pieces of the original meet here, in the order HumanPlayer_Update runs them: sub_411000 and sub_40F760 decide whether a weapon change is pending, the state machine (0x4EC1E0 over off_538678) decides what the human is doing, and 0x462E50 turns the byte it raised into a message to the gun.

The split matters. Nothing in the human counts rounds or reads Rounds/Minute: the firing state asks for a round on every tick the trigger is down and answers on the ticks its cooldown allows. That is what makes a weapon's cadence its own.
The bridge runs after the view has been committed for the tick, because the muzzle is the eye — call , sync the rig, then .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerWeapons.RequestedFireVariant
member.summary: Gets the fire variant was raised with.
member.remarks: Not the same as . The striking state dispatches the animation and then increments the counter — sub_4137E0(human, 8) reads Human+1256 before ++ touches it — so the first strike of a press plays FireAnimation1 and the counter is 1 by the time anything else looks at it. Reading the counter after the increment plays the second clip for the first swing, which is what this exists to stop.

remarks.para: This is Human::GunPickup at 0x45FFC0. A firearm the human does not yet own is added without selecting it, with the payload in its magazine. Medipack is the native exception: its payload is an AMMO_ID_MEDIPACK reserve count, never a magazine charge. When the weapon already exists, retail adds the payload to the matching loose-ammunition entry and never duplicates the gun.

GunPickup::Update supplies the weapon record's clip size as , so authored pickups are one full magazine. Keeping the argument explicit preserves the native message boundary and lets scripted pickups provide a different payload later.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Player.PlayerWeapons.ChargedThrowSpeed(System.Single,System.Int32)
member.summary: Turns a throw's charge into its release speed, in metres a second.
member.param: The weapon's own muzzle velocity — fifteen for both grenades.
How many ticks the button was held.
member.returns: The speed the grenade leaves at.

remarks.para: The curve is retail's, from 0x462E50's category-4 special case: t = clamp(held, 3, 60); s = pow(t·50, 0.7) + t·0.1, times a per-weapon scale — so a tenth-of-a-second tap lobs and a two-second wind-up hurls, on a 0.7 power law rather than a line.

The scale's field (record+1632) is unresolved, so the calibration is chosen and measured in play: a tap throws at of the muzzle velocity — a deliberate short toss that still clears a crate rather than a drop at the feet — and a full two-second charge at , the long hurl. The retail curve shapes everything between.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.SoldierDeath
member.summary: 0x45C440 — the soldier death state that chooses its own animation, and the turn 0x45DAA0 makes before it.

remarks.para: The soldier class has three death states, entries 32, 33 and 34 of its 38-state machine (off_53EC10), and all three carry animation id 0 in the state-to-animation table at 0x53ED10 — which is that table's "this state names its own clip" marker, the same rule the player's table uses. Two of them name a literal (0x45C5A0 plays 24, 0x45C650 plays 25); the third, this one, works the id out.

This corrects the port's own SoldierView.DeathAnimations = [24, 25]. Those two literals are real, but they belong to the two states that are not the general one, and neither is a stand-up-to-ground fall: over the retail sets, 24 starts from a crouch (skeleton 1: root Z 2219 → 1020) and 25 is a 15-tick twitch already on the floor (462 → 523). The clips this function names — 22, 23, 28, 30 and 71 — all start at the standing pelvis height and end on the ground (skeleton 1: 3877 → 524…772). Playing 24 or 25 on a soldier who was standing is exactly what left a corpse upright in mid-air.

member.summary: 0x45DAA0 — turns the dying body to the round, and reports which way it was struck.
member.param: The round's direction of travel, as the damage handler stored it at Human+3360.
The body's forward axis — column 1 of its 3×3, which is what the original reads out of Human+124, +136, +148.
Receives the new heading in radians about Z. Left untouched when the direction is a zero vector.
member.returns: when the round came at the body's front — which is also what a zero direction reports.

remarks.para: The body always ends up aligned with the round: struck from the front it turns to face the shooter (bearing + π), struck from behind it turns to face away. Either way the fall clip then plays along the round's line, which is what makes 28 and 71 read as backwards and forwards — and the retail root motion agrees, 28 travelling −6001 units in Y over skeleton 1 and 71 travelling +9933.
The zero-vector case returns without touching the heading, so a kill that carries no direction (a script's, or a fall) uses the backwards clip.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Player.WeaponWheel
member.summary: The remaster's weapon wheel: held open, the mouse steers a pointer round a ring of the weapons carried, and letting go takes the one pointed at. Not retail: neither game has one; each switches weapons by its keys alone.

remarks.para: The host owns the input: it opens the wheel on its key, steers it with the mouse while it is open, and closes it when the key is let go, handing the pick to the player (). The player takes it on its own next tick, as it would a weapon key. A title's display draws the wheel from , and .

The ring's first sector is straight up and the rest follow clockwise. The pointer is the mouse's travel since opening, held within ; inside it points at nothing new, so the wheel opens on the weapon in hand and a twitch does not move it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.AmmoTracer
member.summary: How a tracer is coloured and faded along its length, as 0x47ABD0 draws it.

remarks.para: This is what the six colour components of an are for. Each live round has a head and a tail parameter along the shot; the colour is interpolated from towards by that parameter and clamped to 0–1 per component. So a 9×19 round runs amber at the muzzle to yellow at the tip.
The brightness then falls off with distance and is floored, so a tracer never disappears entirely.

member.remarks: 2048000 units is 500 metres.

member.summary: How much of the brightness the distance fade can take.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.AmmoType
member.summary: One entry of the ammunition table, as DefineAmmoType (0x47CAD0) fills it.

remarks.para: Built exactly like the weapon table and by the same shape of code: 0x47CAB0 resets the count and walks LOCAL:ammo, and AmmoType_Open (0x47CA40) runs <dir>/ammo.qsc for each sub-directory. Fourteen 360-byte records at 0x5BE3E0. Unlike the weapon call this one is a fixed fifteen arguments — no task classes are named, so there is no tail.
Two lookups exist: by (0x47CD40) and by (0x47CD70). The second is the join a weapon uses — the gun's init at 0x4789C0 takes its weapon record's calibre and caches the ammo record beside it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Ballistics.BallisticProfile
member.summary: How one weapon's rounds fly when the tactical-ballistics option (g_ballistics) is on.

remarks.para: This is remaster behaviour, not the original's. Retail resolves every round as a hit-scan ray in the tick it is fired (); this profile is what turns the same weapon record into a projectile that takes time to arrive, drops under gravity and slows in air. Nothing here is read when the option is off.

Every number starts from data the retail tables already carry and the bullet never used: (metres per second, which GunShotBallistics notes is "carried for the HUD and the AI, not for the bullet"), (whose original consumer was never found), and the calibre's own diameter. That is what makes the flight per-gun rather than per-setting: a 7.62 round is heavy for its face and carries; a shotgun pellet is all face and falls off.

The table lies in three places, and each has a named correction here. Read against the real roster (the port's own dump of a retail installation): the three rocket carriers are category Gun with a 5 m/s muzzle velocity — their real projectile is the missile task — so keeps them hit-scan. The Dragunov says 6000 m/s, a hit-scan era convenience no rifle reaches, so caps it. And most ammunition masses are placeholders (9×19 at 3.5 g, the 12.7 at 2 g — only the 7.62's 12 g is a measurement), so the drag mass is floored at a lead slug of the calibre's own diameter rather than trusted raw; see .

member.param: The muzzle speed, in world units per second.
The quadratic drag constant k in reciprocal world units, so the deceleration in units/s² is k · v² with v in units/s.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Ballistics.BallisticProfile.MassForDragInGrams(System.Int32,System.Single)
member.summary: The mass the drag divides by, in grams.
member.param: The calibre.
What the ammunition table says one round weighs.
member.returns: The table's mass, floored at a lead slug of the calibre's own diameter.
member.remarks: The table's masses are mostly placeholders — 3.5 g for every pistol calibre, 2 g for the 12.7 — and dividing a .50's face by two grams would strip its speed in a hundred metres. No bullet is lighter than lead of its own calibre: the floor is a lead sphere of the flying diameter, doubled for everything but shot because a bullet is elongated where a pellet really is a sphere. The floor only ever raises a placeholder — the one measured mass in the table, the 7.62's 12 g, sits above its own floor and is used as shipped.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Ballistics.BallisticRound
member.summary: One round in flight under the tactical-ballistics option, and its visible trail.

remarks.para: A mutable class rather than a struct because pools and reworks these in place every tick, the way Physics.RagdollBody is owned by its world. Positions are double precision for the same reason every world-space thing here is: a level sits tens of kilometres from the origin, where a float resolves to millimetres.

The trail is part of the round rather than the renderer so that what is drawn is what was simulated — the renderer reads positions, it does not integrate anything. A dead round lingers for so its trail fades out instead of vanishing on the impact frame.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Ballistics.BallisticSimulation
member.summary: The rounds in flight under the tactical-ballistics option, stepped once per game tick.

remarks.para: This whole class is a deliberate divergence, and it is opt-in. Retail's round is hit-scan, resolved entirely in the tick it is fired (); with g_ballistics on, a round instead flies across ticks at its weapon's real muzzle velocity, drops under the engine's own 9.8 m/s² (the same constant the ragdoll falls at — ) and slows by its profile's quadratic drag. With the variable off this class is never constructed and the retail path runs untouched.

Velocity is integrated in substeps for the drag's sake, but each tick casts one segment over the whole tick's chord — the arc a round bends inside 33 ms is millimetres, and one cast keeps a full magazine's worth of rounds no dearer than the hit-scan it replaces. The cast uses the same two delegates the hit-scan path does, in the same both-then-nearer order, so a guard in front of a wall still takes the round and the wall stays clean. Like that path, a surface or body the round's power beats is passed (), an exit crossing passes and arms the stop-at-the-next-entry latch, and anything else stops the round.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Ballistics.BallisticSimulation.MaximumLiveRounds

member.remarks: Not retail's fifteen () — this mode is already non-retail, and a shotgun spawning one round per pellet would exhaust fifteen in two trigger pulls. A sixty-fifth is dropped the way retail drops its sixteenth.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.ExplosionDamage
member.summary: How an explosion's damage falls off with distance.

remarks.para: From 0x416C90, which the human's explosion handler (0x45F9D0) calls, and which is the whole falloff model:
remarks.code: d = |explosion - target| - bodyRadius - radius; if (d < 0) return damageFactor; // inside the blast if (d >= falloff) return 0; // past it return (falloff - d) * damageFactor / falloff; // linear between
remarks.para: An explosion always applies to hit zone 13 — the human's handler hardcodes it. So a blast never lands a headshot and never hits a limb; every target takes the same zone multiplier however it is standing. That also confirms the per-zone array layout independently: zone 13's accumulator is at +712 and its multiplier at +716, which is exactly 608 + 8 × 13.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.ExplosionDamage.Dose(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: How much damage an explosion delivers to a target.
member.param: Centre-to-centre distance from the blast to the target.
The target's own radius, already scaled by .
The blast radius, inside which damage is undiminished.
How far past the radius the damage takes to reach zero.
The explosion's damage factor.
member.returns: The dose, which the caller multiplies by the zone multiplier.

remarks.para: A falloff of zero makes this binary. The retail grenade ships with exactly that, so a grenade does its full damage anywhere inside five metres and nothing at all a millimetre outside — there is no gradient in the shipped game. The order of the two tests is what saves the division: everything at or past the falloff returns before the divide, so a zero falloff can never divide by zero.
Distance is measured to the target's origin and the radii are subtracted, so a target standing on the blast takes full damage regardless of the radius.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.Flashbang
member.summary: What a flashbang does, from 0x47E9A0 and the player's handler for it (0x413090).

remarks.para: This class models the player's whiteout only. IGI1 also broadcasts a separate AIEVENT_FLASHBANG (type 19) to nearby guards; that event drives their scripted panic/stun response, but it does not write the player's whiteout fields and is delivered by the AI renderer. Keeping the two handlers separate prevents a distant world smoke task from flashing the player.
The effect is two independent tests against two different distances, and both can apply at once.
The player callback is distance-only. In particular, 0x00413090 compares the event position with the player's eye and does not perform a world line-of-sight trace.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GrenadePhysics
member.summary: The grenade's physical constants, as the retail data and code carry them.

remarks.para: The numbers come from two reads. physicsobj/physicsobj.qvm's DefinePhysicsObjType rows for TASKTYPE_GRENADE (dumped through this port's own interpreter) give the mass (0.3 kg), the half-extents (0.1 × 0.1 × 0.15 m), a per-surface elasticity of 0.3 on every one of the five collision groups, and the tail pair every entry carries. The same rows' trailing arguments are the grenade class's own: the explode time, 4.0 seconds, and the explosion type — 0 for the frag model 135_01_1, 1 for the flashbang 137_01_1. The task init (0x477040) turns the seconds into ticks at thirty and counts down in the per-tick (0x476AC0), detonating at zero.

The throw itself carries no constant of its own: the round's velocity is the aim direction times the weapon record's Muzzle Velocity — fifteen metres a second for both shipped grenades — exactly as every projectile spawn receives it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GrenadePhysics.TumbleRadiansPerTick

member.summary: What fraction of the surface-tangential speed survives a bounce.
member.remarks: A chosen number, not a read one. The groups carry two further unit values whose use in the solver is unread; a modest tangential loss is what keeps a grenade from skating like a puck without pretending to be the original's friction model.

member.summary: Returns the native placement orientation for a mine or held grenade.

remarks.para: The retail fire bridge at 0x462E50 passes the current weapon orientation in the placement message. The mine callback at 0x4754C0 copies that message's ten orientation words into task +0x70; it does not derive a new pose from the contact normal.

The native basis helper at 0x414A60 stores the supplied forward direction in matrix column two. The mine model's authored contact face is the opposite local axis, so the placed task supplies the reversed weapon direction to that helper. This is why a downward placement ray produces an upright mine instead of an upside-down one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GrenadeSimulation
member.summary: Flies every live grenade, bounces it off the world, and detonates it when its fuse runs out.

remarks.para: The compact port of the grenade's physics-object flight: gravity at the engine's own object 9.8 m/s², one world cast per tick along the tick's travel, a reflected bounce at when it meets a surface, and rest once it is slow on something floor-like. The original's full rigid-body solver (tumbling, the per-surface groups) is deliberately not reproduced — what is kept is every number that decides where a grenade ends up and when it goes off, which is what the game is played against.
Detonations land in for the owner to apply — damage through , the flash through , and whatever is drawn and heard. The simulation itself hurts nobody.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics
member.summary: How a round travels and what stops it, from GunShot's per-tick (0x47B750).

remarks.para: A round is hit-scan and resolved entirely in the tick it is fired. There is no projectile flying over several ticks: the update loops while (remainingRange > 0), casting a ray from the current position to the end of the remaining range, and each surface it meets either stops it, is penetrated, or deflects it. What persists to later ticks is only the visible tracer and the decals.
That is why plays no part in any of this — nothing here reads it. It is carried for the HUD and the AI, not for the bullet.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.MaximumLiveShots
member.summary: How many rounds may be in flight at once.
member.remarks: Fifteen. A sixteenth is silently dropped — 0x47B190 takes the early exit that only bumps the total-fired counter, so the round is counted, consumes its ammunition, and never exists. With the fastest weapon in the game emptying a magazine in 87 ticks this is not usually reachable, but a shotgun firing several projectiles per round can get close.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.MaximumRecordedImpacts
member.summary: How many impacts one round may record for decals.
member.remarks: Ten. Impacts past that are resolved but leave no mark.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.UnitsPerMetre
member.summary: World units in a metre, used to turn the effective range into a distance.
member.remarks: 0x47B190 stores EffectiveRange * 4096.0 as the round's starting range, so the parameter really is in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.PenetrationStepOffUnits
member.summary: How far past a penetrated surface the next ray starts.
member.remarks: 20.48 units — five millimetres. Without it the next cast would hit the same face again and the loop would not terminate.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.EqualPenetrationChance

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.TracerInterval
member.summary: What a gun's tracer counter is set to: the passes that go undrawn before the next one draws.
member.remarks: Ten (0x47B560, 0x47C1F6), counted per gun and per pass of the march, so a plain burst draws one pass in eleven. A deflected round, or a pass a surface's bite let through, draws regardless.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.TracerLifetimeTicks

member.summary: Turns a weapon's effective range into the distance a round may travel.

member.returns: The range in world units.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.Penetrates(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Decides whether a round gets through what it hit.
member.param: The weapon's .
What the surface or target resists with.
A uniform sample on 0–1, drawn only when the two are equal.
member.returns: when the round carries on.

remarks.para: The rule is not a threshold, and it is not monotonic. A margin of one or more always gets through; a margin of exactly zero gets through six times in ten; and anything else stops — including a margin strictly between zero and one, which is a narrower gap than the equal case that succeeds. That looks like an oversight in the original, but it is what it does, so it is what this does.
The original also requires the ray to have named an object before it will let a round through, so a hit on nothing in particular stops it whatever the margin.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.DeflectionChance(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The chance a round glances off rather than biting.
member.param: The surface's own limit, in degrees. Zero means the surface never deflects anything.
The angle between the reversed travel direction and the surface normal, as 0x4B2B30 returns it.
member.returns: The probability, which the caller compares a uniform sample against.

remarks.para: The expression is (limit − (π/2 − incidence)) / limit with the limit in radians. A round arriving square on the surface has an incidence of zero, giving a large negative number and no chance of deflecting; a round arriving almost parallel has an incidence near π/2, giving a value near one. So it is a grazing-angle ricochet, and the surface's limit sets how oblique the approach has to be.
The result is deliberately not clamped — the caller only ever compares it against a uniform sample on 0–1, for which any negative value is as good as zero.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunShotBallistics.CanDeflect(System.Boolean)

member.summary: What a round does at a surface it enters: first the graze, then the bite.
member.param: The weapon's .
The struck face's game material.
Whether the trace named the object it struck.
The arrival angle off the normal, as gives it.
Whether this round has glanced before.
Draws a uniform sample on 0–1, called only where the original draws one.
member.returns: Whether the round stops, goes through, or glances off.

remarks.para: One rule for every round, because 0x47B750 is one routine for every round: the player's, a guard's and a mounted gun's alike. A glance is tried while the round may still deflect, against the surface's own ricochet limit; failing that, the round goes through only when the trace named an object and lets it.

A guard firing from behind a fence is the case that needs it. The water tower's railing on mission 1 is Fence (resistance 0) and a sniper's Dragunov carries power 3, so the probe watched every one of the tower guard's rounds strike that railing 4.3 m out and carry on to the player.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunTiming
member.summary: The gun's clock: how Rounds/Minute becomes a tick count, and the counters that hang off it.

remarks.para: Everything here comes out of one expression the original writes five times over — three times in Gun_Fire (0x478BA0) and twice in the per-tick (0x478640):

It is a double divide and multiply, truncated toward zero by an __int64 cast, in that order. Doing the arithmetic in single precision, or rounding instead of truncating, changes the cadence of most of the roster: at 400 rounds a minute the exact value is 4.5 ticks and the gun uses 4.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.HeldGun
member.summary: A weapon in someone's hands: the roster record, the magazine, and the clock between rounds.

remarks.para: This is the original's 432-byte Gun task, reduced to the fields the firing path touches. Its two entry points are the per-tick 0x478640 and the message the human sends every update, which the class binds to 0x479780 — not to Gun_Fire directly. 0x479780 calls Gun_Fire (0x478BA0) and then, only if a round went off, samples the view recoil.

The human never decides when a round goes off. The weapon state machine raises a byte every tick the trigger is down and this class answers on the ticks its own cooldown allows. Rate of fire, burst length and the magazine all live here.

So a weapon with no record — the knife, whose Calibre ID is -1 — never runs out and never spends anything.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.HeldGun.Fire(System.Boolean,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom,System.Nullable{System.Single})
member.summary: Sends the gun one tick's trigger message.
member.param: Whether the human asked for a round this tick.
The muzzle, in engine units.
The barrel's direction — the view's +Y axis, already unit length.
The view's +X axis, which the cone is opened across.
The view's +Z axis, the cone's other axis.
The stream every sample is drawn from, in order.
Optional charged-throw speed; otherwise the weapon speed is used.
member.returns: What happened.

remarks.para: This is 0x479780 around 0x478BA0, in the original's order: the gate, then one cone sample per , then the round's bookkeeping, then — only when a round actually went off — the recoil.

The draw order is part of the behaviour. A projectile takes four draws (three multiplied into the radius, one for the bearing) and the recoil takes an unbounded even number, because it rejection-samples a unit disc two draws at a time. Reproducing a shot means reproducing that.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.HeldGun.SampleRecoil(OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponType,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom)
member.summary: Samples one round's view kick.
member.param: The weapon fired.
The stream, which this consumes an unbounded even number of draws from.
member.returns: The pitch and yaw kick, in radians.

remarks.para: 0x479780's second half. The random part is drawn from a disc, by rejecting pairs outside the unit circle, so the two components are correlated: a shot that kicks hard upward cannot also kick hard sideways. Two independent axis samples would be a squarer, and wrong, distribution.
The fixed part is added on top, so a weapon with no random terms — the Glock — kicks by exactly its every time.

member.remarks: The speed keeps of itself, after more of fall, and the round moves by it. The first build adds the x speed to the position straight from the register (fst, not fstp: the product before it is stored) and the other two as stored; at the sequel's 24 bits the two are the same.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.MissileConfig
member.summary: The per-missile flight parameters the retail Missile task reads from its config struct (cfg = *(task+436)+724, consumed by the integrator at 0x00428D00 and the smoke emitter at 0x00428630).

remarks.para: A retail launcher does not carry these in its DefineWeaponType row — that call only hands the missile projectile its model name (). The flight behaviour lives in the task config, keyed by . The clean-room engine has no task-config parser, so the values here are transcribed from the reversed integrator and grouped into the per-type presets the retail rockets fly with.

The LAW 80 / RPG-18 is a rocket: 0x00428910 clears its steering inputs so it holds the launch facing, and 0x00428D00 ramps a throttle from launch to full and drives the body forward under thrust with no grenade gravity.

member.remarks: A LAW/RPG holds its line — thrust dominates and the trail reads as flat over any range the player fires it at, so gravity stays off. A dropped is the one body that falls.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.MissileConfig.MotorBurnTicks
member.summary: Gets how long, in ticks, the rocket motor burns — thrusting and laying smoke.
member.remarks: a1+2148 is the burn countdown: 0x0042939A subtracts cfg+292 each tick, and while it is non-zero the missile thrusts and — with cfg+280 set — smokes (the gate at 0x00428445). Once it reaches zero the body coasts and the integrator adds its idle wobble. Three seconds of burn covers any range the player fires a LAW over.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.StatusScreenLayout
member.summary: Where the in-game HUD puts everything, as StatusScreen and the weapon's own HUD handler compute it.

remarks.para: The HUD is a task of its own — StatusScreen, 1264 bytes, registered at 0x486900 with the resource prefix STATUSSCREEN: bound to LOCAL:screens/game/status/. Its render (0x486F30) draws its children and then sends one message to the weapon in hand, which the Gun class answers with 0x479D20. So every part of the HUD that depends on what you are carrying is drawn by the weapon, not by the screen.

Everything is anchored as a fraction of the current resolution, so the HUD follows the window rather than being authored at 640×480 and centred the way the menus are. Sprite and font dimensions stay in authored pixels; the renderer's UI scale magnifies those dimensions for modern displays while these original fractional anchors keep every element in the correct part of any aspect ratio.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponAnimationTable
member.summary: Which of a weapon's thirteen animations each action plays.

remarks.para: Transcribed from 0x4137E0, which is the whole of the weapon animation dispatch: a switch on the action picks one full-body and one upper-body clip out of the weapon record, then hands them to 0x489F20 and 0x489ED0.

The table is where the upper-body split becomes concrete, and the split is between two skeletons rather than two tracks on one. 0x489F20 plays the full-body id on bone 0 of the first-person view rig — human->view->boneObj, which 0x464660 built from skeleton 5 — and 0x489ED0 plays the upper-body id on bone 1 of the human's own skeleton-0 rig, with orientation type 5 over the root orientation at Human+1616.

So a weapon's full-body ids are ids in 005.iff and its UpperBody* ids are ids in 000.iff. An earlier note here read the full-body ids as simply not resolving in the player's set; they resolve, in the other set. RetailHumanViewTests checks every full-body id of every one of the 24 weapons against 005.iff.
The blend is 0.4 seconds for the standing and moving actions and immediate for firing, reloading and — a shot has to look instant.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponAnimationTable.TimedFireStart(System.Single)
member.summary: How much of a clip skips, given one uniform sample.
member.param: A draw on 0–1 from the engine's own stream.
member.returns: The clip time to start at, in the clip's own units.

remarks.para: The original computes flt_A54658 * (rand01() * 0.175) * 30.0 and hands it to sub_4D65B0, which writes it to the clip's +44. +44 is the clock — sub_4D4B60 does clip[+44] += clip[+40] and compares +44 against the duration — and the rate is +40, which a different function sets. So a shot's animation starts part-way in rather than playing at a random speed. An earlier note here had it the other way round.
flt_A54658 is 4800 / 30 = 160, set once by sub_4D2D30(30.0). The same constant converts a blend from seconds to ticks, which is the cross-check on its value.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponConfigRegistry
member.summary: The weapon roster as weapons/weaponconfig.qvm declares it and the runtime consumes it.

remarks.para: The script is an ordinary task tree, so loading it is just running it against the task system, and it describes all twenty-four weapons in the same field order as the live path. Mission startup applies each record to the matching entry before gameplay begins.

It is not dead weight, though. A WeaponConfig instance is 1800 bytes, which is exactly the 32-byte task header plus the 1768-byte runtime record, and its extra fiftieth parameter — Is weapon selectable when empty — lands at the very offset the live loader hardcodes to 1. So this is the same struct, declared a field further on: an intended replacement for DefineWeaponType that shipped without ever being wired up. That makes it a genuine cross-check on the live reader and the authoritative source for shared runtime tuning, which is what the parity tests verify.

The shot's line, its end less its start; a stab's unit direction.

The sending game's own context, whole: both games fill the same six fields (the intersection, the damage, the shot vector, the shooter, the weapon and the ammunition), in their own types. A target of the same game reads it; one of another game reads the fields above.

The tally of the player who fired it, which a soldier of either game counts its hit and its kill on; for a round no player fired. Not retail: the display's hit and kill marks.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponTaskParameters
member.summary: How many arguments each projectile and weapon task class reads from a DefineWeaponType call, and what it turns them into.

remarks.para: This is why the call is not a fixed-length one. 0x413F90 reads argument 47 as the projectile task type, then hands the call to that class's parameter reader with a cursor starting at 48; the reader consumes as many arguments as it wants and writes the cursor back. The weapon task type is read at the returned cursor, and its own reader then consumes the rest. Retail argument counts are 49, 50, 52 and 53 — a reader that assumed 49 would mis-read six of the twenty-four weapons.
Each entry below is transcribed from the class's reader. The two that matter beyond arity:

item.description: The zoom readers (0x4732F0 for the MP5SD and the Dragunov, 0x470CE0 for the binoculars) take a field of view in whole degrees and store its half-angle tangent. The halving is integer division — cdq; sub eax, edx; sar eax, 1, truncating toward zero — so the Dragunov's 5° becomes tan(2°), not tan(2.5°).
The binoculars store their three angles out of order: the first two land in slots 1 and 2 and the third in slot 0, so the script's 5, 90, 70 reads as minimum, maximum, default.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponTaskParameters.DegreesToRadians
member.summary: The degrees-to-radians factor the zoom readers use, as the single-precision constant at 0x53367C.
member.remarks: Stored in the executable as a (0x3C8EFA35), not a double, so it is a little short of the exact value. The multiply and the tangent then happen on the x87 stack at extended precision before the result is rounded back to a .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponTypeRegistry
member.summary: The runtime weapon table: the roster the firing, HUD and AI code actually read.

remarks.para: This is not weaponconfig.qsc. 0x413B70 resets the weapon count and walks LOCAL:weapons with File_WalkTree, and WeaponType_Open (0x413A90) runs <dir>/weapon.qsc for every sub-directory it finds. Each of those scripts is a single DefineWeaponType call. The parallel declaration loads afterwards and describes the same twenty-four weapons in the same field order, but its task ctor only zeroes its own storage — nothing at runtime reads it.

Two consequences worth stating. The call is variable length because the projectile and weapon task classes read their own parameters from its tail (). And the WEAPON_ID_* symbols get their values here, as each weapon is read, which is what the pattern registration was waiting for.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.BakedLightmaps
member.summary: A path-traced bake of a level's object lightmaps, composited into ready-to-upload pages and keyed the way the renderer samples them: by lightmap entry name, then page index.

remarks.para: This is the hand-off between the bake and the frame. The expensive tracing () and the compositing here are pure CPU and run on a worker; the renderer takes the finished pages and swaps their pixels in where the shipped .olm ones would be sampled. Nothing here touches the graphics API, which is why the whole thing can be built off the render thread and cached to disk.

Several of a model's draw records can name one page, each covering a different island of it, so a page accumulates across every target that shares it. Uncovered texels stay black; they are atlas space no surface maps to, and the page clamps rather than repeats, so the black does not reach a sampled texel.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.BakedLightmaps.Page
member.summary: One page's dimensions and its row-major, width-fastest LINEAR radiance, an uncovered texel zero.
member.remarks: The radiance is kept linear and unclamped -- the high dynamic range the bake produced -- so the renderer can encode it either as an LDR page (clamped to one) or as an HDR page (divided by a headroom then sRGB-encoded) depending on the mode, without the bake having to know which.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.BulletMarks
member.summary: The marks rounds and blasts have left on the world, and the rules for adding one.

remarks.para: The bullet does not choose its mark, and neither does the material alone. The shot resolution records an impact and 0x4083C0 dispatches it to the material's GunShotEffect handler (0x438440). That handler picks the texture and size, then asks the struck object to take the decal (0x438508). The decal only exists if that object's type answers the decal message.

Only two base classes register a handler for it, both in 0x47CF70: RigidDynCubeObj (0x47D380), which every placed collision object descends from, and SplineObjSegment. Several descendants register a null handler to refuse it — see . Terrain has no object at all: the trace's terrain pass zeroes the struck task (0x4CC2A0), so the ground is never marked.

Everything else is 0x47D380's own bookkeeping, reproduced by . Marks are kept per object, at most on one. At most objects carry marks at once. A mark landing on top of an existing one is skipped. A mark overhanging an edge is dropped by 0x47D920's four-corner test.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.BulletMarks.Poses
member.summary: Gets or sets where placements are when a mark is made.
member.remarks: This must be the pose the round struck -- the collision index's -- so that the mark's place in the object's frame is the face it hit. Without it marks stay where they were made.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.BulletMarks.MaximumSurfaces
member.summary: How many objects may carry marks at once.
member.remarks: 0x47D03A sizes the per-object decal pool at four. When a fifth object is struck, 0x47D3D0 frees the pool entry whose last mark is oldest, and every mark on it goes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.BulletMarks.MarksPerSurface
member.summary: How many marks one object keeps before its oldest is overwritten.
member.remarks: The ring in 0x47D806 holds 200 and wraps.

member.remarks: 0x47D661: the dot product of the two normals against 0.9.

remarks.para: A collision face's fourth field selects a row of its own mesh's TAMC table. The collision resolver translates that local selector through TAMC's global-material field before it creates the , so the hit's Material is already the shared game-material row that owns the decal effect.

The local selector must not be used as a shared material ID here: the same selector value can mean different global materials in different meshes. The effect's texture and size still come from the resolved material row, including the material's no-mark guard.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CampaignLimitedMissionCatalogue
member.summary: A title's missions cut to the opening stretch of its campaign: the first so many along the progression, and nothing else.

remarks.para: For a build that offers only part of the game -- the browser build offers the first six missions. The cut is made here, at the one table every route into a mission already consults, rather than at each route: the campaign list, the retail menu's fills, a save slot, -mission and a finished mission's successor all look their mission up in the catalogue, so a mission this does not know is one none of them can reach, and none of them has to know there is a limit.

Counted along , the order the game is played in, not by id and not in scan order. A mission the campaign never reaches -- a mod's extra level -- is outside the opening stretch by definition, so it is not offered either.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CarDynamics
member.summary: The retail CAR force model, run once per 30 Hz physics tick.

remarks.para: Retail drives a car entirely through forces on a rigid body. Car::Tick (0x42ECA0) smooths the two controls, runs the suspension sweep (0x42EF00) and hands the body to the shared step 0x4FC0E0(body, 44.600887, 0.97, 0.9). That first constant is gravity: at 4096 units to the metre and 30 ticks to the second, 44.600887 units per tick squared is 9.80 m/s². The other two are the per-tick retention applied to linear and angular velocity.

Per contacting wheel, 0x430D10 applies a drive force of EngineForce * throttle * g / drivenWheelCount less the body speed, directed along the body forward axis rotated by that wheel's steering angle (MaximumSteerDegrees * pi/180 * steering), then the tyre model 0x430960 opposes the contact point's slip: the slip direction is taken into wheel space, scaled by the lateral and longitudinal friction of the wheel body, taken back out, and applied with a magnitude of slip * mass * 0.1 while the tyre grips, dropping to normalLoad * 0.24 once the slip passes 4 * normalLoad / mass. Steering is therefore emergent -- the front wheels push the nose round and the rear tyres resist the resulting sideslip -- rather than a yaw rate written straight into the transform.

This is the planar reduction of that model: the cutscene cars run on level ground, so the suspension's only contribution is the normal load it carries, which at rest is exactly mass * g shared between the contacting wheels. Roll and pitch, and the vertical degree of freedom, stay with the authored transform.

member.summary: Rides the springs, returning how far the body rises this tick.
member.remarks: The wheel sweep (0x42EF00) casts from wheelZ + travel + 4096 down to wheelZ - 2048 and reads the compression as (travel + 4096) - distance -- which is how far the wheel's origin sits UNDER the surface. It pushes the body up by compression / travel * stiffness * mass * g, so at rest every wheel sits a quarter of its travel into its spring for a stiffness of 0.5. A wheel driven past the full travel keeps it and its force grows by another 1 + depth / 4096, and the body is lifted clear of the deepest of them. Gravity is the whole weight at the origin. Without this the body holds whatever height it was handed: no settle when it is boarded, and no ride over the ground it crosses.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CinematicActor.IsMovingPlatform(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Whether a ground contact with this task can parent a staged Human.
member.remarks: Retail Human_GroundCollision (IGI.EXE 0x462390) tests the contacted task's moving-platform flag (task+0x64) before calling Human_SetParent (0x463310): a non-platform contact detaches through 0x463550 instead, and an already-parented Human keeps its slot without recapture. The flag is type-derived once at task init (init zeroes it, then TaskType_IsDerivedFrom at 0x401CF0 sets it), so it is immutable per task family. Boundaries confirmed in both Ghidra and r2; the igi.pdb (IGI1) publics independently confirm neighboring owners (Human_DamageApply at 0x412440, Human_RunUpdate, Human_ViewCam). Port mapping, forced by the authored Level 1 landing (land_ground_2 at CutScene_1201.nTick > 0.25*GAME_FREQUENCY onto the passing wagon while the insertion heli hovers 6 m above it): Train/Car/Elevator are platforms; Heli/Plane airframes never capture through ground contact (their riders are direct QVM children, which bypass the ground pass entirely).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CoincidentSkins
member.summary: Finds a model's coincident skins: triangles lying in the same plane as another of the model's, overlapping it and facing the other way -- the two faces of a sheet modelled with no thickness, an awning's top and its underside.

remarks.para: The original culls back faces, so of such a pair it only ever draws the face turned to the camera. A mesh drawn two-sided -- a sector, which encloses the viewer and so is never culled whole -- draws both at the same depth, and which wins a pixel then turns on rounding: the sheet flickers between its two faces as the camera moves, and under a jittered projection every frame while it stands still. Drawn culled, the skins of a pair are exactly one face from any side, as the original's are.
Each subset's skins are moved to the end of its index range and counted (), so a renderer drawing the subset two-sided can draw that tail culled. The rest of the subset keeps its order.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CollisionStaticGrid
member.summary: The broad phase: a sparse 2D grid over the entries' build-time bounding spheres.

remarks.para: The flat scan this replaces touched every placed object's sphere for every ray — the AI's lines of sight, every soldier's ground snap, every dropped gun's contact probe, all against the whole level. A ray now touches the entries of the cells it passes, which for the vertical ground probe is one cell.

Two-dimensional on purpose: a level is kilometres across and metres tall, so a Z axis would cut nothing while tripling the buckets. An entry whose sphere spans an unreasonable number of cells goes to the list and is tested every query instead of being written into hundreds of buckets.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ConditionalContainerTask
member.summary: A level's ConditionalContainer, in either title: a container whose children are in the world, and run, only while its Condition holds, exporting isRun.

remarks.para: Both games run the same handler, Project I.G.I.'s 0x4874E0 and I.G.I. 2's ConditionalContainer_RunHandler (igi2 0x520EF0): a condition, when there is one, is run in the float walk and chopped into the isRun byte; with none, isRun keeps what it had. While the container runs, children taken out of the world are put back (ConditionalContainer_RegisterChildren, igi2 0x520D20) and then run; otherwise children still in the world are taken out (ConditionalContainer_RemoveChildren, igi2 0x520DC0), each setting the in-world byte after it has told the children. Last, the tick it starts its Run at start script runs, and the tick it stops its Run at stop. What the titles decide differently, the level run's says.

The three parameters are the ones level data declares (Task_DeclareParameters("ConditionalContainer", "Condition", "VarString", "Run at start", "VarString", "Run at stop", "VarString")). The children stay tasks throughout, so their exported variables keep resolving while they are out of the world.

Why Project I.G.I. needs this. Level 1 places its intro and outro cut-scene actors inside containers gated on cut-scene state that is false during ordinary play (ConditionalContainer_4001 "Intro cutscene", 4007 "Outro Cutscene"), among them a second David Jones on the player's own model. The player and the real guards sit under ConditionalContainer_1495, whose condition !4001.isRun && !4007.isRun holds during play. settles the first game's containers before the first tick, and render, spawn, AI and collision paths read .

member.summary: Runs retail's registered CarAI callback (0x425DE0) once per game tick.

remarks.para: CarAI does not move its car. It decides steering, throttle and brake and sends them to the car as a channel packet (0x426510: ch0 steering, ch1 throttle, ch3 brake), which the car's own receiver (0x42EA10) turns into physics -- the same path an AnimTask-driven car takes. The car therefore pulls away as its smoothed throttle rises: probed on Mission 7, the checkpoint APC crawls at 1-4 km/h for six seconds and reaches its cruise near 35 km/h after eleven.

While the car's vision holds a target (0x426000: retained 600 ticks) CarAI leaves its route and drives at 20 km/h towards the graph node nearest the target, stopping within three metres of it and turning in place to face the target (0x4262F0).

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneCarAi.CarAiThrottle(OpenIGI.Game.World.CarAiState)
member.summary: Opens or closes the throttle towards the desired speed (0x426260).
member.remarks: The car's speed is read in world units a tick and converted to km/h (× 108/4096). The throttle moves one hundredth of the shortfall from the car's own smoothed throttle -- all in one register, truncated once -- and the brake comes on when told to halt or when the car is more than 5 km/h too fast.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneCarAi.CarAiRouteSpeed(OpenIGI.Game.World.CarAiState)
member.summary: The route speed, eased for the heading and for the turn at the node (0x4255A0).
member.remarks: Beyond ten metres of the current node the speed falls with the heading error to it. Within ten metres: mid-leg the look-ahead resolves back to the current node, so there is no turn; at a leg's last node the turn is the angle at the node between the way back to the car and the way on to the next leg's destination, so carrying straight on slows to about 5 km/h; before a Quit or End the speed runs down with the square of the distance. This is what the original computes, dead look-ahead included.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.GroundContactToleranceUnits
member.summary: The narrow vertical band in which an airframe has touched supporting geometry.
member.remarks: Contact is resolved after the native-style integration step. This small band catches the exact rest case as well as the following tick's shallow penetration without affecting a genuinely airborne path.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.MeasureGroundRestOffset(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Measures a parked helicopter's rest height above the ground under its authored pose.
member.remarks: The authored pose of a landed helicopter sits its skids on the surface, so the distance from the pose down to the terrain is the model's own rest height. Returns when the pose is not within the near-ground query's reach, meaning the helicopter is airborne and no rest height applies.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.TryFindSupportHeight(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double@)
member.summary: Finds the highest supporting surface height under a point, preferring an elevated placed object (a pad, crate or rooftop) over lower terrain.
member.param: The body position, in world units.
Receives the highest supporting surface height found.
member.returns: when at least one surface answers; when neither the terrain nor the collision index reports a surface under the point.
member.remarks: Retail's terrain half (0x4CBE40) and placed-model sweep (0x4CDB20 -> 0x4C7770) are two answers for the same question. The higher of the two is the surface the body actually rests on: a heli parked on a pad must rest on the pad's top, not the terrain below it. Both queries run and the higher answer wins, so an elevated collision surface takes precedence over terrain without losing the terrain answer when no object is present.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.RestCollisionHelisOnSupport
member.summary: Keeps a helicopter from sinking through the terrain during contact recovery.
member.remarks: Retail's Heli collision flag prevents a descending body from penetrating a supporting surface; it does not replace the scripted collective or cyclic controls with a pad lock. Airborne helicopters are untouched while the query finds no nearby support. The landing-height search is widened a little above the body (see ) so a body that dips under a ridge or a rising slope still finds the surface it just crossed and rides it back up, instead of falling forever once the downward-only search loses it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.KeepHelicopterAboveGround(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask,OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneTransformState)
member.summary: Holds a collision-enabled helicopter on the surface it has reached, and notes its contact and landing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.LogAirframePath(System.Int32,System.String,OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask,OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneTransformState)
member.summary: Samples the live Heli/Plane tick every fifteenth physics tick, at Trace in the Airframe.Path log category (OPENIGI_LOG=Airframe.Path=trace).

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneGroundSupport.TryGetLandingHeight(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double,System.Double@)
member.summary: Finds the height a helicopter should rest at under a body position.
member.param: The body's current position, in world units.
The model's measured rest height above a supporting surface.
Receives the height the body should rest at when one is found.
member.returns: with when a supporting surface is under the point; when nothing holds the body there.
member.remarks: The terrain query mirrors retail's terrain half (0x4CBE40) but not the placed-model sweep (0x4CDB20 -> 0x4C7770), so a heli landing on a pad, crate or rooftop finds nothing and would sink straight through. When the terrain misses, cast the collision index down from well above the body and rest on the solid object the ray hits instead. A NaN rest offset from the terrain measurement does not disable the object fallback: a heli resting on a pad measures its rest height from the pad's surface below the body.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneRuntime
member.summary: Runs the authored CutScene, EditCamera, timer, container and animation timelines.
member.remarks: Timing and interpolation reproduce the retail handlers: a 30 Hz integer clock, depth-first camera flattening, duration scaling, non-uniform cubic Hermite interpolation, per-shot smooth flags, and transition-latched link/target tracking. The host only supplies presentation and the few game natives referenced by level expressions.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneRuntime.CollisionIndex
member.summary: Gets or sets the solid-object index used to find a supporting surface for vehicles.

remarks.para: Wired by the host when a level has placed pads, crates, garage floors or rooftops that a vehicle stands on. The terrain half mirrors retail's 0x4CBE40; the object sweep mirrors retail's placed-model sweep (0x4CDB20 -> 0x4C7770). Main thread only.

Every mission wants this: a car's suspension probes it for the surface under each wheel, and a great deal of what a vehicle stands on is placed geometry rather than terrain -- the Mission 1 outro truck starts on a garage floor a few centimetres above the dirt, and without the objects its wheels settle through the floor onto the terrain. Setting it no longer rests the helicopters as a side effect; call for that.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutSceneTask
member.summary: A level's cut-scene task — the original's CutScene, carrying the parameters level data declares for it and exporting the three script variables other tasks read off it.

remarks.para: The fourteen parameters are the ones level 1's objects.qvm declares (Task_DeclareParameters("CutScene", …)), in that order — the registry verifies a class against the declaration, so they have to be present and match by type. The exported variables are the ones the original's symbol registrar binds (0x4F4FB0): isRun (a byte at +96), isFinished (a byte at +97) and nTick (an int at +100).
reproduces the original Run/Reset/Start/Stop transitions, advances nTick, and latches isFinished after the final nested EditCamera duration.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneVehicleBodies.VehicleSoundSources
member.summary: Every live vehicle's sound inputs, as its update left them this tick.
member.returns: One entry per active, undestroyed Car, Heli, Plane or Train car.
member.remarks:
A plane instantiates su27 while its "Play sound" holds (0x433690), as a helicopter does helicopter_1 (0x4316D0). Both answer their sounds' parameter query with a two-entry array (0x434A30, 0x432BB0; laid out by 0x4E6AB0 as a count, then the values) that their physics step fills after each step (0x433B50, 0x431E30): parameter 0 the thrust (+1824), parameter 1 whether it is above 0.01. plane_01 reads parameter 1, so a jet sounds at its curves' "on" point whenever its engine is running.
Every car of a train sounds too (0x42B700): train_loop_1 for a locomotive pulling wagons, train_loop_2 for anything else, unless its "Play Sound" expression reads 0 -- and no IGI1 level writes one. Its two parameters are its locomotive's thrust five times over, held to 0.8..1, and whether that thrust is over a thousandth.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneVehicleBodies.VehicleOccupants
member.summary: Gets every vehicle in the world at its current origin, as CRITERIA_VEHICLE counts them.
member.remarks:
0x4F4560 walks the global vehicle list (dword_A76C40) and tests each vehicle's origin (+32): every Car and Heli, whatever drives it. Mission 7's escape truck is an AnimTask's, and the areas it drives through -- the timer that releases it past the checkpoint and the two gates that open for it -- only ever counted the CarAI cars.
A vehicle joins the list when it is created (0x42E180) and leaves it only when it is destroyed (0x42E940); deactivation (0x4F44A0) clears its active flag and leaves it listed. So a vehicle behind a closed ConditionalContainer still counts where it stands: mission 7's ending hides the truck under CutScene 1200, and the truck in AreaActivate 177 is what keeps that scene's container open.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.CutsceneVehicleBodies.BindVehicleWheels(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,System.Func{System.String,System.Single})
member.summary: Binds every car's drawn wheels to its physics record, in the order both are authored in.

member.remarks: A car's wheels arrive as TASKTYPE_WHEEL magic-object attachments, one placement each, in the same order as the record's wheel entries -- on the Mission 1 truck that pairing puts both steered, driven entries exactly on the two front wheels. Their offsets from the body origin are what the drive force and the tyre torque are applied at, so the physics reads them from the model rather than guessing an axle layout.

member.summary: A helicopter's moving parts: its rocket pods and its sliding door (0x4F4660 runs them).

remarks.para: A Heli's update (0x4316D0) tells its door to open or shut from its "Open door" expression, then runs its children; its AnimTask's packet (0x431B70) runs the parts before the flight step, on every packet but the set-up, and the set-up makes them again (0x4F4820, 0x4F4800).
Only the Hind (700_01_1) carries either: four pods and one door.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleObjectRegistry.TryDestroy(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement,System.Single)
member.summary: Applies one weapon hit to the exact placement or owner.
member.remarks: Retail has no search here: the round's trace (0x47B750) hands its damage message to the struck task's own type handler and nothing else, so a hit that names no destructible destroys none. The damage is the firing weapon's Damage Factor (the round's +56, copied from weapon +1620; the knife sends the same field), and a pane only breaks once the sum reaches its drawn threshold (0x449B00) -- a Glock round at 0.25 takes three to six. A placement is the stronger identity -- a wall of the Building that owns a pane names the Building, and must not fall back to that pane through the owner.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleObjectRegistry.ApplyExplosionHits(OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleObject,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Func{OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleObject,System.Boolean},System.Int32)
member.summary: Applies one native Explosion0 contact to every authored destructible in its blast.
member.param: The object that owns the blast, which must not be hit by its own fireball.
The explosion centre in engine units.
The full-damage radius.
The outer contact range after the full-damage radius.
The damage delivered by a full-strength contact.

The id of the weapon whose record the blast carries as its source (Explosion0+0x84), or 0 for a blast that carries none.
member.returns: The exact glass and explosive objects whose native hit callbacks should run.

remarks.para: Retail does not destroy only the nearest object: Glass_ExplosionHitHandler and ExplodeMagicObj_ExplosionHitHandler are both registered as Explosion0 collision callbacks. The fireball therefore visits every authored object in its contact envelope. Marking the state before returning is important: a chain reaction must not enqueue the same object twice.
A car is not returned. Its handler (0x42FB40) only starts it dying — and only for a blast the LAW 80 fired () that reaches it at all — and takes it from there.

member.summary: One tick of a dying car's destruction, 0x42E5A0.
member.remarks: The first tick sets the blasts off and starts a countdown — ten ticks after a single blast, thirty after one per explosion point. When it runs out the car spawns its wreck (0x4F3390, nothing when the record names none), deletes its children (0x401780), gives up its world object (0x4F4820), is switched off (0x42FC80) and only then raises isExploded. The car tick skips all of it once isExploded is set.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleVehicleBlasts.StartVehicleBlasts(OpenIGI.Game.World.DestructibleObject)
member.summary: The blasts 0x42E5A0 sets off on its first tick.

remarks.para: With no explosion points, one Explosion0 at the car's origin, sized from the car's own bound r (its largest scale times MESH+0x78): damage 1, radius r/4, falloff r/20, full range r/200, three fragments and one fireball, going off at once.

With them, one per point at that magic vertex: damage 1, radius 12288, falloff and full range 3072, three fragments and two fireballs, each after its own rand % 30 ticks. Every one plays explo_03_l and posts the 25 m explosion event, and hands over no source record.
0x480FE0 draws three values for the fireball's drift and 0x4810A0 three for its spin from the same global stream; they are drawn here too so that each point's delay is the one the original rolls.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.DirectionalLightSettings
member.summary: The level's sun, read from its Dirlight task.

remarks.para: Every reading here is measured rather than assumed — taken from a probe over the retail data, because nothing recorded these parameters' names and the only statement of what a script Angle means was a doc comment.
This closes a standing item carried out of M6: the "residual dimness" left after the diffuse × lightmap composite was matched is the missing directional term, and this is the data behind it.

member.param: The world-space unit vector pointing towards the sun. World Z is up.

member.summary: Turns the keyframe's two angles into a world-space direction towards the sun.
member.param: The ELEVATION above the horizon, in radians.
The azimuth, in radians.
member.returns: The unit direction towards the sun, in the world's Z-up frame.

remarks.para: As both binaries compute it: IGI.exe sub_527320 and igi2ed 0x6573C0 build (cos β cos γ, −cos β sin γ, sin β). So Beta is an ELEVATION and Gamma is the compass bearing, which is the plain reading of a light that is placed by pointing it.

What was here before took the forward row of the engine's Euler composition, and that is Row3 of RotationZ(γ) · RotationY(β) — but Row3 of a Z rotation is (0, 0, 1), so the product's third row is the Y rotation's alone: (−sin β, 0, cos β). Gamma fell out of the arithmetic entirely. Every level's sun stood in the same vertical plane whatever bearing its authors gave it, and elevation and azimuth were swapped besides — which is why Beta had to be described as a zenith angle to make the numbers look plausible.

The old note reasoned from the elevations the wrong formula produced looking reasonable at noon. They did; a sun that ignores its bearing still rises to a believable height. Reading the two binaries settles it in a way that squinting at outputs cannot.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.DistanceFieldAtlas
member.summary: Every model's distance field packed into one volume, so a shader can reach all of them.

remarks.para: A shader cannot hold an array of textures the way the CPU holds an array of fields. It can hold one volume and an index, so the fields are laid side by side in a single 3D texture and each one records where its corner sits. A trace that wants the field of model seventeen reads its slot and offsets every sample by it.

A uniform grid of slots, not a tight packing. The fields differ in shape — a lamp post is tall and narrow, a floor panel is wide and flat — so packing them tightly would save perhaps a third of the volume. It would also put a different arithmetic in the shader for every model and a search in the builder, and the saving is a few megabytes of a texture that is already small. Every slot is the size of the largest field, and a model that does not fill its slot leaves the rest unread.

Voxels stay isotropic, which is not a detail. Each field is baked with the same voxel spacing on all three axes, so a stored distance means the same thing in every direction. Normalising models into a fixed cube instead would make the spacing depend on the model's proportions, and a distance measured through a stretched grid is not a distance — a sphere trace stepping by it would overshoot along the squashed axis and walk through walls.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.DistanceFieldBake
member.summary: Bakes a level's distance fields off the frame, and hands them over when they are ready.

remarks.para: The same handover uses, and for the same reason recorded there: a multi-second job on the thread holding a live GL context stops the process answering, hands the GPU no work for the whole of it, and loses the context to the operating system's watchdog. Loading a mission that way died with exit 0xCFFFFFFF.

The split is where the GL is. Tracing the geometry is arithmetic and moves to a worker freely; the texture upload cannot, because a GL texture belongs to the context that made it. So the worker produces the fields and the atlas, and the render thread collects them and uploads.
A lockstep capture waits rather than polls, so a reference image either contains the field or does not — never whichever frame the worker happened to reach.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.DoorState
member.summary: One door's state machine — the Door task's update (0x446D10), transcribed.

remarks.para: A door carries an open-command latch (+656, toggled by a use — sub_447DA0 is a plain XOR) and two motion channels driven toward the latch's targets every tick: the swing (current angle +396 toward Max angle +320 or zero, stepping |maxAngle| / (openTime × 30) degrees a tick) and the slide (fraction +312 toward one or zero, stepping (L / (openTime × 30)) / L, L the slide's length). When both channels sit at their targets the door is fully closed (+410, targets zero) or fully open (+409); while either moves, both flags are clear.

The use state the interactions read (sub_447D70): 0 fully open, 1 fully closed, 2 moving with the latch set (opening), 3 moving with it clear (closing). The AI's walker opens on 1 and 3 — a closing door is re-opened — and waits on 2 ("Waiting for door to open").

The registry evaluates the task's authored conditions around this state machine: the open expression only while fully closed, the close expression only while fully open, and the locked expression every tick. The ticks-open counter (+664) is exposed for those conditions. The mid-swing doorway ray that re-opens a closing door off a human standing in it is driven by .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ElevatorSplineFrame
member.summary: The frame an Elevator's spline gives it at a point on its track, which turns the car's authored orientation into the one it is drawn with.

remarks.para: 0x43D960 places a car one of two ways. With the Elevator's Linear set (+396) it interpolates between the first and last waypoint and leaves the orientation alone -- every lift shaft in the game. Otherwise it walks the spline with 0x4FEC10, which hands back a frame as well as a point, and unless Force orientation is set (+397) the drawn orientation (+112) becomes the authored one (+288, which 0x43DDB0 copies into +112 on reset) times that frame.

The frame is the spline's own. At track position nought it is the first waypoint's matrix (+272, 0x4FEC10's LABEL_13); past that it is the matrix of the segment the position lies in, a position exactly on a waypoint belonging to the segment that ends there. A Linear Segments spline gives each segment one piece whose matrices are all a turn about Z to the chord's heading (0x4E4530: 0x4B2D00 on the chord, then 0x4B3BE0 on the heading) -- and that heading is atan2(y, x) except for a chord with no X at all, which 0x4B2D00 calls heading nought rather than either quarter turn.

Mission 12's cutscene gondola (Elevator 1667) is the car this is for: authored at 271 degrees on a cable heading 91 degrees, it is drawn at about 2, side-on to the camera, and the port drew it at 271 -- a quarter turn out. A curved spline's frames (slerped Hermite tangents) are not ported: no IGI1 Elevator rides one unforced, and returns for it so the car keeps its authored frame.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ElevatorState
member.summary: The deterministic movement state for one retail Elevator task.
member.remarks:
The native elevator updates its platform and children together through Elevator_UpdatePosition and Elevator_UpdateChildPosition. The port keeps the same single position source and exposes the previous sample for render interpolation and collision. Floor expressions are commands: a held expression does not skip through every floor.
The original moves a spline parameter (+388) along the spline's segment lengths, its speed and brake in those units (0x43D6E0), and places the car on the straight line between the knots (Linear, 0x43D960). The port keeps the car's position, and measures each step and the brake in the segment's own length: a bent segment's length is its sampled cubic's, longer than the straight run, so the car covers the run more slowly. Every shipped lift that is not Linear has straight segments, which the car follows knot to knot either way.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.EmissiveTextureSurvey
member.summary: Finds the textures a level treats as light sources, by reading what the artists baked around them.

remarks.para: Why this has to be inferred at all. I.G.I. declares no lights. A survey of level 1's task tree turns up a Dirlight, a GlobalLight and 290 lightmap records, and nothing else — no omni, no point, no spot. Every lamp on a wall is geometry with a texture, and the light it appears to cast was painted into a lightmap by hand. So a renderer that stops using the bakes, as the dynamic lighting model does, has no way to know a lamp is a lamp.

What gives them away. A lightmap records how much light reached a surface. For nearly every surface in a level that is some fraction of the sun or the sky. For a lamp's own fixture it is not: the artist painted it bright, because it is the thing doing the lighting. So a texture whose lightmap is consistently near-white, across every place the level uses it, is a texture the artists treated as a source — and that is a far more reliable signal than the diffuse texture's own brightness, which merely says the thing is pale.

Consistency is the discriminating part. One bright sample is a surface in sunlight. The same texture bright in twenty different places, indoors and out, is a surface that carries its own light. The survey therefore reports the share of a texture's uses that are bright as well as the mean, and ranking on the share is what separates a lamp from a wall that happens to face south.

What it is NOT. This ranks textures by how they were LIT, and being brightly lit is not the same as being a light — level 1's highest-scoring texture of all, baked pure white across every one of its thirty uses, skins the office cabinets. It is also blind in the other direction: four of that level's real ceiling fittings score exactly nought, because those rooms were lit without painting the fitting bright. So this does not decide which textures are lamps and is not consulted on it; reads the geometry instead, and records why. What this is good for is a starting list for materials.json and for any level export's emissive materials — it says which textures are worth looking at, and someone still has to look.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.EmissiveTextureSurvey.BrightThreshold

member.remarks: Well above what the sun alone puts on a surface in these levels, so that a sunlit wall does not qualify. Lower it and the survey fills with south-facing concrete.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.EmissiveTextureSurvey.MeanLuminance(OpenIGI.Formats.World.ObjectLightmapImage@,OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshGeometry,OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshSubset@)
member.summary: Averages the luminance of the part of a lightmap page one sub-mesh actually covers.

remarks.para: The sub-mesh's own corner of the page, not the whole page. The page is an atlas of one MODEL's surfaces, and that is not local enough: a ceiling model carries its slab, its beams and the one small tube bolted to it in a single .olm, so averaging the page divides the tube's near-white by the whole dark ceiling around it and the brightest thing in the room scores like concrete. That failure is why a page-wide survey needs a hand-written list of lamp textures to catch what it missed. Measuring only the texels this sub-mesh's own lightmap UVs reach takes the dilution away, and the list with it.

The bounds are a rectangle rather than the exact footprint. A lightmap atlas is packed so that a sub-mesh's chart occupies a contiguous block, and the padding around one is either black — which is skipped below — or a bled copy of the chart's own edge, which is the same light. So the rectangle costs nothing in practice and saves rasterising every triangle into the page.
Fully black texels are skipped. An atlas is padded, and counting its empty margin would drag every page towards zero in proportion to how wastefully it was packed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.EmissiveTextureSurvey.Bounds(OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshGeometry,OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshSubset@,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: The texel rectangle a sub-mesh's lightmap UVs cover, clamped into the page.
member.remarks: UVs come out of a pack file and are not guaranteed to sit inside the unit square -- a chart can be authored slightly over its edge, and a malformed record can be anywhere at all. Clamping is what keeps a bad one costing the accuracy of one measurement rather than reading past the page.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds
member.summary: What a footstep sounds like, and how far it is heard — the rules of 0x463920.

remarks.para: Animation event 1010 is by far the commonest event in the retail animation data — 117 of 245 — and it is deliberately absent from the animtrigger table, because a table entry names one fixed sound and a footstep depends on what is underfoot. This is where that choice is made instead.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.EventId
member.summary: The animation event a footstep is.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.TerrainMaterialName
member.summary: The material a step on bare terrain lands on.

remarks.para: The ground query 0x462390 does not read a material out of the ray hit. It asks the task that was hit — dword_A9A6E0[hitTask.Type] dispatches a probe message, and the answer lands at offset 76 of the cached hit block, which is Human+1772, the field the footstep handler reads. So the material is a property of the thing underfoot, not of the geometry.

The terrain answers too, and it is not always Ground. It has no task, so the leaf query answers for itself: 0x4CB050 ends by calling 0x4CB810, which takes the low byte of the terrain material's first field — argument 1 of CreateTerrainMaterial, long mistaken for a flag word — and uses it to select the same per-level material array a mesh face selects with its own index. So the ground under your feet outdoors names a game material exactly as a crate does.

Across the campaign that field takes two values: 1 (Ground) in levels 1–6, 9, 10, 13 and 14, and 20 (Snow) in the four snow missions, 7, 8, 11 and 12. Every terrain material within a level agrees, which is why can answer for the whole map; the name below stays only as the fallback for a level that declares nothing.

What is not modelled: the per-point half. The original reaches its terrain material through a message-13 broadcast at the hit position, so in principle two regions of one map could answer differently. No retail level does — every material in a level carries the same value — so picking any of them gives the retail answer.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.TerrainGameMaterialIndex(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyDictionary{System.Int32,OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainMaterial})
member.summary: The game material index the terrain of a level declares, or null when it declares none.
member.param: The level's terrain materials, keyed by id.
member.returns: The row to look up in the game material table.
member.remarks: Every terrain material in a retail level declares the same index, so the first is the answer. A level that somehow disagreed would need the original's per-point message-13 lookup; taking the lowest id keeps that case deterministic rather than dependent on dictionary order.

member.remarks: Transcribed from the twelve dwords at 0x53F318, which the handler walks with a per-human cursor advanced (i + 1) % 12. It is not a permutation: the first six use each sound once, the second six are an irregular tail in which 3 appears twice and 0 not at all. Authored by hand, so it is copied rather than generated.
