member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.RainSoundName(System.Int32)
member.summary: The wet layer a step lays over its own sound while the level's weather is on.
member.param: The cycle slot the step took, 0 to 5.
member.returns: The definition name, walk_rain_1 through walk_rain_6.

remarks.para: 0x463920 builds it with sprintf(buffer, "walk_rain_%1d", slot + 1) and plays it as well as the material's own sound, at the same position and the same pitch. It is a second voice layered on the first, not a replacement — walking on metal in the rain is the metal step and the wet step together.
The gate is 0x416FB0, which returns a single global byte. That is the level's weather flag, not a shelter test, so standing under a roof does not stop it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.CrouchedVolumeScale
member.summary: How much of its volume a crouched step keeps.

remarks.para: 0.66 (0x3F28F5C3, in both 0x45A7F0 and 0x463920). The handler tests Human+829 — the crouch byte — and, when it is set, sends the started voice a two-float message, -1.0 and 0.66 (0x4E6C60). The second is the volume the voice keeps; the -1.0 reads as "leave the other alone", which is how the same message is used elsewhere, though that half is inference rather than something traced to a handler.
The same crouch test also skips the AI hearing event entirely, so crouching is both quieter to the ear and completely silent to a guard.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.NamesAWalk(OpenIGI.Game.World.GameMaterial)
member.summary: Reports whether a material names anything to walk on.
member.param: The material a probe struck.
member.returns: when every one of its six walk sounds is empty.

remarks.para: Six rows of the retail table name no walk sound at all: Air, Water, Flesh, BloodyFlesh, HumanCollision, MetalLadder and MetalFence. None of them is a floor, and the original never asks them: 0x462390 takes the material from the ground task it is already standing on, through a message dispatch, rather than from whatever a fresh downward ray happens to strike first.

This port has no ground task to ask, so it casts that ray — and near the player it lands on human-collision volumes, which named nothing and left every step on placed geometry silent. Treating a row that names no walk as "not the floor" and going on to the ground beneath is what keeps the port's answer the same as the original's.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.Pitch(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom)
member.summary: The pitch a footstep plays at.
member.param: The engine's generator.
member.returns: A ratio between 0.8 and 1.3.
member.remarks: The original computes rand() * 0.5 + 1.0 - 0.2, which is the same thing written the way the compiler folded it. Two steps on the same surface are never quite the same sound, and this is the whole of why.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.HearingRadiusInUnits(OpenIGI.Game.World.GameMaterial)
member.summary: How far away a step on this material is heard by the AI, in engine units.
member.param: The material under the feet.
member.returns: The radius in engine units.
member.remarks: The handler posts its hearing event with the material's own argument-5 number times 4096, so the ground decides how far a footstep carries as well as what it sounds like — gravel gives a sneaking player away where carpet does not.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.LandSound(OpenIGI.Game.World.GameMaterial)
member.summary: The sound the ground makes when a body lands on it.
member.param: The material under the feet.
member.returns: The definition name, or empty when the material names none.

remarks.para: Both airborne states play this on contact and they play it identically: the falling per-tick (0x40BE40) and the jump's (0x40BBD0) each read the material pointer at Human+1772, add 276, and hand that straight to the sound bank. That lands on the field straight after the six 32-byte walk names, which the same handler reaches at +84 + 32·slot. The reader 0x407F50 confirms the order from the other end — it stores the name, three reals, a flag, argument 5, then six walk names, the land name, the rain name, six bullet names and two spare — though at its own offsets, which run 32 lower than the pointer these two states hold.

It is not the fall-damage sound. player_fall_1..3 come from 0x408460 and only when the drop actually hurt; this one plays on every landing, hurt or not, and it is what a harmless hop off a crate sounds like. It takes no pitch variation and no volume change.

The shipped bank holds land_ground_1 through land_ground_5 and nothing else of the kind, so every row names one of those five however hard the surface is — material.qvm gives Air the first and Wood the fifth. A row naming none lands in silence.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.FootstepSounds.Probe(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)

member.returns: The probe's start and end, in engine units.
member.remarks: A separate cast from the one that found the ground height: the original probes from 0.05 m above the ground point down to 0.5 m below it, which is short enough not to punch through a floor into whatever is under it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.GunShotEffect
member.summary: What one GunShotEffect a material declares does to the surface it is on.
member.param: The first flag the class reads.
The second flag.
The mark a round entering the surface leaves, or empty for none.
The mark a round leaving it leaves, or empty for none.
How wide the mark is, as authored.
The impact effect's model.

remarks.para: Read from 0x4387B0, the GunShotEffect class's parameter reader. It consumes six arguments and stores the two texture names as 24-character fields, the size multiplied by 4096 into world units, and the model as 32 characters. It then resolves each texture name and leaves a handle at +88 and +92 — zero when the name is empty.

That zero is load-bearing: the shot resolution refuses to record an impact at all unless the struck material's block has a non-null +88. A material naming no texture leaves no mark and costs nothing, which is how Air and Water work.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.GameMaterial
member.summary: One row of the game material table — what a surface is made of, and what happens when it is hit.

remarks.para: DefineGameMaterial (0x407F50) fills a 616-byte record per material, and SetActiveMaterial chooses which row is being filled. So a material's index is its row, which is what makes a collision face's fourth field usable: it selects one of these directly.

The call is variable length for the same reason the weapon roster's is — it names two task classes and each consumes its own parameters. Retail names TASKTYPE_GUNSHOTEFFECT for both, so every row is 36 arguments.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.GameMaterial.IsSightTransparent(System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether a line of sight passes through this global material row.
member.param: A row of the retail material table.
member.returns: for the see-through surfaces a sight ray must ignore: Water (2), Glass (14), Fence (18), MetalLadder (22) and MetalFence (23).
member.remarks: Retail's binocular detector culls contacts by sector/portal visibility, which glass panes and chain-link fences do not bound, so a guard behind them stays visible. This reimplementation approximates that with a sight raycast; those materials must therefore not count as occluders. Air (0) is deliberately excluded — the terrain trace reports material 0 by default, and treating it as transparent would let contacts be seen straight through a hill.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.GlobalDistanceFieldSettings
member.summary: How the level's distance field is resampled into clipmaps around the camera.

remarks.para: A trace cannot afford to consult every object in the level at every step. A clipmap is the standard answer: a small grid that follows the camera, holding the distance to whatever is nearby, so a step is one texture fetch regardless of how much geometry the level contains.

Several of them, each twice the size of the last. One grid cannot be both fine enough to resolve a doorway and large enough to reach the horizon. Nesting them gives fine detail where the ray starts — which is where it takes most of its steps — and coarse detail far away, where a ray is crossing open ground and a metre of error costs nothing.

member.param: How many nested grids. Each covers twice the extent of the one inside it at the same voxel count, so each costs the same to build and store.
Voxels along each axis of every level. The cost of a rebuild is this cubed, so it is the dial that matters.

How many metres across the innermost level is. Its voxels are this divided by .
The world these cover IS in metres — WorldScene divides every raw coordinate by 4096 on load, and the player's eye sits 1.8 above the ground to prove it. This was 4096 for a while, on a theory that the units were raw and a metre was a hundred of them; that made the finest voxel 64 metres, so the sun trace started its rays 96 metres off every surface and called a hit anything within 32 — which in a built-up level is everywhere, and every card sat in shadow.
How many cells each level is divided into for culling. Each cell holds the list of objects that reach into it, so a voxel consults a handful of candidates rather than the whole level.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.GlobalDistanceFieldSettings.Default
member.summary: Gets the settings the shipped presets use.

remarks.para: Spelled out rather than written new(): for a record struct that is the ZERO instance, not the primary constructor's defaults, and a resolution of nought builds nothing while reporting success. That trap has already cost this project one silent stage.

A 16-metre near extent (not the 64 the record defaults to) is what seals interiors. Changing it costs nothing -- the voxel count is the same either way, this only chooses how much world it covers -- so the near level is pulled in to a 0.25-metre voxel, fine enough to register the building's walls. At 64 the finest voxel was a whole metre, thinner than any interior wall, so the radiance cache's probe rays sailed through the walls of a sealed room and came back carrying the daylight sky: a windowless office lit as if it had a skylight. The trade is far reach, which drops from 512 metres to 128; validated on mission 1 as ample -- the sealed base-floor office now darkens to its own ceiling tubes while the windowed office still fills through the glass.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.GunPickupRegistry
member.summary: Finds and resolves the original game's automatic world weapon pickups.

remarks.para: GunPickup's proximity handler at 0x46D230 tests the Human's origin (+32, sent every tick by 0x410F70), not its feet, against the pickup: planar distance must be less than 2867.2 units (0.7 m) -- or the model's bounding radius, when that is larger -- and vertical distance less than 4096 units (1 m). It does not require aiming or the activate key. On success it sends the human the weapon id plus one full magazine, marks itself for deletion and publishes PICKEDUPWEAPON….
Presentation owns the sound and notification; this registry owns only the level data, range test and task lifetime.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.IBakedLight
member.summary: The light a level bakes at a point: what its lightmaps say of the ground or floor there, not what is drawn.

remarks.para: The scale is the one both games' lightmaps share as they draw: nought is dark, and one shows a surface as bright as its texture. I.G.I. 2 stores a texel as a byte times 2/255 and draws it doubled, so its own lightmaps reach two; Project I.G.I. multiplies its surfaces by their lightmap once, so its brightest texel is one.

I.G.I. 2 asks this of the face under a human's feet as it stands (Human_GroundCollision), and sees its player by it. Project I.G.I. never asks it: its terrain cells hand their pages only to the terrain's draw lists (TerrainLightMap's event 15 at 0x4F82B0, read by 0x4D14E0). A level of it answers so that another game's rules can.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ICollisionWorld
member.summary: A level's walls and ground, as anything that moves through it or looks across it asks of them.

remarks.para: Each game keeps its own collision -- Project I.G.I.'s placed objects and terrain octree, I.G.I. 2's object tree and height grid -- and answers its own retail queries exactly. This is the part of them that is the same question in both: is there a wall between two points, and where is the ground under one. A camera kept out of walls, a body set down, or another game's soldier brought into a level asks this, and works in either game.
Not a replacement for the retail queries: a game's own code keeps calling them, in their own precision and order.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.LevelCollision.DaylightCast
member.summary: Gets daylight's line through the level, as the lighting bakes cast it: every door shut, glass and chain-link passed, and the terrain blocking wherever it is nearer than the first solid object.

remarks.para: A bake ray passes through glass and chain-link the way a line of sight does (), so daylight reaches a room through its windows instead of stopping at the pane. It steps a hair past each see-through face and casts on until it meets something solid or leaves the level; a portal polygon (a doorway or window opening) the cast skips anyway. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.IGroundHeightField
member.summary: The ground a level puts under a body: how high it is, and which way it faces.

remarks.para: Two games, one question, two completely different answers. Project I.G.I. stores its ground as an octree of geometry blocks and answers by descending it to a leaf and intersecting a triangle; I.G.I. 2 stores a grid of height samples and answers by interpolating four of them. Nothing about either shape survives into the other, and the body standing on the result does not care: it asks how high the ground is at a point and which way the surface faces, and both games can say.

This is deliberately not "the terrain". A terrain is also a thing you ray-trace through, draw, bake lightmaps from and block sight with, and those stay on the concrete type that can do them — and TerrainSightBlock still take a , because there is nothing to share yet. What is behind this seam is only what the player's feet need, which is the part I.G.I. 2 can already answer.

The window is part of the contract rather than an implementation detail. The original's own ground query is a segment test — Terrain_GetNextZHandler (igi2 0x572E80) accepts a surface only when its height lies between the two ends of the probe, and Project I.G.I.'s (0x4CB050) reaches below its origin — so a query is asking "is there ground in this stretch", never "how high is the ground somewhere below".

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBake
member.summary: A probe bake running off the frame, and the handover of its result to the render thread.

remarks.para: takes about three seconds in Release and half a minute in Debug. Called inline during a level load that already owns a live window, that is not a stall: the process stops answering, the GPU sees no work for the whole of it, and Windows' watchdog takes the context away — loading mission 1 from the menu died with exit 0xCFFFFFFF. So the trace runs off the main thread and the frames keep going out while it does.

The upload cannot move with it. A GL texture belongs to the context it was made on and the context belongs to the render thread, so the worker produces a plain array of coefficients and the main thread collects it with and hands it to the device. Nothing here touches the graphics API.

The cast handed in must be safe to call while the game runs, because by the time the trace finishes the game is running: doors open, and reads the set that records which ones. is the cast that answers this, and it is the one the bake wants for its own reasons anyway.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker
member.summary: Traces a level once and records what each probe in an can see.

remarks.para: The whole cost of a probe volume is the geometric question — what can this point see — and in this game that answer never changes. The levels are static and each mission's sun is a fixed direction, so the transfer is traced here, once, and relighting afterwards is a multiply by whatever colour the sun and sky are that frame.

Rays go out on a Fibonacci sphere rather than a random or axis-aligned set. Random directions clump, which shows up as probes that disagree with their neighbours for no reason the geometry explains; axis-aligned ones miss the diagonals that matter most in a corridor. The Fibonacci spiral is the cheapest construction that spaces points near-evenly on a sphere, and it is deterministic, which matters because a probe bake that differs between runs is a level that lights differently each time it loads.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.RaysPerProbe
member.summary: How many directions each probe is asked about.
member.remarks: Enough to resolve a doorway, few enough that a level of several thousand probes bakes in the time a level already takes to load. The result is first-order spherical harmonics, which cannot represent more detail than this anyway.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.Bounces
member.summary: How many times the light is allowed to bounce through the volume.
member.remarks: One bounce is a surface lit by the sun and the sky and nothing else, which leaves a room the sun never reaches almost dark -- the light that fills such a room is what has already reflected two, three, four times off its walls. Each extra pass re-traces every probe reading the light the last pass left on the geometry, so the series converges on the true multi-bounce answer. It is a one-time cached bake, so bounces cost nothing at runtime and the count is set for convergence, not speed. With the feedback carried at the surface's re-emitted radiance (see ) the per-bounce gain is albedo times how much of the gather the geometry catches, which is below one, so the light settles geometrically: at the grey retail albedo (~0.4-0.5) an enclosed room is within a per cent of its limit by the fourth pass. Five leaves a pass of headroom for a brighter-walled room without tracing the whole grid twice for a gain no surface still shows. This is the difference between an interior that reads lit and one that reads like a cave, and it is why the sun through a window fills the room rather than only its floor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.SunlitBounce
member.summary: How much more a sunlit surface bounces than a sky-lit one.
member.remarks: The sun is far brighter than the sky it shares the hemisphere with, so a wall in sunlight is a far stronger secondary source than the same wall in shade. This is the only route by which sunlight reaches the indirect term, and it has to be the only one: the lighting pass adds the direct sun itself, shadow-mapped, so a probe that also carried a lobe pointed at the sun would count it twice.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.IndirectFeedbackScale
member.summary: Undoes the SH projection scale when reading light back for a further bounce.
member.remarks: The zeroth SH basis constant, Y0 = 0.282095. omits it, so a gathered value comes back at 2*sqrt(pi) times the radiance it represents; multiplying by Y0 cancels that, which is what stops the bounce feedback from compounding a factor of ~3.5 per pass and running the light away in enclosed rooms.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.PublishesPerPass
member.summary: How many times a single bounce pass hands over its progress before it finishes.
member.remarks: The pass publishes a snapshot roughly this many times, spread across the rows it traces, so the field the game shows advances steadily over the pass rather than once at its end -- enough that the light reads as resolving in continuously. The render thread coalesces to the newest, so a larger number only smooths the fill; it does not cost an upload each time.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.IrradianceProbeBaker.SunBiasInUnits
member.summary: How far off a surface a shadow ray starts, in engine units.
member.remarks: Without it every shadow ray begins exactly on the surface it is testing and immediately hits it, so nothing is ever found to be in sunlight.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ITitleWorldBuilder
member.summary: Turns a title's loaded level into the shared scene everything downstream consumes.

remarks.para: Behind a seam because the walk is per title and nothing downstream is. — a position, an orientation, an instance, a pack, a mesh and a lightmap name — is a shape both games have, and the world renderer, the collision index and the soldiers' ground probe all take it unchanged. How a level becomes that is not shared at all: knows Project I.G.I.'s task names, its parameter names and even its security-camera model ids, and opens the two packs that game has; the sequel declares different types, resolves models through a table over four packs whose order decides which name wins, and binds its lightmaps by task id.

The host called the first game's walk directly, so a second title loaded a mission and got the first game's reading of it — which for I.G.I. 2 means almost nothing placed, quietly. That is the same shape of failure the sky had: everything loads, nothing says a word, and the world is empty.

A third lookup in the composition root rather than a member of IGameTitleRuntime, for the reason the presentation provider is a second one: the reference graph forbids joining them, because OpenIGI.Game references OpenIGI.Engine and so Engine cannot name a . What matters is that all three are resolved in the one place allowed to name either game.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LadderClimbLine
member.summary: A ladder's climb geometry: the segment between its bottom and top, divided into the discrete steps the original climbs it in.

remarks.para: The bottom and top are the ladder model's magic vertices 2 and 3 in world space — the two points the ladder constructor (sub_440280) reads to size the ladder, and the two the mount (sub_4113E0) and the per-tick climb (IGI2 HumanPlayer_ClimbLadder 0x4A0B30) place the human between.

The ladder is climbed in whole steps. The constructor divides the bottom-to-top height by and truncates, giving ; the climb tracks an integer step from 0 (foot) to (head), and the human's position along the ladder is bottom + (step / StepCount) · (top − bottom) — exactly the fraction IGI2's HumanPlayer_ClimbLadder forms.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LadderClimbLine.StepLengthUnits
member.summary: World units per climb step — 4096 · 0.3 = 1228.8, one rung's spacing (0.3 m).
member.remarks: The constructor scales the height by 0.0008138020833333334 = 1/1228.8 and truncates it into an integer step count; IGI2's climb uses the same reciprocal (0.0008138020509957453, the single-precision rounding of the same value).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector
member.summary: Decides which of a level's textures are lamps, from the shape of the geometry that draws them.

remarks.para: Why the lightmaps alone are not enough. asks what the artists BAKED around a texture, which is the strongest single signal there is — a surface painted near-white everywhere it appears is a surface the artists treated as a source. But it is evidence about light and not about objects, and it says yes to things that are lit rather than lighting: a pale sign under a lamp, a vending machine's advert panel, a white door at the end of a sunlit corridor.

What this asks about instead is the object. A ceiling lamp is a specific shape in a specific place: small, above head height, flat, facing down, and painted in near-neutral white rather than in a brand's colours. None of those alone means anything — plenty of small flat things hang from ceilings — but together they describe a light fixture and very little else, so that is the test.

And that shape test is not, on its own, nearly enough. Measured over the fourteen retail levels it proposed 423 sub-meshes of which 263 were not lamps — soldiers, chairs, toilets, filing cabinets, security cameras, dropped weapons — because "small, pale, flat and above head height" describes a mounting bracket as exactly as it describes a batten. So it is now a second opinion rather than the whole answer: a sub-mesh is admitted only when it is also SKINNED like a fitting, with one of the texture pages this level's own catalogued lamps draw from. See FixtureTextures for why that is the fact that separates them, and why it is the texture and not the model name that has to be asked.

The bake is not used as a second source, and that was measured rather than assumed. Letting a high survey score make a texture emissive on its own would be wrong twice over. It says yes to surfaces that are bright because they are LIT — level 1's highest-scoring texture of all, baked pure white across thirty uses, is a panel that skins office cabinets, and it glowed. And emission means something strong in this renderer: an emissive surface is UNLIT, it stops receiving light entirely, so a half-confident emitter does not glow faintly, it turns into a flat shadeless slab.

Using the bake the other way round — as a veto — fails on the same level for the opposite reason: 316_01_1 and 316_02_1, two pages of level 1's LIGHT model itself, score exactly nought in the survey across all twenty-seven of their uses, because the artists lit those rooms without painting the fittings bright. The two signals genuinely disagree about real lamps, and the bake is the one that is wrong about them, so it decides nothing here.

Confirm once, then trust the SUB-MESH — not the texture. A texture is shared: the page that skins a ceiling fitting also skins the panel it is bolted to and, in level 1, the side of an office cabinet. Confirming the texture and glowing it everywhere is what put a blown-out wedge across a garage soffit and a flat white slab down that cabinet, and a size cap on the drawing geometry does not save it — the cabinet's panel is smaller than a fluorescent batten. So what is remembered is which MODEL AND MATERIAL SLOT passed, and only those draw as lamps.

Model and slot rather than the individual placement, because that is the level the answer lives at: a model is a lamp model wherever the level puts it, and a corridor of six identical tubes is six placements of one model. Testing each PLACEMENT would light one tube in six, since only the tidily modelled instances pass the shape test; testing each texture lights the furniture.

The output is still a proposal. Everything here is inferred from art that was never authored to be read this way, and the fixtures file exists so a wrong answer is corrected by editing a list rather than by editing this class — see .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MinimumHeight
member.summary: How far above the level's ground a fixture must sit to be a lamp, in metres.

remarks.para: To keep out floor clutter — a pale crate, a white barrel — which no other test here excludes. Measured from the level's own ground rather than from zero, because this game's world sits tens of kilometres from the origin.

Low, and deliberately so, because the datum it is measured against is poor. GroundHeight is the MEDIAN height of the level's placements — a fact about the whole level, which says nothing about the floor of the room a fixture is in. At head height it threw away a 2.4 m office ceiling strip, normal straight down and 11 cm thick, for sitting 1.72 m above that median. Measured on level 1: 1.8 m admits 21 sub-meshes and 1.2 m admits 23 — the two it gains are real ceiling fittings — while dropping to nought admits 44, and those twenty-one are the crates and barrels this exists for. So the floor sits where the curve is flat.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MaximumWidth
member.summary: The widest a lamp fixture is, in metres.
member.remarks: A fixture, not a ceiling. Three metres takes the longest fluorescent batten in the game and stops well short of the ceiling panels a lamp is mounted on, which are the thing most likely to share its texture and its height.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MaximumThickness
member.summary: The thickest a lamp fixture is, in metres.

member.summary: The largest a fixture may be in ANY direction to count as a compact fitting, in metres.
member.remarks: The size that separates a wall lamp from a wall PANEL. A bracket fitting is a little box; the things a bare size test would otherwise admit are flat sheets — a cabinet's side, a door, a sign — which are small in two directions and not in the third. Six tenths of a metre is comfortably larger than any fitting in the game and smaller than any panel that was mistaken for one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MinimumCompactSize
member.summary: The smallest a compact fitting may be in its THINNEST direction, in metres.
member.remarks: A fitting is a solid little object. This is what stops a decal, a sticker or a paper-thin quad from qualifying as one by being small in all three directions at once.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MinimumBrightness
member.summary: How bright a lamp's own diffuse texture reads, 0 to 1.
member.remarks: The DIFFUSE, not the lightmap: a lamp is painted pale because it is a lamp, and this is the one piece of evidence here that does not come from the bake at all. Low, because a tube's texture page carries its dark housing as well as its bright glass.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MaximumSaturation
member.summary: How colourless a lamp's own diffuse texture reads, 0 (grey) to 1 (saturated).
member.remarks: This is the term that separates a lamp from an advert. A fluorescent fitting is white, grey and steel; a soda machine's lit panel and a warning sign are bright in the bake for the same reason a lamp is — the artist painted them so — but they are RED, and no light fixture in this game is.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.LampRadiance
member.summary: How much light a lamp should appear to give off, whatever colour it is painted.

remarks.para: A radiance to reach, not a multiple to apply. Emission is albedo times a strength, so one strength for every fixture makes a lamp as bright as its own texture happens to be: a near-white tube came out at six and clipped to a flat white block, while the grey fitting in the next room came out at two and read as a pale panel. They are the same kind of light, and how dark the artist drew the housing is not a fact about how brightly it burns.

So each texture's strength is this divided by how bright the texture is, and every fixture in the level arrives at about the same brightness. Three, which is what a typical fitting reached under the old flat six — so the ones that already looked right are unchanged, and it is the outliers at either end that move.
Uniform in the MEAN only. Within one fixture the bright glass still outshines its dark housing, because this scales the texture rather than replacing it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.MaximumStrength
member.summary: The most a lamp's own texture may be multiplied by.
member.remarks: A texture only just past would otherwise ask for a strength high enough to turn every speck of noise in its dark half into a light. This is the point past which a fixture is simply drawn too dark to be normalised into a lamp.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.Lamps
member.summary: Which sub-meshes of a level are light fixtures.
member.param: The textures those fixtures draw with. What the light extractor gathers for.

Every sub-mesh that is a lamp — keyed by model and material slot — and the multiple of its own albedo it emits at. A draw is a lamp only if it is in here; see the type's remarks for why the texture alone is not enough.
The strength lives HERE and not on the texture because one texture is not one brightness. A level's floodlight, its ceiling fitting and the lamp over its door all draw with the same page, and a floodlight is not a reading lamp. Keying the strength by sub-mesh is what lets an authored list say so.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.FixtureTextures(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene)
member.summary: The texture pages a level's own light fittings are skinned with.

remarks.para: The shape test alone cannot do this, and that was measured rather than feared. Across the fourteen retail levels it proposed 423 sub-meshes and 263 of them were not lamps: soldiers, chairs, toilets, sinks, filing cabinets, security cameras, telephones, computer monitors, dropped weapons and ammunition boxes. A HOLDER — the bracket the user's report named — is a pale grey plate 1.2 m across and 15 cm thick, hanging 6 m up with its faces summing straight down. So is a fluorescent batten. No measurement of that geometry separates them, because there is nothing left in the geometry to measure.

What does separate them is that the artists SKINNED lamps as lamps. This game's own model catalogue names its fittings — LIGHT, LAMP_CIELING, FLOODLIGHT, STREETLAMP, HANGER_LIGHTS and the rest — and those models draw from a small set of texture pages. A holder is skinned with a holder's page, a camera with a camera's; neither shares one with anything the artists called a light. Gathering the pages the level's OWN named fittings use, and admitting nothing else, drops all 263 and keeps every one of the 146 real fittings.

Textures rather than the names themselves, because a lamp is not always its own model. A garage's ceiling strip is a sub-mesh of the garage shell — model GARAGE_INTERIOR, which is no more a lamp than a wall is — and the same is true of an elevator car's ceiling light. Judging by the model's name would lose both. They are skinned with the fitting's page, so judging by the page finds them: the six garage strips and the elevator light survive with nothing named by hand.

A page is shared, so this is a gate and not a verdict — the shape test still has to agree, and what passes both is still keyed by sub-mesh rather than by texture. One family survives that should not: an office cabinet skinned with the ceiling lamp's own page, seven sub-meshes across the fourteen levels. That is what 's lamp: false is for.

The catalogue is not complete — it names 523 of the game's models — and a fitting it does not name contributes no page, so a level lit entirely by uncatalogued fittings would come out dark rather than wrong. None of the fourteen is: every level carries between eight and thirteen named fittings. Naming the model in the manifest is how such a level would be corrected, and the manifest is read before this gate rather than through it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.IsNamedLightFixture(System.String)
member.summary: Whether the game's own catalogue calls a model a light fitting.
member.param: The drawing instance's name, such as 316_01_1.
member.returns: when the artists named this model a light or a lamp.
member.remarks:
The catalogue holds 523 distinct names and exactly fourteen of them contain LIGHT or LAMP — LIGHT, LIGHTS_FLAT, LIGHTS_ROUND, LAMP, LAMP_CIELING, LARGE_LIGHTS, MEDIUM_LIGHTS, HANGER_LIGHTS, FLOODLIGHT, STREETLAMP, COMM_TOWER_LIGHT, ALARM_LIGHT and its two destroyed variants — and every one of them is a light fitting. Nothing else in the catalogue contains either word, so the substring test needs no list of its own to maintain.
The destroyed variants count. A shot-out alarm light is not a light any more, but it is skinned with the same page as the working one, and it is the PAGE this is gathering.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.IsFixtureShaped(OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshGeometry,OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshSubset@,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement@,System.Double)
member.summary: Whether one sub-mesh, where it stands, is shaped and placed like a ceiling lamp.
member.remarks:
Small and above head height, and then EITHER facing along the vertical — a ceiling fitting presenting its lit face to the room below — or compact in every direction, which is what a wall bracket looks like when its faces sum sideways and the vertical test cannot see it.
The normal comes from the winding rather than from the authored vertex normals, which face inward on this game's interior shells; summing the raw cross products weights each face by its own area, and a fixture whose faces cancel — a closed box — falls through to the compact test rather than passing the vertical one by accident.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.Look(System.String,OpenIGI.Engine.Resources.ResourceRegistry,System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.String,OpenIGI.Game.World.LampDetector.TextureLook})
member.summary: A texture's mean brightness and mean saturation, cached per name.

remarks.para: Brightness is the mean of each texel's largest channel, and saturation the mean of (max - min) / max over the texels that are not nearly black — black texels have no hue to average, and counting them would call every dark texture grey.

Resolved through the pack's own naming. A bare texture name is not a path this game's resource layer will accept — it throws rather than returning false — which is why an earlier attempt at reading these came back white for every texture in the level.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampManifest
member.summary: The lights the game has, named by hand rather than inferred.

remarks.para: Why an authored list exists at all. I.G.I. declares no lights, so works out which geometry is a fitting by its shape and its texture. That inference is good but it is still an inference: it misses fittings whose model does not look the way it expects, and it occasionally lights furniture. Somebody who has walked the level with the target readout open knows the answer outright, and this is where they write it down.

One list for the whole game, not one per level. A model is a global asset: 226_01_1 is the same ceiling fitting in all fourteen missions, and it binds the same textures in every one of them — verified for every model the game names a light, across all fourteen. Nothing about a lamp changes between missions, so keying this by mission only meant re-stating the same answer up to fourteen times and, in practice, forgetting it thirteen: the file named ten models for mission 1 and left every other level to the detector alone.

Additive, not exclusive. Naming a model here makes it a lamp; it does not switch the detector off for everything else. A fitting modelled INTO a building shell — a garage's ceiling strip, an elevator car's light — has no model of its own to name and is still found by shape, so the two run together. lamp: false is how a detection that fires on the wrong thing is struck out without touching any code.

A model is not all lamp. A vending machine is a cabinet with one lit panel and a monitor is a desk with a screen on it, so an entry names which of the model's sub-meshes emit, by the texture each draws with. Naming none lets the brightest sub-mesh be chosen, which is right for a fitting whose glass is plainly its brightest part and wrong for the two cases above — hence the option.
Data rather than code, and loaded the way the material and fog files are, so a level can be re-judged by editing a file rather than by rebuilding.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhotocells
member.summary: The photocells that put a level's lamps on at dusk and off at dawn.

remarks.para: A lamp that follows the daylight is not switched by the clock but by how light it is, through a sensor with a threshold, a delay and a dead band -- and it is the spread in those three that makes a real dusk look the way it does: a few lamps blink on while the sky still glows, then most of a yard in a ragged run over a minute or so, then a straggler well after dark. Every lamp switching at one sun height reads as a level being toggled.

So the lamps are wired into circuits, as a real site is. Lamps that stand near one another share one: one photocell and one contactor, so they get their supply at the same moment and then each takes its own time to strike. Some fittings carry a cell of their own, and switch alone. Each circuit has its own threshold -- a dirty cell, one shaded by a wall, one facing the last of the western sky -- a dead band above it so a cloud passing at dusk does not flick the yard off and on, and a reaction delay re-rolled every time it trips. On top of that every lamp adds a little jitter of its own.

The light it is given is the sine of the sun's elevation, so the thresholds are sun heights: a threshold of nought trips as the sun touches the horizon. That keeps the spread honest at any speed the clock runs: the same ragged dusk takes a minute of a forty-minute day, and a fraction of a second of the scrub keys, without either one needing to be tuned for.
It only ever touches , the daylight's side of each circuit. The wall switches and the faults stay the player's.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhotocells.NewCircuit(System.UInt32@)
member.summary: Wires a new circuit: its photocell's thresholds and its own generator.

remarks.para: A street-lighting photocell switches on at a few tens of lux, and most of these trip with the sun between the horizon and four degrees over it. That is earlier than a real cell would, on purpose: the picture is dark well before the sun is under -- by the time it touched the horizon the yard read as night -- and circuits that waited for four degrees under left lamps dark in a dark yard for a minute of the day's clock. About one in eight is an early one -- shaded, or dirty enough to read dusk an hour soon -- and comes on with the sun still several degrees up, which is the lamp somebody always notices burning in daylight.
The dead band is a couple of times the switch-on light, as on real cells, so the morning trips at a higher sun than the evening did.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhotocells.ReactionDelay(System.UInt32@,System.Boolean)
member.summary: How long a circuit's photocell waits after it trips before its contactor closes or opens.
member.remarks: Real cells are built to wait, so a car's headlights do not put a street out. Mostly a second or two here; about one trip in ten is a lazy one that takes a few seconds more, which is the circuit still dark after its neighbours are lit. It took up to fourteen, which in a yard already dark read as a lamp that was broken rather than late.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics
member.summary: The curves a lamp moves along: how it goes out, how it comes on, and how a failing one stutters.
member.remarks: Static, and working on one lamp's state at a time, so that keeps the switches, the supply and the order lamps are stepped in, and this keeps the physics of a fitting. Every draw comes from the lamp's own generator, in the order the board always drew them, and every sound is raised into the board's list at the instant the light does the thing it is the sound of.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.FlashSeconds
member.summary: How long a tube's flash holds, in seconds, once the starter opens.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.DipEndSeconds
member.summary: When a tube's flash has dropped back nearly dark, as the arc settles or fails.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.Cooling(System.Single)
member.summary: How much of its output a lamp still gives out, this long after the current stopped.

remarks.para: Two decays added, because a fitting going out has two things happening in it and they run at very different rates. Most of the light stops within a couple of mains cycles — an arc extinguishes, a filament's surface cools — and that is the fast term, around 35 ms. What is left is thermal mass and phosphor persistence, and it lingers for a fifth of a second as the ember or the afterglow everybody has seen and nobody would describe.
A single exponential gets the timing right and the LOOK wrong: it is either fast enough to be a snap or slow enough to be a dissolve, and never both. The sum is what reads as a light going out.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.Warming(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LampEvent})
member.summary: How far into coming back on a lamp is, from nought to one.

remarks.para: A tube does not fade up. It draws a dim glow across the cathodes, strikes — one hard flash, far brighter than the dim it came from — drops nearly dark again as the arc settles, and only then climbs to full over a few tenths of a second as the mercury warms. That sequence is the whole reason a switched-on lamp reads as a lamp; a linear ramp reads as a slider being dragged.

Not every fitting does it, so not every lamp here does: a fixture whose generator says otherwise simply warms, the way a filament does. A corridor whose lamps all strike in the same way at the same moment is the artefact that says a single effect is being played on all of them.
The sounds are raised from here, at the instant the light does the thing they are the sound of.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.Striking(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LampEvent},System.Single)
member.summary: A tube on a glow starter coming on: preheat, flash, and as many goes as it takes.

remarks.para: The starter is a little neon bulb with a bimetal strip in it. It glows, the strip warms and closes, current heats the tube's cathodes -- the dim orange glow at each end -- and then the strip cools and springs open, and the choke's kick across the tube is the flash. If the arc holds, that is the lamp lit; if not, the starter closes again and the whole thing repeats. A warm tube on a good starter catches first time in a tenth of a second. A cold one at dusk often does not: a second go, a third, now and then a tube that blinks half a dozen times before it holds, which is the one everybody notices.
And it does not catch at full. Cold mercury is thin vapour, so a tube lit after a day standing dark comes up at half or two thirds of its brightness and creeps the rest of the way over a few seconds.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.Igniting(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LampEvent},System.Single)
member.summary: A discharge lantern coming on: the ignitor's crackle, a dim arc, and a long climb.

remarks.para: A sodium or metal-halide lamp has no cathodes to warm. An ignitor fires pulses of a few kilovolts across the tube, every half-cycle of the mains, until the gas breaks down -- an audible crackle and nothing much to see but a faint spitting -- and then the arc holds in the starting gas, dim and the wrong colour, and climbs as the metal in the tube vaporises. A real one takes minutes. This takes seconds, because a dusk the player is watching is not minutes long, but keeps the shape: dim at first, then most of the way quite quickly, then the last of it slowly.
A cold tube does not always break down on the first burst, and the ignitor pauses and tries again.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.WarmingTint(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@)
member.summary: What colour a lamp coming on gives out, before it is giving out its own.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.RollStrike(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@)
member.summary: Rolls one go of a tube's starter: how long it preheats, and how bright the flash is.
member.remarks: A cold starter's bimetal takes far longer to close and open than a warm one's, which is the long orange-ended pause before a tube at dusk first blinks. A flash that fails is a weaker one -- the arc barely formed -- and the one that takes is the full flash.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.ColdStrikeAttempts(System.UInt32@)
member.summary: How many times a cold tube's starter fails before it catches.
member.remarks: Mostly none or one. Now and then a tube is stubborn and blinks several times over a few seconds, and that rare one is worth more to the scene than any amount of the common case.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampPhysics.StepBroken(OpenIGI.Game.World.Lamp@,System.Single)
member.summary: Advances a failing lamp, in the phase it is currently stuck in.

remarks.para: A broken fluorescent is not noise. It is a loop of four recognisable states — a dim glow at the cathodes, a burst of rapid restrikes, a stretch of running unsteadily, and darkness — and what makes it read as broken rather than as a flicker shader is that the durations are wildly uneven and the transitions are not a cycle. Random per frame gives white noise, which looks like a fault in the renderer; this looks like a fault in the lamp.
Every phase's brightness is a function of the phase's own clock, never of the frame, so the same fault plays out identically whatever the frame rate is.

member.returns: when the lamp has just begun a burst of restrikes, which is heard.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard
member.summary: The switch on the wall for every lamp a level has, and the filament behind it.

remarks.para: says where a level's lamps are and how bright they would be; this says which of them are currently giving that out. Everything downstream — the punctual lights in the deferred pass, the emission on the fixture geometry, the emitters the surface cache bounces off — multiplies by , so the three can never disagree about whether a lamp is on. A lamp that lights a floor without glowing reads as a room lit by nothing; a lamp that glows without lighting reads as a decal. The same holds while it is switching.

Nothing here happens instantly. A light switch is a step function and a light is not: a real fitting takes a couple of hundred milliseconds to die and rather longer to come back, and it is the SHAPE of those two curves that makes the difference read as a lamp rather than as a texture being swapped. The curves are in and and each is documented with what it is modelling.

Everything is driven from a seconds delta and a per-lamp deterministic generator — never from the frame counter — so a lamp behaves the same at 30 fps and at 300, and so a row of ceiling tubes does not strike, stutter and fail in unison. That last part matters more than it sounds: identical flicker across six fixtures reads as one shader effect, not as six broken tubes.

Two things decide whether a lamp is fed, and this keeps them apart. The wall switch is the player's (); the supply is the daylight's (), which a photocell closes at dusk and opens at dawn. They are in series, as in a real installation: a lamp somebody switched off stays off when night falls, and comes on by itself at dusk if they switch it back on during the day. A lamp the supply brings up starts COLD -- it has stood dark all day -- and that start is longer and less certain than flicking a switch on a lamp that was lit a minute ago.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.IgnitorSeconds

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.SetSupply(System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Closes or opens the daylight's side of a lamp's circuit, the way a photocell does.
member.param: The fixture's index.
Whether the supply is to be on.

remarks.para: Nothing happens to the light of a lamp somebody has switched off at the wall -- the supply is on the far side of the switch -- but the supply is remembered, so switching it back on later finds it lit or dark as the daylight says.

A lamp brought up this way starts cold: a tube may need several goes of its starter and then glows short of full for a few seconds while it warms, and a discharge lantern's ignitor may crackle more than once before the arc holds, after which it climbs to full over many seconds rather than a fraction of one. That is the start a lamp gets after standing dark all day, and it is most of what makes a dusk read as lamps rather than as a switch being thrown.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.SetSupplyImmediately(System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Sets the daylight's side of a lamp's circuit with no transition at all.
member.param: The fixture's index.
Whether the supply is to be on.
member.remarks: For a level opening, which has to open with its lamps already in the state its hour puts them in: a night mission whose every lamp strikes as the first frame appears, or a noon whose outdoor lamps fade out over the loading screen, is the lamps visibly reacting to the level being loaded rather than to the time of day. Silent, for the same reason.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.TintOf(System.Int32)
member.summary: Returns what to multiply a lamp's colour by while it is cooling.
member.param: The fixture's index.
member.returns: A multiplier per channel; white whenever the lamp is not cooling.

remarks.para: A filament does not merely get dimmer when the current stops — it gets COLDER, and a colder black body is redder. The last thing anyone sees of a lamp being switched off is a brief orange ember, and leaving it out makes the fade read as an opacity ramp rather than as a light going out.

Applied to the cast light only, because the geometry's emission is a scalar multiple of the surface's own albedo and has no channel to carry a tint. By the time the shift is strong the lamp is at a few per cent of its output and its panel contributes nothing to the frame, so the two disagreeing there is not visible; at the start of the fade, where the panel is still bright, the shift is nearly nothing and they agree.

And a lamp coming on is not its own colour yet either. A tube's cathodes glow orange before the arc strikes; a discharge lantern's arc starts in the wrong gas -- the pink-red of a sodium lamp's neon starter fill, the blue-green of a metal-halide's mercury -- and only reaches its own colour as it reaches its own brightness. Under the same reasoning as the ember, the light carries it and the fixture does not.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.Switch(System.Int32)
member.summary: Switches a lamp off, or a switched-off one back on.
member.param: The fixture's index.
member.returns: The mode the lamp is now in.

remarks.para: A broken lamp switches off like any other, and comes back broken: the switch and the fault are different facts about the fitting, and pulling the breaker does not repair a tube.
Switched on while the daylight has its supply off, the lamp stays dark and will light when the supply comes on; switched off, it stays off whatever the supply does.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.Break(System.Int32)

member.remarks: Breaking a lamp that is switched off arms the fault without switching it on — it will flicker when somebody turns it back on, which is how a failing tube actually announces itself.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard.TryPick(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double,System.Int32@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Finds the lamp the crosshair is on.
member.param: Where the view is, in world metres.
The way it looks. Need not be normalised.
How far to look, in metres.
Receives the fixture's index.
Receives how far along the ray it stands, in metres.
member.returns: when a lamp is under the crosshair.

remarks.para: Against the fixtures rather than against the geometry, because a fixture is what there is to switch: the extractor merges a lamp's triangles into one light wherever they stand, and a ray test against the housing's mesh would find the model the lamp is part of rather than the lamp.

Nearest along the ray wins rather than closest to its axis. That is what a crosshair means — the thing in front — and it is also the only rule that stays stable as the view turns, since a tie-break on angle swaps between two lamps for a sub-pixel movement of the mouse.
It answers nothing about what stands between: a wall is not in the fixture list. The caller casts against the world to check that, which it can do because it already has the level's collision.

member.summary: Finds the lamp nearest a point, for binding a placement's glowing geometry to a light.
member.param: Where to look from, in world metres.
How far to accept, in metres.
member.returns: The fixture's index, or -1 when nothing is near enough.
member.remarks: The fixture list is the merged conclusion about a level's lamps and the placement list is the level's own; there is no key joining them, because a fixture can be the emissive faces of several placements at once and a placement can be nowhere near the fixture its texture contributed to. Proximity is what actually relates them, and it is exact enough: two lamps closer together than this were merged into one fixture in the first place.

member.summary: One simulation tick of the level as the original runs it: a single depth-first walk of the task tree in authored order, each task running its own update -- which decides whether, and when, its children run.

remarks.para: The original has no grouped passes: Flow_Update walks the root's children, and a type that wants its subtree to tick walks its own children from inside its update (Task_UpdateChildren, 0x488700), before, after or in the middle of its own work. So a task reads this tick's state from everything before it in the tree and last tick's from everything after.

It is I.G.I.'s . Subsystems bind the update of the tasks they own; a task nobody bound behaves as a plain container and walks its children -- except Static and Idle, whose update is a no-op in the original, freezing everything beneath them. A runs the shared handler under the first game's rules (). Unlike I.G.I. 2's run, the walk does not pass over a task already marked deleted.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixture
member.summary: One light a level appears to have, proposed by reading where its emissive geometry stands.

remarks.para: This is a proposal, not a declaration. I.G.I. declares no point lights at all, so nothing in the level data corresponds to this type — it is the conclusion of two inferences stacked on each other. infers which textures the artists treated as sources, from how bright they painted the lightmaps around them; then infers a light from every place such a texture is drawn. Both steps produce a list for someone to look at rather than an answer to be trusted, and a fixture that turns out to be a reflective sign rather than a lamp is a normal outcome, not a bug.

Everything but is soft. The centroid of a lamp's triangles is a fact about the geometry and is as exact as the transform that produced it. and are not facts about anything: they are what a plausible light of this size and colour would do, from a formula with a tunable constant in it. They exist so the list can be loaded and looked at, and they are expected to be edited afterwards.
A default-constructed is the zero instance — no texture, no area, at the world origin — and never something the extractor produces.

member.param: The emitter texture that contributed most of this fixture's area, as the pack names it. A cluster can draw with more than one emitter texture, so this identifies the dominant one rather than the only one.
The centroid of the cluster's triangles, in world space and in metres.
How far the light is proposed to reach, in metres. Derived from and the colour's luminance — see DefaultRadiusScale for the derivation and for how arbitrary the constant in it is.
The light's colour, linear and normalised so the brightest channel is around one. Supplied to the extractor per texture; white when the caller had nothing better.
The total surface area of the cluster's triangles, in square metres. The emitting area, which is what makes a strip light stronger than a bulb.
The radius in metres of the smallest sphere about containing every vertex of the cluster — the fixture's own size, as distinct from the size of the region it lights.
How many emitter triangles were merged into this fixture. Carried for review: a fixture built from one stray triangle deserves more suspicion than one built from a whole lamp housing.

The way the fixture faces, as a unit vector in world space, or zero when it does not face anywhere in particular.
A lamp is not a bare bulb hanging in a void: it is a housing with an opening, and it throws its light out of that opening and nowhere else. A ceiling tube lights the floor under it and leaves the slab it is bolted to dark. Treating every fixture as an omnidirectional point is what puts a bright disc on the ceiling above every lamp in the level — light appearing on the one surface that is physically behind the emitter — and it is visible from anywhere in the room.
So this is the area-weighted average of the fixture's own face normals, flipped downward: it is where the geometry looks, measured from the geometry. Zero is honest and not a failure — a lamp modelled as a closed box has normals that cancel, and a fixture that cannot say which way it faces is better lit as a point than as a spot pointing at a guess.

The long axis of the fixture's emitting face, a unit vector square to , or zero for a fixture that faces nowhere.
A fitting is a rectangle, not a disc: a fluorescent batten is over a metre long and a hand wide. Its shadow rays are aimed at points on THAT rectangle, as a rect light is sampled on its own area. Aimed at a disc a quarter of a metre across instead, half the points hung in the air beside the glass, and from a wall at a grazing angle each frame's rays clipped the housing or not at random -- the black speckle under every ceiling and beside every lit panel.
Half the emitting face's extent along , in metres.
Half the emitting face's extent across it, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixture.Intensity
member.summary: Gets how much light the fixture is proposed to emit, in relative units.

remarks.para: The emitting area weighted by the colour's luminance, which is the power a Lambertian emitter of unit radiance would put out. It is deliberately relative: the retail data records no radiance anywhere, so there is no absolute value to recover, and the only honest thing to report is the ratio between one proposed fixture and another. A renderer scales the whole set by one number it picks by eye.
Derived rather than stored, so that it cannot drift out of step with the area and colour it is computed from.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor
member.summary: Proposes where a level's lights are, by finding every place it draws a texture the artists treated as a source.

remarks.para: Where this sits. answers "which textures are lights" and stops there — on level 1 it answers 236_01_1, thirty uses, baked pure white on every one. That is a name, not a place. This is the other half: given the names, walk the level's placements and their geometry the same way the survey does, take every triangle whose subset draws with one of those textures, and put it in world space. What comes out is a cloud of triangles that are lamps, and the remaining question is how many lamps.

Why clustering is the whole problem. A single wall lamp is a dozen triangles, and averaging all of a texture's triangles together would put one light in the middle of the level. Averaging none of them would put a light on every triangle, which for a strip light is a row of a hundred overlapping sources costing a hundred times what one costs. The useful answer is between the two, and it is found by asking which triangles are near enough to be the same object — see for what "near enough" means and why it is a gap rather than a size.

The output is a starting list for a human to review. This inherits the survey's stance deliberately, and stacks another inference on top of it: the survey says which textures are worth looking at, and this says where each one is drawn — neither says that the thing found is a lamp. A bright reflective sign, a window frame catching the sun in the bake, a decal on a crate: all of them come out of here as proposed fixtures, and someone still has to look. Hence
rather than Find, and hence being carried through to the reviewer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.DefaultClusterDistance
member.summary: How far apart two emitter triangles may be and still belong to the same fixture, in metres.

remarks.para: This is a gap, not a size. Triangles are joined transitively, so a fluorescent tube five metres long stays one fixture as long as no two consecutive triangles along it are further apart than this. What the threshold has to separate is the gap within one lamp from the gap between two lamps — and those two distances are far apart in these levels. A lamp housing's triangles are tens of centimetres from each other at most; two lamps face each other across a corridor several metres wide, or sit a bay apart along a wall.

1.5 m sits in that gap with room on both sides, and errs towards splitting rather than merging. That is the safer direction: two proposed lights where there is one is visible in a review and costs a duplicate, whereas one light hovering in the middle of a room because two wall lamps merged looks perfectly reasonable in the list and wrong in the frame.

The known limit of measuring between centroids. The distance is between triangle centres, not between their surfaces, so a single triangle spanning much more than the threshold reads as far from its own neighbour — a four-metre panel modelled as two triangles has 1.9 m between their centroids and splits in half. Accounting for each triangle's own size would fix that at the cost of an unbounded search radius in the grid below, and the geometry that provokes it is rare: lamps are small, and large emissive panels in these levels are tessellated. It is left as it is, and the threshold is a parameter for the level where it is not.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.DefaultRadiusScale
member.summary: How far a fixture's light reaches, as a multiple of the fixture's own radius.

remarks.para: The radius is extent × scale × √luminance, and the square root is the one part of it that is derived rather than chosen. Cut an inverse-square falloff off at a fixed threshold and the cut-off distance goes as the square root of the emitted power; power goes as area times radiance, so a fixture twice as bright reaches √2 times as far. Scaling on the fixture's own extent rather than on its area then keeps a long thin strip light from claiming the reach of a compact source with the same total area.

The multiplier itself is a guess. The retail data records no radiance for any of this — the bakes are the only evidence, and they record where the light landed rather than how strong it was. 12 puts a typical wall fixture, a quarter of a metre across, in charge of the three or four metres around it, which is about what the lightmaps in those corridors show. It is a number to start looking from, not a measurement, and it is a parameter for that reason.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.MinimumRadius
member.summary: The smallest influence radius any proposed fixture is given, in metres.
member.remarks: A floor rather than a correction. A lamp modelled as a single small quad has an extent of a few centimetres, and the scaled radius would then be smaller than the lamp's own housing — a light that lights nothing, which reads in a review as "the extractor missed it" rather than as "the geometry is small". Two metres is close enough to nothing that a false positive stays cheap.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.PlacedMesh
member.summary: One drawable mesh and where in the world it stands.
member.remarks: Plain geometry and a transform, rather than a . A placement names a MefModel, a type only a real pack file can construct, so a test that wanted to check the arithmetic would first have to load a level. Taking the mesh and the transform directly puts every decision this class makes — which triangles count, where they land, how they group — behind an argument a test can build by hand, and leaves the scene walk with nothing in it but a loop.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.ToWorld(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.PlacedMesh@)
member.summary: Takes a model-space position into world space.
member.remarks: The same composition uses, and it has to stay the same: a fixture placed by a different convention from the one the renderer draws its own lamp with sits somewhere the player can see is wrong. The orientation is orthonormal and applied as a row-vector multiply, so drawing with it means transposing it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Cluster(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Triangle},System.Single)
member.summary: Groups triangles that are near enough to each other to be one fixture.

remarks.para: Union-find over a spatial hash. The grid's cells are exactly the joining distance across, so every triangle near enough to join is in this cell or one of the twenty-six around it, and the pass costs a constant per triangle instead of the square of the count. Nothing more elaborate earns its keep here: the input is the few hundred triangles a level's lamps amount to, not the level.

Joining is transitive by construction, which is the property that makes the threshold a statement about gaps rather than about sizes — a long fixture stays whole however much longer it is than the distance, provided it has no hole in it that big.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Describe(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Triangle},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32},System.Func{System.String,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f},System.Single)
member.summary: Turns one cluster of triangles into the fixture it proposes.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.EmittingRect(System.Collections.Generic.List{OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Triangle},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32},OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Measures the rectangle a facing fixture emits from.

remarks.para: The long axis is the principal axis of the cluster's vertices in the plane square to the facing, each triangle's corners weighted by a third of its area, so a batten's rect runs along its tube whatever angle it was placed at. The half-extents are how far the vertices reach along that axis and across it, measured from the fixture's centroid -- the point the lamp is lit from -- so the rect covers the glass the light comes out of and nothing beside it.
Nothing for a fixture that faces nowhere: the renderer lights and shadows that as a point.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Facing(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double)
member.summary: Turns a cluster's summed face normals into the direction it throws its light.

remarks.para: Zero unless the faces agree. The sum of the cross products is area-weighted by construction, so its length against the summed lengths says how much of the fixture's surface points one way: a flat tube's underside is near one, and a lamp modelled as a CLOSED BOX is near nought, because its top cancels its bottom exactly. That second case is not a failure to fix, it is the geometry saying this fixture has no single face — and the honest answer is no direction, which the renderer lights as a point rather than as a spot aimed at a guess.

Turned downward where it points up, because a fixture is mounted on something. The winding this is derived from is not consistently outward in this game's models — the ceiling lamp and the ceiling it hangs from can disagree — so the sign carries no information and the mounting does: a lamp lights the room, never the slab it is bolted to. For a fixture whose normal is near horizontal, a wall bracket, the flip barely moves it, which is the right amount of opinion to have about a case this evidence cannot settle.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.Dominant(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.ValueTuple{System.String,System.Double,System.Int32}})
member.summary: Picks the texture that contributed most of a cluster's area.
member.remarks: Clusters span textures rather than being built per texture, and this is the consequence. A fixture is a place, and a lamp whose glass and whose housing are two different emitter textures is one lamp — clustering each texture separately would propose two lights standing inside each other, which is both wrong and expensive. The cost is that a fixture can only name one texture as its origin, and the largest contributor is the most useful one to name when a reviewer goes looking for the thing in the level.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureExtractor.MountFinder
member.summary: Finds what a fixture with no facing of its own is mounted on, and faces it away from that.

remarks.para: A round wall lamp is a dome, its faces as much one way as another, so rightly cannot read a direction off it and the renderer lights it as a point. But a lamp bolted to a wall gives the wall's far side none of its light, and a point does: on the software path a point lamp's cube of maps draws nothing nearer than its near plane, which has to clear the fitting's own housing, so the wall a hand's breadth behind it was not drawn either -- and mission 1's round lamps inside the security building lit the plinth, the column and the canopy's edge outside it, where the traced shadow had them dark. Facing away from its wall, the lamp lights its room and nothing behind it, on both paths.

The wall is read from the level rather than from the fitting's winding, which this game's models do not keep consistent: the nearest surface of any OTHER placement within the fitting's own size of its centre. Only a wall or a ceiling counts. A lamp standing on a desk or a floor keeps lighting as a point, which is what a bulb on a stand does.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureStore
member.summary: Reads and writes a mission's proposed list beside its other authored data.

remarks.para: The fixtures are an inference -- see and -- and the whole point of writing them down is that the inference can be looked at and corrected. A level that lights a reflective sign as though it were a lamp is fixed by opening this file and deleting a line, not by editing the extractor. So the file wins over the survey whenever it exists, exactly the way authored material detail wins over the detail derived from a texture: the survey runs once to propose the list, and from then on the file is the truth.

Writing the file also takes the emissive survey's lightmap decode off the load path. The survey exists to propose the list the first time; once the list is written, a load reads it and never touches a lightmap for this.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixtureStore.Version
member.summary: What this file's shape and the detection behind it are worth.

remarks.para: A file is a CACHE of an inference as much as it is a place to correct one, and the two pull in opposite directions: an edited file must survive, and a file written by a detector that has since been improved must not. The version settles it. Raise it whenever the detection changes in a way that would give a level different lamps, and every stale file is re-surveyed once and rewritten; leave it alone for a change that would not, and every edit anyone has made is kept.

6: the hand-written manifest covers the whole game rather than mission 1 alone, so every level gets the fittings and the lit panels only mission 1 had been given. 5: nothing is inferred to be a lamp unless it is skinned with one of the texture pages the level's own catalogued fittings draw from, which drops 263 of the 423 sub-meshes the shape test had been proposing across the fourteen levels — every soldier, chair, camera and bracket among them. 4 gave each lamp sub-mesh its own emissive strength, so one texture can be a floodlight on one model and a reading lamp on another. 3 moved emission from the texture to the sub-mesh, 2 added the direction a fixture faces, and version 1 was a bare array — which is what an absent version reads as. 7 added the emitting rectangle (long axis and half-extents) the lamp's shadow rays are aimed at. 8 faces a fitting with no facing of its own away from the wall or ceiling it is mounted on.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightmapBake
member.summary: A path-traced object-lightmap bake running on a worker, and the hand-off of its finished pages to the render thread.

remarks.para: The bake -- direct sun, sky and several bounces of indirect over every lightmapped surface -- takes seconds. Run inline during a level load that already owns a live window it is not a stall but a hang: the process stops answering and the driver takes the context away, exactly as the probe bake found (). So the tracing runs off the main thread and the frames keep going.

The texel maps and the triangle BVH are built by the caller on the main thread, because resolving each surface's albedo reads the resource registry the render thread also uses. Everything the worker does -- tracing against the collision cast and the triangle BVH, then compositing -- reads only immutable data and the shut-doors cast, both safe to touch while the game runs. The upload stays on the render thread: hands back plain pixel arrays for the device to turn into textures.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightmapBaker
member.summary: Bakes path-traced object lightmaps: per-texel, coloured, multi-bounce indirect for the static world.

remarks.para: The successor to . That volume bake has a hard quality ceiling -- it traces the colourless collision mesh and stores a low-frequency grey L1-SH field at metre spacing, so its bounce is monochrome, flat and coarse. This bakes into the meshes' own lightmap UV channel (the second UV set format-1 and format-3 meshes carry), so every texel is a real surface point that can be path traced to a coloured, high-resolution, multi-bounce answer. It is the right trade for I.G.I.: the geometry is static and the sun is fixed per mission, so the whole thing bakes once and is cached.

Phase 1 (this file): coloured geometry and the texel map. For every lightmapped surface it rasterises the draw record's triangles into its lightmap page's UV space and records, per covered texel, the world position and normal it belongs to -- the map every later phase traces from. The tracing (direct sun and sky, then the multi-bounce colour bleed), the BVH it traces against, seam dilation and the runtime swap are the following phases. A is here so the texel map can be verified on its own -- a correct one reads as a UV-space unwrap of the object with its world normals -- before any light is traced.

member.summary: Smooths the baked radiance with an edge-aware à-trous filter, taming the ray tracer's noise.
member.param: The baked targets, their filled.
How many à-trous passes, each at twice the previous spacing.
How far, in metres, radiance is allowed to blur across a flat surface.
