remarks.para: A per-texel Monte-Carlo estimate is noisy, and more rays only buy so much before the cost is not worth it; the standard answer a baker reaches for is a denoise that averages a texel with its neighbours but refuses to blur across the geometry the atlas packs side by side. This is that: a joint bilateral à-trous, weighting each neighbour by the B3-spline kernel, by how near it sits in the WORLD (so two islands that touch in the atlas but face different walls do not bleed into each other), and by how alike its normal is (so a convex edge stays an edge). Uncovered texels are left alone and never contribute.
Runs on the bake worker after the bounces and before the pages are composited, so the smoothing is baked into the cached result and costs nothing at runtime.

member.param: Where the pages are filtered: all at once where the scheduler can, a page a slice where not.
Stops the filter part-way, for a level left during its bake.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LightmapBvh.Narrow(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Narrows a ray's live range to one slab of a box.
member.remarks:
The NaN case is a real bug this had, not a hypothetical. A ray parallel to an axis has a zero in that component of its direction, so the reciprocal is an infinity; if its origin also lies exactly on one of the box's two planes for that axis, the extent is zero and the product is zero times infinity, which is NaN. and propagate NaN, so the range came back NaN, the final comparison was false, and the node was rejected — the traversal quietly discarded geometry the ray genuinely meets.
Checked against a full search over every triangle, that lost 240 of 3,456 axis-aligned rays: a ray fired straight down from just above the ground reported open sky. In a bake that is a texel lit that should have been shadowed, on a level whose architecture is almost entirely axis-aligned, in a result that is cached and never compared against anything.
A ray in that position lies exactly on the boundary of the slab, so the slab constrains nothing and the axis is skipped. Erring towards keeping the node is the safe direction: a node kept costs a triangle test, a node dropped costs the hit.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedMission.PacksInLoadOrder
member.summary: Gets every pack the mission has open, in the order the game opens them.

remarks.para: Project I.G.I. opens two — a per-location common pack and the level's — and a mission that names no list falls back to exactly those, in that order, which is what it has always used.

I.G.I. 2 opens four, and that is read rather than assumed: Game_CreateHandler (igi2ed 0x4469A0) calls MTP_Load five times, for common, new, the location's, the level's and finally editor — the last under a "Loading editor..." caption and from LOCAL:editor/, so it is the editor's own and no part of the game. The first four are the game's, in that order, and MTP_VirModel_GetPtr returns the first match walking from the head, so the common pack shadows the level's rather than the other way about.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedPack
member.summary: A pack opened and bound: its .mtp tables, its models keyed by name, and the archives its textures live in.

remarks.para: This is Pack_Open (0x4CEFA0) followed by Pack_Bind (0x4CF080): load <dir>textures/<name>.res and <dir>models/<name>.res into the resource registry, then walk the pack's INST records resolving each instance's model and per-slot textures.

Models are keyed by the bare name because that is the id space MODS defines, and the archive's own entry order is not that order. The original leans on the resource registry for the same effect: exploding models/<pack>.res registers each model under LOCAL:models/<name>.mef, which is exactly the key Model_Load then asks for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedPack.AnimationSetRoot
member.summary: The directory a pack's BANM animation sets load from.
member.remarks: Not the pack's own directory: 0x4CF910 prefers a second root whenever it is non-empty, and Mission_Load pins that root to the literal "LOCAL:common/" (0x415C92) before either pack opens. The shipped sets are at common/anims/; the pack directories hold no anims/ at all.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedPack.PackAnimationSetRoot
member.summary: The name a set carries when the pack's own models archive is where it lives.

remarks.para: I.G.I. 2 ships no loose .iff anywhere and has no common/anims/ directory at all: its bone animations are entries in the same common/models/<pack>.res the meshes come from, named LOCAL:anims/<set>.iff, and the archive registers them under exactly that name. common.res holds 254 of them beside its 466 models and new.res holds 990 and nothing else — the two counts the pack's own BANM list names.

The two games also split them differently. Project I.G.I. ships one file per skeleton with every clip inside it, which is why its player is built from 000.iff alone; the sequel ships one file per clip — 005_02.iff, 005_03.iff — and no whole-skeleton file exists to read. Assembling a skeleton's clips into one set is character work and belongs with it; what happens here is only that the clips are found and parsed instead of being reported absent.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedPack.TryGetTextureName(System.String,System.Int32,System.String@)
member.summary: Resolves the diffuse texture a draw record samples, for a model named directly.
member.param: The model's name, as level data spells it.
The draw record's material slot.
Receives the texture's bare name.
member.returns: when nothing in the pack answers for that model and slot.

remarks.para: A material belongs to an instance, not to a mesh — the slot indexes the instance's own material range — so a caller holding only a name has to find the instance that uses it. Both spellings resolve: a name that is itself an instance's, and a name that is the mesh an instance points at. Level data uses the first for placed objects and the second for a forest stand, whose Model parameter names the tree mesh.

The first instance using a mesh wins. Two instances of one mesh with different materials would be two differently textured objects, and nothing in the retail data does that for the meshes reached this way — a tree is a tree.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.LodModelChain
member.summary: A model name resolved to its chain of detail levels — the original's "LOD virtual model".

remarks.para: 0x4CED50 builds one of these by loading the requested name and then incrementing the last character of the name and loading again, stopping at the first name that does not resolve or once it has five. So 435_01_1 pulls in 435_01_2 through 435_01_5, and a name ending in something other than a digit still works because the step is character arithmetic, not a parse.
This matters well beyond drawing: every level is baked one lightmap per level of detail, so the length of this chain is what decides how many .olm entries an object contributes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MagicGunMount
member.summary: The authored limits of a gun a vehicle model carries (TASKTYPE_AISTATIONARYGUN).

remarks.para: A tank's cannon, its coaxial machine gun, an APC's gun and a helicopter's nose gun are not authored in a mission script. They are attachments of the vehicle's model, and DefineMagicObj gives each one a longer argument list that 0x46FA50 parses: the weapon's model, the arc and pitch limits, the ammunition, both turn rates, the turning sound, a barrel spin rate and a minimum range.

The weapon is found by that model name, not by a WEAPON_ID_*: the gun's constructor (0x46EAE0) hands it to 0x413C00, which returns the weapon row whose model string matches. So 614_03_1 is the T80 cannon, 123_01_1 the M2HB, 601_05_1 the APC gun and 700_12_1 the helicopter's MIL gun.

member.param: The weapon row's model name (argument 3).
How far either side of the mount the gun may turn (argument 4, +40); 360 or more turns freely.
The highest elevation (argument 5, +32).
The lowest elevation (argument 6, +36).
The rounds the gun carries (argument 7, +44).
How fast the barrel elevates (argument 8, +48, stored per tick).
How fast the gun traverses (argument 9, +52, stored per tick).
The looping sound while the gun turns (argument 10, +56).
The barrel spin added on each firing tick (argument 11, +88, stored per tick).
The gun holds fire at anything closer (argument 12, +92, stored in world units).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MagicObjectRegistry
member.summary: The magic-object table: the map from a model attachment's name to the object that hangs off it.

remarks.para: This is what makes a level bigger than its script. 0x4DFA50 walks the attachments of every placed model, looks each name up here, and spawns a child object carrying the definition's model at the attachment's position and orientation — then does the same to that model's own attachments. A level-1 garage whose script node has no children at all still ends up with 64 pieces this way.
The table is filled by running magicobj/magicobj.qvm, which is nothing but 387 DefineMagicObj(name, model, TASKTYPE_*) calls.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MefMeshBuilder
member.summary: Turns a loaded .mef model into buffers a graphics device can hold.

remarks.para: The vertex layouts already match — is deliberately the original's 40-byte model vertex — so this is really about the index buffer. A model's draw records index its vertices two different ways depending on the mesh format: a lightmapped model's indices are relative to the record's base vertex, the other two formats index the whole array. Flattening resolves both to absolute indices in one buffer, and each record becomes a naming its range and its material slot.

The material slot is carried through rather than resolved here: a slot names a position in the instance's list, so the same model drawn by two instances wears two different sets of textures. Only the caller knows which instance it is drawing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.MefMeshBuilder.RepairWinding(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Vertex3D[],System.UInt16[])
member.summary: Makes every triangle wind to agree with its vertices' own normals, so a front face exists.
member.remarks: Public because it is not only this builder's business: anything that assembles world geometry from a model's raw draw records has the same unwound triangles and must be repaired the same way, or back face culling removes it. Spline segments are bent into shape rather than built here, and were the case that proved it.
member.param: The mesh's vertices, whose normals point out of the surface.
The triangle-list indices, rewound in place.
member.remarks: The flattened draw order does not wind uniformly -- some triangles face out and some in -- which is why the world pass could not cull: culling either facing dropped real walls. But every vertex carries a normal the lighting already trusts, and it points out of the surface. So a triangle's intended front is the side its vertex normals face; where its winding disagrees (its own cross product opposes the vertex normals) the two indices are swapped to bring it into line. With every triangle then wound the same way relative to its outward normal, back-face culling has a consistent facing to remove -- which is what stops a thin object's two coincident faces from fighting over the same pixel, and halves the indoor fill besides. A degenerate triangle, whose cross product is near zero, is left as it is.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MenuStringTable
member.summary: Resolves a menu item's Text Resource key to the localised string it names.

remarks.para: Transcribed from Menu_GetString (0x418EA0). A key is not a label: MenuText carries "Single Player", and the text is fetched from the language archive under LOCAL:<languageDirectory>/<key>, where the directory is the language name. The retail archive is language/<lang>/menusystem.res, whose NAME/CSTR pairs are registered as LOCAL:english/Single Player and so on, so the resource registry resolves them once the archive is registered.

A missing key is not an error. The original formats "RM: <key>" — resource missing — caches it, and draws that on screen. Translators saw the untranslated entries in place rather than a blank menu, and reproducing it keeps a partial language pack usable instead of silently empty.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardAxis
member.summary: Which of the six axis directions a mesh card faces.

remarks.para: A card faces outwards, the way a surface normal does, and the orthographic capture that fills it therefore looks the other way: a card sits above the model and its camera looks down.

The numbering is load-bearing and must not be tidied into something more readable. Opposite directions differ in the low bit alone, so (int)axis ^ 1 is the direction facing the other way and (int)axis / 2 is the axis it lies on. uses both, and so will the shader-side table that indexes the six cards of a model by direction.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCard
member.summary: One oriented rectangle a model is approximated by: an orthographic view of it along one axis, and the page of the surface cache that view is captured into.
member.param: Which of the six directions this card faces.
The centre of the rectangle, in the model's own space. It lies on the face of the model's bounding box that faces , so it is where the capture's near plane sits.
Half the rectangle's extent along .
Half the rectangle's extent along .
How far the model extends behind the card. The capture's orthographic range runs from to , so this is its far plane.
How many texels the card gets along .
How many texels the card gets along .
The fraction of the model's surface that faces this card's axis, in the range 0 to 1. The shares of a model's six directions sum to one.

remarks.para: The surface cache answers a question a triangle mesh cannot answer cheaply: a ray landed here — what does this surface look like and how is it lit? Answering it by finding the triangle and its material means a mesh traversal per ray. Answering it from a card means one projection and one texture fetch, because the model's albedo, normal and depth have already been rendered flat through these six views and left in an atlas.

Six axis-aligned views rather than a fitted set of arbitrarily oriented ones. Fitting would cover a slanted roof with fewer texels, and would cost the lookup its cheapness — an arbitrary card has to be found before it can be sampled, whereas which of six axes a hit normal most faces is three comparisons. This game's architecture is boxes, huts, crates and gantries, which the axis-aligned six fit almost exactly.
A default-constructed is the zero instance — a degenerate card facing +X with no extent and no texels — not a sensible default. They come from .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker
member.summary: Reduces a model to the handful of oriented rectangles the surface cache captures it through.

remarks.para: Every model gets up to six cards, one per axis direction, and each is an orthographic view of the whole model along that axis. A later stage renders albedo, normal and depth through each view into an atlas page; the lighting then runs over those pages rather than over the level's triangles, and a ray that lands anywhere on the model reads its answer out of whichever page faces the way it hit.

The card's rectangle is the model's bounding box projected onto the axis's plane, not a tight fit around the triangles that face that way. The tight fit is the obvious improvement and it is wrong: what the capture renders is the whole model seen from that direction, including every triangle that faces slightly away and every one behind them. Cropping the rectangle to the contributing triangles crops the render, and the surface that falls outside it has no entry in the cache at all — which reads, at trace time, as a hole in the geometry rather than as a slightly worse approximation. A later reader tempted to shrink these rectangles should read this paragraph twice.

A triangle counts towards both directions of the axis it faces. I.G.I.'s models are single-sided art from 2000 — a floor panel is one quad, a wall has no back, and the inside of a hut is the outside's other face. A ray hitting that floor from beneath is a perfectly ordinary event in a bounced-light solution, and if only the direction the normal points had accumulated area then the panel would have a card above it and nothing below, so the ray would find no surface to read. So the area is counted twice, once each way, and a flat panel comes out with a card above and below and none on its four edges — which is exactly the set that describes it.

The normal is the triangle's own, from its winding, not the interpolated vertex normal. Vertex normals in this game's art are smoothed across corners, so the three vertices of a cube's corner triangle point in three different diagonal directions and none of them points at the face the triangle actually lies in. Smoothing is a shading convenience; which way a surface faces is geometry.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker.MinimumResolution
member.summary: The fewest texels a card is given on either in-plane axis.
member.remarks: Below this the capture stops describing the surface and starts describing its average colour. Eight is cheap enough that giving it to a card that barely deserves one costs nothing.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker.MaximumResolution
member.summary: The most texels a card is given on either in-plane axis.
member.remarks: The cap exists because a single card's cost is quadratic in it and because this game's largest models are hangar walls whose texture is a tiling sheet — a page four times the size resolves nothing further, it just repeats the same detail at four times the bandwidth.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker.DefaultTexelsPerUnit
member.summary: How many texels one world unit of a card's surface is given by default.
member.remarks: Calibrated against what these models are, the same way the distance field's resolution was: a crate is about a metre across and a hut about eight, so this gives the crate the floor of eight texels and the hut sixty-four. The surface cache is a source of indirect light, which is low-frequency by nature — bounced light needs to know that a wall is red, not where its rivets are.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker.DefaultMinimumAreaShare
member.summary: The share of a model's surface a direction needs before it is worth a card.
member.remarks: Two percent. A model's six shares sum to one, so a direction that describes nothing at all sits at zero and even a cube's least-represented face sits at a sixth; the threshold only has to separate "a genuine face of this model" from "the four one-quad edges of a floor panel". Set it much higher and the top edge of a wall — a real surface that real light lands on — stops being captured.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshCardBaker.MinimumDepth
member.summary: The shallowest orthographic range a card is given, in world units.
member.remarks: A single quad has no thickness along the axis it faces, and an orthographic volume whose near and far planes coincide has no depth range to rasterise into — the capture would come out empty or, worse, undefined. A centimetre is far below anything this game models and comfortably contains a flat panel.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshDistanceField
member.summary: How far every point in a box around a model is from that model's surface, and which side it is on.

remarks.para: The structure the realtime GI track traces through. A ray marched against triangles has to test every triangle it might cross; a ray marched against a signed distance field asks one question at each step — how far is the nearest surface — and takes a step exactly that long, which cannot overshoot. A ray crossing empty space clears it in a handful of steps regardless of how much geometry is nearby, and that is what makes tracing a whole level affordable.

Dense rather than sparse, deliberately. The usual layout stores only bricks near the surface, because most of a volume around an open-world mesh is empty and storing it is waste. I.G.I.'s models are crates, doors, huts and gantries: at the resolution below a whole model is a few tens of kilobytes, and the entire game's model set is smaller than one of its texture packs. Sparse bricks would buy memory this game does not need and cost an indirection on every one of the millions of samples a frame takes.

Distances are stored as bytes. A sphere trace needs to know how far it may step, not the distance to the millimetre — an error of a fraction of a voxel costs a step, never correctness, and the alternative is four times the memory and four times the bandwidth on the hottest read in the renderer.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshDistanceFieldBaker
member.summary: Turns a model's triangles into the signed distance field the realtime GI track traces through.

remarks.para: Three problems, solved separately because each has a different right answer.

Distance near the surface is exact, and computed the only way it can be: the closest point on every triangle within reach. It is confined to a narrow band around the geometry, because doing it for every voxel is the product of two large numbers and doing it near the surface is the product of two small ones.

Distance far from the surface is propagated outwards from that band by sweeping, rather than measured. A sweep costs one pass over the voxels per direction and gives a distance that is very slightly too large along diagonals — which for a sphere trace is the safe direction to be wrong in only if it is under, so the sweep uses the true diagonal spacing rather than a chamfer approximation and the residual error is a fraction of a voxel.

The sign is the hard part, and the reason is the data. A closed mesh can be tested by casting one ray and counting crossings. I.G.I.'s models are not reliably closed — they are game art from 2000, with open backs, coincident faces and single-sided walls — and one ray through an open mesh gives a confidently wrong answer for an entire column of voxels. So three rays are cast, one down each axis, and the majority wins. A hole has to line up with two axes at once to fool it.

Runs off the render thread. Every level's models together are seconds of work, and the reason that matters is recorded on : a multi-second job on the thread holding a live GL context loses the context to the operating system's watchdog.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshDistanceFieldBaker.DefaultResolution
member.summary: How many voxels the longest axis gets by default.
member.remarks: Chosen against what this game's models are. A crate is a metre across and a hut is eight, and at this resolution both get voxels of a few centimetres — fine enough that a sphere trace lands on the right side of a wall, coarse enough that a level's models fit in a few megabytes.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshDistanceFieldBaker.Propagate(System.Single[],System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Spreads measured distances outwards over the voxels that had none.
member.remarks:
Eight sweeps, one per corner of the grid, each carrying the running minimum along with it. Two sweeps per axis would only propagate along axes; going corner to corner is what lets a distance travel diagonally, which is how most of a volume is actually reached.
The step added between neighbours is the true Euclidean spacing, not the one-per-cell a chamfer transform uses. A sphere trace steps by whatever this says, so a distance reported larger than the truth is a step through a wall — and a chamfer transform's diagonal is exactly that.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MeshRaySearch`1
member.summary: One line's search through one model's collision mesh: the box the faces must reach, the nearest crossing so far, and the sphere-tree walk and face test every model and spline-segment line handler of both games shares.

remarks.para: Project I.G.I.'s model ray (0x4C1840) and I.G.I. 2's line handlers (RigidDynCubeObj_TraceLinesHandler, igi2 0x58B3B0, and SplineObjSegment_TraceLinesHandler, 0x5B7390) walk the same tree and test faces the same way: a padded box around the line, a plane test, a barycentric test on the face's dominant axis, and a tie window that lets a face a little behind the best through when it faces the line and the best does not.

What each build chose differently is a parameter: its pad and tie window and how it compares a value that is not a number (), the order a handler sums the plane distance in () and the sphere distance in (), and the precision. Each float the disassembly stores is stored.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionDescriptor
member.summary: One mission's descriptor: the eleven values a level's mission.qvm passes to DefineMission.

remarks.para: The original keeps these in a 1192-byte record inside a fixed table at 0x5C1590 (Mission_GetDescriptor, 0x485170, is a linear scan of it for a matching id). The table is empty in the executable image — every entry is written at runtime by the DefineMission native (0x484F60), which is why searching the binary for the mission list finds nothing.

Level 1's whole mission.qvm is a single call: DefineMission(1, "Mission 1 Name", "Mission 1 Desc", "", 2, "missions/location0/level1", "missions/location0/common", "missions/location0/level1", "location0", "level1", "mission1.spr").

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionLoader
member.summary: Loads a mission: the ordered sequence Mission_Load (0x415B30) performs, from the descriptor lookup to the level's task tree.

remarks.para: The order is the specification. Each step depends on the ones before it — the MISSION: alias has to exist before the terrain path resolves, both packs have to be open before objects.qvm names a model, and the search directory is re-pointed between the two pack opens because a pack's archives are addressed relative to it.

Steps this does not perform yet are logged, not skipped silently. AI graph files are detected here; the desktop host still parses them and applies the AIGraph world offset. A caller can see exactly what a loaded mission is missing from .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionObjectiveRuntime.ExtraMessageHoldSeconds
member.summary: Gets or sets extra seconds every status message is held on screen for.

remarks.para: Added to each message's authored Duration. The authored values are short — two seconds is the common case, and the hold does not begin until the last character has been typed, so a long message can be fully readable for under a second before it goes.

This is not free of consequences, which is why it is a setting and defaults to zero. The hold ending is what raises isFinishedDisplay and starts nTicksSinceFinishedDisplay, and mission scripts gate on both — several LevelFlow expressions wait for a message to finish before they complete a level. Extending the hold therefore delays those triggers by the same amount. A delay is all it is: nothing is skipped and no expression changes its answer, the mission simply reaches it a few seconds later. Left at zero the timing is the original's exactly.

remarks.para: Some game events create a StatusMessageScreen child directly instead of running an authored StatusMessage task. GunPickup does exactly that at 0x46D3A7, formatting PICKEDUPWEAPON%s from the weapon's display name and posting it through 0x485970. These messages share the same twenty-four slots and display state as mission messages but do not alter script variables or the map-computer log.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionObjectiveRuntime.DisplayedMessages
member.summary: Gets the messages on screen now, in the slot order the original draws them in.

remarks.para: Slot order, not send order, because that is what the player sees. 0x486650 puts a new message in the lowest free slot and 0x486020 walks the array from zero, so when a message in the middle of the column finishes, the next one to arrive drops into the hole it left rather than onto the bottom. Sorting by send tick instead would be tidier and would not match.
Empty on almost every tick of a mission, so it is a lazily-walked view over the slot array rather than a list rebuilt thirty times a second for a renderer that usually draws nothing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionObjectiveRuntime.ClearMessages
member.summary: Empties every message slot, as the StatusMessageScreen_ClearMessages native does.

remarks.para: The native (0x485AD0) walks all twenty-four slots through 0x4868D0 and releases each occupied one with 0x485D20, ordinary messages and cutscene subtitles alike. Levels 1-14 run it from their gameplay container's Run at start, so the intro's messages do not carry over into play.

Releasing a slot is not silent: 0x485D20 marks the owning StatusMessage task as finished (isFinishedDisplay = 1, nFinishedDisplay = now, nTicksSinceFinishedDisplay = 0), exactly as if its hold had run out. Scripts that wait on a cleared message still see it end. Messages without a task, such as weapon pickups, just leave the screen.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionObjectiveRuntime.ClearCutsceneMessages
member.summary: Removes subtitles that belong to a cutscene which the player skipped.
member.remarks: Cutscene messages share the same slots as ordinary status messages. Releasing them here prevents a subtitle from surviving the camera hand-off and being drawn as a normal gameplay message.

member.summary: Advances level state with alternate player projection and liveness information.
member.param: The player's primary world projection, when one exists.
The player's team, for criteria that name a team (CRITERIA_HUMAN0).
An alternate projection of the same logical player in world units. The two positions contribute at most one player to each area. The host chooses projections according to its camera/body policy.
Whether the logical player can occupy authored areas. A dead player contributes no occupancy, matching the retail human-registration scan used by AreaActivate.
member.remarks:
These tasks precede the mission's AlarmControls in retail update order. Keeping this phase separate lets the desktop host preserve that ordering while evaluating the remaining objectives and messages after the rest of the simulation tick.
AreaActivate::Update (0x5048A0) clears nActive, queries the authored oriented volume and sums matching occupants. The volume's criteria names whose occupants count: a team (CRITERIA_HUMAN0 counts team 0 — the player and the friendly squad — while CRITERIA_HUMAN1 counts team 1, the guards) or the player object itself. Dead humans are not occupants, exactly as the detection scan unregisters a corpse. The renderer reports every brain to preserve isDead bindings, so this query also excludes soldier tasks outside the live task world, just as the collision-body pass does.

member.summary: Puts the areas and edit variables into the level's update walk, so each updates where the tree places it (0x5048A0 counts, then walks its children; 0x4889B0).
member.param: The level walk.

Reads the soldiers where they stand when an area counts them.
Reads the player where it stands when an area counts it.
member.remarks: An area scans the registered humans and vehicles at the moment it updates (0x5048A0), so it sees what the tasks before it in the tree did this tick and what those after it did last tick. Without a source the host's last report stands in (, ).

member.remarks: The mission runtime is built from the level's task tree before the soldiers exist, so the script variables it binds (isDead) and the AreaActivate volume counts both read from this snapshot. member.summary: Runs the objective definitions and publishes the rows of the one that ran last.
member.remarks: 0x467410: a definition whose Objectives Valid is empty or holds becomes the computer's, and each of its rows takes its Complete and Failed flags from its expressions -- off where a row has none. One that does not hold leaves everything as it was, so the computer keeps the last that ran, flags and all. Running it at construction, before the host has a player to report, latches the level's opening state.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionRegistry
member.summary: The table of mission descriptors, built by running every mission.qvm under LOCAL:missions.

remarks.para: This is Mission_InitRegistry (0x484F30): register the DefineMission native and the MISSION_NEXT_MISSION_UNDEFINED constant, empty the table, then walk LOCAL:missions recursively (0x4B1420) running each mission.qvm it finds (Mission_Open, 0x484E60).

The scan is a startup step, not part of loading a mission. Mission_Load looks a descriptor up by id as its very first action, long before any level script runs, so the table has to be complete beforehand — and a retail mission.qvm holds nothing but its one DefineMission call. An earlier note placed Mission_Open inside Mission_Load; it is not called from there at all, and running a mission.qvm twice would trip the original's own "not unique" abort.

member.summary: Walks the missions in campaign order — the NextMissionId chain from an id.
member.param: The id the walk starts at; defaults to .
member.returns: Each mission in the chain, ending at .
member.remarks: The order is the chain's, not the table's. is in the order the startup scan happened to find each mission.qvm — a directory walk, so alphabetical, which puts level 10 before level 2. The campaign's real order is declared: every descriptor names its successor, and that is what the retail menu's three fill natives (0x405660, 0x4056F0, 0x405760) walk. A descriptor pointing at itself, or at a mission already visited, would otherwise spin, so visited ids are tracked.

member.summary: Walks every registered mission, the chain first and anything it does not reach after it.
member.returns: The chain in campaign order, then the unreachable missions by ascending id.
member.remarks: What a mission browser wants, as opposed to the campaign's own progression: the chain is the truth about the order, but a mission the chain does not reach — a mod's extra level, an installation with a broken descriptor — still exists and should still be listed rather than silently vanishing. stays the faithful walk for the retail menus.

member.summary: Resolves the string keys a mission's own data carries — objective rows, computer highlights, status messages — to the localized text behind them.

remarks.para: Why this is not just . That table resolves a menu label, and a menu label is addressed the way Menu_GetString (0x418EA0) addresses one: by building LOCAL:<language>/<key> and asking the registry for that. Mission data does not work that way. Its archives — objectives.res, messages.res, computer.res — are registered whole, and the entries inside them keep their own names, so a status message's M4_MSG_1 is registered as M4_MSG_1 and nothing else. Asked for LOCAL:english/M4_MSG_1 the table misses and hands back its RM: placeholder, which is exactly what a mission's messages showed before this existed.

So the registry is asked first, by the raw key, and the menu table is the fallback. That order also keeps the retail behaviour for a key that genuinely is missing: still produces RM: <key>, which is what the original puts on screen rather than a blank.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.ObjectCollisionEntry.TryCastRetail(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double@,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldRayHit@)
member.summary: Casts a ray at this model with the original's own arithmetic ().
member.param: The ray start, in world units.
The ray end.
The nearest hit so far as a fraction of the ray; a hit must be nearer to count.
Receives the contact, reported as reports one.
member.returns: Whether this model was struck nearer than .
member.remarks: The original transforms the ray into the model's frame, rounds it to single precision and accepts a face up to and including the ray's end (t ≤ 1 as a float). A human's wall sweep ends its re-cast exactly on the wall it has just slid off, so that boundary decides whether a slide into a corner is accepted or refused: the original's test meets the wall, the sweep slides again and again, and after ten casts it refuses the move (0x461A70). The double-precision test here stopped a hair short.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ObjectCollisionIndex
member.summary: The placed objects a level is solid with, and the ray cast against them.

remarks.para: The terrain octree says where the ground is; this says where the walls are. A model's collision geometry is its HSMC chunk group () — a separate, far coarser mesh than the one that draws, which is why a crate can be a box to walk into and a hundred triangles to look at.

Units. A 's position is in metres — the scene builder divides by for the renderer — while a collision mesh's vertices and the player's own position are in world units. The conversion happens once, here, at build time. Getting this wrong puts every object 4096 times too far away, which reads as no collision at all rather than as an error.

What this is not. The original reaches its objects through the broad-phase octree that 0x4C6940 commits positions into, and through 0x4CDB20's shape dispatch. Neither is read. This walks a flat list, rejecting on each object's bounding sphere first. It finds the same surfaces; it does more work to do it.

member.content: The casts and queries: every ray, trace and box the live world asks of the index.

member.param: Where the ray starts, in world units.
Where it stops.
Receives the nearest contact.

remarks.para: For the probe bake, which wants both halves of that sentence. A door standing open when the bake runs would be traced as a hole in the wall it is part of, and the field is static, so the hole would still be there once the door shut.

It is also the only cast safe to run off the main thread. reads , which mutates whenever a door moves; this touches nothing but the entry array, which never changes after . Ordering the bake before the doors open would answer the first point and not the second.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.ObjectCollisionIndexBuilder.IsElevatorShaftVolume(System.String)
member.summary: Gets whether a placement is an invisible elevator-shaft collision volume (instance name colbox*, task class EditRigidObj). These authored boxes sit at every elevator doorway. Retail does not register them for the human trace — the player boards a lift with its door open and the door's own leaf provides the closed-state block — so keeping them solid to the player blocks boarding (observed as the "can't enter the cab" bug on M3/M8). They remain in the default world collision (level zero) so bullets and visibility still respect them.
member.param: The placement's instance name.
member.returns: when the object is an elevator-shaft collision volume.

member.summary: Gets whether any placement is owned by a task descended from an Elevator task.
member.remarks: The engine excludes elevator-shaft collision boxes from the human trace so the player can board a lift, but only on levels that actually contain elevator machinery. Levels without elevators (M9/M10) author colbox* objects as ordinary static collision the player must hit, so this level-wide check keeps those solid rather than letting the player walk through them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.Particles.Particle2DBleeding
member.summary: One body's blood, the effect both titles' engines throw where a round enters flesh: a mist at the wound and drops thrown forward along the round and back towards the shooter, each body keeping one mist system and one drop system, made anew once the last has burnt out.

remarks.para: The order is the original's own, and so are its draws from the run stream: the mist first, taking none; then the forward count, drawn before any of its drops; each drop its spin, then thrown within its cone by the engine's own stream; then the back count and its drops along the wound's reversed direction. The stain a wound leaves on what stands behind it and the stain a drop leaves where it lands are each title's own, against its own world, and come before (the wound's) and after (the collider's) this.

The mist plays its sprite's frames over its fifteen ticks, a whole number of ticks to a frame (15 / frames: seven frames show two ticks each, the last held a tick longer), and fades through its alpha; the drops fall and fade likewise.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.Particles.Particle2DSystem
member.summary: A system of 2-D particles, Particle2DDynCubeObj: the mist and drops a wound throws, the puff a round kicks off a wall, smoke, a rocket's trail. Both titles' engines run the same code (Project I.G.I. 0x4FDF00 makes one and 0x4FD660 steps it; I.G.I. 2's Particle2DDynCubeObj_New and _RunHandler), in the original's x87 arithmetic.

remarks.para: The particles sit in slots; one that dies swaps places with the last live one, so the order changes as they die, as the original's pointer table does. A system that is empty when it runs deletes itself (it is self-destructing from creation).

Each tick a particle gains the system's acceleration, moves by its speed, turns by its spin and grows by the system's size delta; an animated system's particle steps its frame. Then its life ticks down, or, once spent, its intensity fades; it dies at no intensity or no size.

A system with a collider checks each live particle every fifteen ticks, in a phase given when it is added: its countdown is taken down, and at nought a line from where it was last checked to where it is joins the tick's batch and the countdown reloads. The batch is traced at once, each strike answered, and its particle dies. The particle that dies is the one the line was made for by its index when the lines were made: an earlier death this pass may have swapped another particle into that slot, and then that one dies instead, as in the original.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RadioRuntime
member.summary: One Radio task: an ExplodeObject that chatters while it is on.

remarks.para: TASKTYPE_RADIO (0x43AD80) registers under ExplodeObject (word_54097C), so its damage, explosion, destroyed model and isExploded are the family's, in . What the Radio adds is isOn (+576, exported as %s.isOn on activation, 0x43B1C0) and its update, 0x43AF90, run after the ExplodeObject update each tick:

list.item: once exploded (+400) it is off; otherwise an authored On expression decides, and a radio with none keeps what it had (off, from its constructor 0x43AF20);
while on and silent, it counts down +572; at zero it plays one of its four Radio sounds (rand % 4) and waits 150 + rand % 150 ticks after that sound has finished;
switched off, it cuts the sound it was playing and, on the tick it goes off, plays its Shutdown sound once.

remarks.para: Both draws come from the engine's global stream and are made whether or not the chosen name resolves: every shipped radio (mission 7's Radio_3366, mission 11's Radio_201) authors no sounds at all, yet a lit one still rolls every few seconds.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RailroadPath
member.summary: A retail Train's railroad: the SplineObj's polyline and the coupler walk over it.

remarks.para: The original never evaluates the rail's curve while a train runs. Each waypoint's segment keeps the polyline Segment_Build (0x4E4530) sampled from the Hermite between it and the waypoint before (), and 0x4FEC10 walks that: the first coupler sits the train's scalar position along it, each later one where a sphere of the car's coupling length about the coupler before crosses it. A car is then laid on the chord between its two couplers (), not on the curve.

Evaluating the curve itself put every car below the original wherever the rail bends upward: Mission 1's intro wagon 607_01_1 ran 0.6 m low down the hill into the valley, so Jones, welded to it there, sat 0.64 m high inside the crate he leans on once the wagon reached the flat, where the two agree again.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RayCapsule
member.summary: Ray against a capsule — the analytic human body test used to make soldiers solid.

remarks.para: A capsule is the set of points within radius of the axis axisA..axisB. This is the same 0.55 metre by 1.8 metre shape uses for human-versus-human separation, so a soldier's collision body matches the body the renderer already uses to keep two soldiers apart.

Like , this is geometry, not a transcription: the original never needed a capsule because its human bodies were registered collision meshes. It exists so the player's existing wall sweep can treat a living soldier as a wall, which is the behaviour retail got from that mesh registration.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RenderSurfaceProbe
member.summary: Names the texture on the drawn surface a ray meets.

remarks.para: Why the collision trace cannot answer this. A model is two meshes, not one: the collision mesh the world trace walks, and the render mesh the G-buffer draws. They are different geometry with different triangle counts, and nothing indexes one to the other — so a contact from knows the object and the game material row, and cannot know which texture is on the face that was struck. The renderer's material — roughness, metallic, whether the surface reflects — is keyed by TEXTURE NAME in materials.json, so naming a surface there means knowing that name, and there was no way to get it out of a running game.

So this traces the render mesh itself, over the same ray, and reports the texture of the nearest draw record it crosses. One placement per probe, on a keypress, so a linear walk of the model's triangles is the right shape: the object has already been chosen by a broad-phase the collision index ran.

Triangles are carried to world space rather than the ray to model space. The inverse of a placement's orientation is its transpose, and this codebase has two conventions that have already cost a bug apiece; the forward transform is the one LightmapBaker and both build their world triangles with, so using it here means this agrees with them by construction rather than by argument.

member.summary: Ports the retail Heli live update (0x431B70), its force helper (0x431E30), Rotor::Tick (0x42D440), and the force accumulator at 0x4EC6A0. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RetailMissileBody
member.summary: A missile in flight as Project I.G.I. flies one (Missile, registered at 0x427FF0): a physics object pushed by its motor, steadied by its fins, steering as its type says, and set off by the first thing it touches.

remarks.para: Fired (0x429A30) facing as its launcher faces, along that frame's forward column at the launcher's speed, its thrust full and its fuel its type's; its wings are its type's with the first two mirrored across it as the third and fourth (0x429EF0).

Each tick (0x428390) it steers by its type (+284), lays smoke while it has fuel (0x428630, drawing the missiles' own stream), then moves (0x428D00): its thrust eases toward full, its pitch, roll and turn rates toward their ideals, its frame turns by pitch then turn, a burnt-out missile wobbles, its motor pushes it while it has fuel, it burns some, and unless it may rest the air acts on its wings and the shared step moves it. Touching anything, it goes off ().
The same engine module as I.G.I. 2's missile (Missile_Move), with the first game's own operand order and register use, and two steering kinds the sequel dropped (the Hind's and the keyboard's).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RetailPrecipitation
member.summary: Both games' weather as the originals simulate it: eighty drops or flakes in one tile of the ground, falling through a layer and coming round to its top again, which the drawing repeats over every tile and layer around the eye.

remarks.para: Project I.G.I.'s Rain_Update (0x499CF0) and I.G.I. 2's Rain_UpdateParticles are the same: the weather fades in or out by a sixtieth a tick as it is told to fall or not; while any of it shows, every drop falls (rain 2048 units a tick, snow a tenth of that) and wraps round its layer; a flake also drifts, picking a new drift every thirty to fifty-nine ticks, and crosses into the next tile's group when it leaves its own; and new drops are let in at the layer's top, one per 307.2 units fallen, until there are eighty.
The two draw from their own stream, never the level's, which only places drops in the picture; both are this generator, seeded as is.

member.summary: Advances one 30 Hz tick as a RotatingObject's update (0x439090), with its x87 arithmetic.

remarks.para: Switching off zeroes the target speeds themselves (+316..+324), and nothing writes them again: the post-load handler (0x4395D0) is the only other writer. An object switched off, even for one tick (Mission 8's fan is on while !Switch_260.isPressed, a three-tick pulse), runs down to rest and stays there.

Each speed steps toward its target by its acceleration (+300..+308) over a thirtieth of a second. The clamp compares the register's unrounded value, so an axis with no acceleration never changes speed. Each angle (+340..+348) gains its speed over a thirtieth, and is wrapped only from above.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.SceneDistanceField
member.summary: Every placed object's distance field, in one structure that can be asked about the whole level.

remarks.para: answers "how far is this point from this model". A trace needs "how far is this point from anything", and that is this: one baked field per distinct model, and an instance per placement holding where it stands.

One field per model, not per placement. A level draws the same crate two hundred times, and the distance field of a crate is a property of the crate rather than of where it is standing — so the bake is shared and the placement contributes only a transform. On level 1 that is the difference between baking seven hundred fields and baking a few dozen.

This is the reference implementation, and it exists to be disagreed with. The clipmap the GPU builds is an approximation of exactly this answer, sampled onto a grid, and there is no way to tell a wrong clipmap from a right one by looking at the frame it produces. Having the exact answer available on the CPU is what makes the approximation checkable.

A placement names a model, but which mesh describes it is a question with two defensible answers — the collision hull, which is what the AI sees, or the drawn surface, which is what light actually falls on. This takes the second, and takes it as an argument so the choice sits with the caller and the bake stays testable without a level.

member.summary: The coarsest voxel a field may bake to before it is discarded, in metres.
member.remarks: Coarseness, not size. An earlier attempt cut on the model's extent, which throws away buildings; what actually disqualifies a field is its voxel, because every field gets the same voxel count. A crate bakes voxels of centimetres and the largest buildings a few metres, and those all describe their surfaces usefully. The sky and level-bounds shells span kilometres, so their voxels come to hundreds of metres — and such a field is worse than absent: its band is as coarse as its voxels, one byte step spans tens of metres, every true distance in the playable space quantises to noise, its bounds cover the whole level, and the union takes a minimum. That noise is what stopped the sun trace in mid-air. Sixteen metres keeps every model whose surfaces a trace can actually land on and drops the shells whose answers were never real.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.SceneDistanceField.Sample(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: How far a world-space point is from the nearest surface in the level.
member.param: The point, in world space.
member.returns: The distance to the nearest surface. The fields are unsigned — this game's meshes are single-sided shells with no meaningful interior — so both sides of a wall read as clearance from it, and near zero means at a surface.
member.remarks:
The minimum over every instance, which is the correct combination for a distance field and the reason a union of shapes is free: the nearest surface to a point is the nearest surface of whichever object is nearest, and taking the smaller of two distances says exactly that.
Instances whose box the point lies outside contribute the distance to that box, so a point in open ground still gets a usable answer rather than the sentinel — which is what lets a trace take a long step through empty air instead of creeping.

member.returns: A description of the nearest instance and what it reported.
member.remarks: For diagnosis only. A union hides which member decided the result, and when the union is wrong that is the only thing worth knowing -- reasoning about which model it might be, at the scale these levels run to, is guesswork.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.SceneDistanceField.TryTrace(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single,System.Single@)
member.summary: Marches a ray until it meets a surface.
member.param: Where the ray starts, in world space.
Its direction. Expected to be unit length.
How far to march before giving up.
Receives how far along the ray the surface was met.
member.returns: when a surface was met within the distance.

remarks.para: Sphere tracing: step by exactly the distance to the nearest surface, which by definition cannot pass through one. A ray crossing open ground clears it in a handful of steps however much geometry stands nearby, and a ray grazing a wall slows down of its own accord as it approaches — neither behaviour needs a bounding hierarchy or a step size chosen in advance.

The step floor is what keeps a grazing ray from taking thousands of ever-smaller steps and never arriving. It costs the trace the ability to resolve detail below that size, which is the right trade at the resolution these fields are baked to anyway.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorInsideSphere
member.summary: A sector object's optimal inside sphere: SectorObject_GetOptimalInsideSphere, the same function in both engines (IGI.exe 0x4DF500; igi2 e/3/sectorobject.c).

remarks.para: One sphere that encloses every room of a building and everything the rooms carry. Each room's mesh sphere () is collected, then each of its attach objects' in turn, all in their own model space -- the original never moves them into the building's frame -- and the two nearest are merged until one is left. A building with no room is given its own mesh's sphere.

Project I.G.I. reads it while drawing: an object farther than its radius from its centre is outside the building the camera stands in (QCube_CallHandlers, IGI.exe 0x4D12C0). I.G.I. 2 still computes and copies it but no longer reads it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorInsideSphere.Merge(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.ValueTuple{OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single}})
member.summary: Merges spheres into one, as the original does.
member.param: The spheres, in the order they were collected.
member.returns: The single sphere left, or when there were none.

remarks.para: Each round finds the closest pair by centre, the first strictly nearer in collection order winning a tie. Two spheres with one centre keep the larger radius; a sphere inside the other is dropped; otherwise the first becomes the sphere spanning both -- centred halfway between their far edges along the line joining them -- and the second is dropped.
Dropping moves the last sphere into the dropped one's place, which is how the original's pool removes an element, and is what decides which pair is met first in the next round.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorPortalProjection
member.summary: The projection both titles' sector culls share: what screen box a portal covers, and whether a sphere falls in a window.

remarks.para: Sector_IsPortalVisible is one function in both engines -- IGI.exe 0x4DD7F0 and igi2.exe 0x587D10 carry the same plane test from the portal's first face, the same 409.6-unit relief behind it, the same near plane at 0.04096, the same outcodes against the display area and the same triangle clipper (IGI.exe 0x4DAB50, igi2.exe 0x5865B0). What differs between the titles is the walk that calls it and what the result culls, which each title keeps for itself.
Everything here is in world units, about a camera whose rows are the view's right, up and forward axes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorPortalProjection.NearPlaneZ
member.summary: The view-space depth below which a vertex counts as behind the near plane.
member.remarks: 0.040959999 in the original, which is 0.04096f exactly. It is used twice: as the outcode test at igi2.exe 0x58823A and as the plane SectorObject_CheckTriangle clips to, passed in as the constant 0x3D27C5AC at 0x588376.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorPortalProjection.BackFaceRelief
member.summary: How far behind a portal's plane the camera may stand and still see through it.

remarks.para: Measured, not rounded. The comparison at igi2.exe 0x5880C8 is fcomp ds:__real@4823D70B, and 0x4823D70B is 167772.16f, whose square root is 409.6 exactly. The value compared against it is a squared distance, so the threshold is a distance of 409.6 world units.

What the distance is measured between was not obvious from the original's code and had to be worked out. The original calls Real32x3_ProjectPointToPlane (0x561A70) with the camera-relative position of the portal's plane point, the unit plane normal as the direction and its negation as the plane normal, then squares the distance between the point and its projection. Substituting the normalised normal into that function collapses the whole thing to dot(portalPoint − camera, planeNormal)²: the perpendicular distance from the camera to the portal's plane, not the distance to the portal itself. A camera a kilometre to one side of a wall but level with it is still within the relief.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.Sectors.SectorPortalProjection.VertexScratchCapacity
member.summary: The most vertices the original can transform for one portal.
member.remarks: Sector_IsPortalVisible transforms into MultiMesh_TransformedVertex_t atVertex[100], a stack array with no bound check. The widest portal the 24 shipped levels place has 28 vertices, so the limit is recorded rather than enforced.

member.summary: Projects one portal and returns the screen box it covers, or refuses it.
member.param: Where the viewer is and which way it faces.
How view space becomes pixels.
Where the sector the portal belongs to stands, in world units.
How that sector is turned, as the world renderer turns it.
That sector's portals.
The portal.
The rectangle the sector itself is being seen through.
Receives the portal's own screen box, clipped to the display area but not intersected with — the original leaves that to the caller.
member.returns: when nothing can be seen through this portal.
member.remarks: Sector_IsPortalVisible (IGI.exe 0x4DD7F0, igi2.exe 0x587D10) minus its first step, the open/closed byte, which has no object to read here and is the caller's business.

member.summary: Clips one portal triangle and widens a box by whatever survives.

remarks.para: SectorObject_CheckTriangle (igi2.exe 0x5865B0) does this by splitting the triangle against one plane at a time — near, then left, then top, then right, then bottom — recursing on the extra triangle when one vertex is outside and two are in, and widening the caller's box by the three surviving vertices at the end.

This is a convex polygon clip in the same order, not a line-for-line port of that recursion. The two produce the same set of points: splitting a triangle against a half-plane and clipping it as a polygon give the same intersection, and only its extreme points reach the box. The clip order still matters and is preserved, because the near plane's interpolation happens in view space and is then reprojected, while the four screen planes interpolate the pixel positions directly — the original does exactly that split, and doing it the other way round bends the outline.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.ShelterHeightField
member.summary: How high the solid world stands over every square of ground: the level's roofs, awnings, walkways and containers, seen from directly above.

remarks.para: What it replaces. "Indoors" used to mean inside the axis-aligned bounding box of a task named Building_-something, and everything that cares whether the sky can be seen — the fog, the falling rain, the splashes, the standing water — asked that one question. It is wrong in both directions, and measurably so. On mission one a quarter of the ground inside those boxes has no roof over it at all (a building standing at an angle to the world axes fills barely a third of its own box, so the box swallows the apron in front of it), while two fifths of the ground that genuinely is under a roof lies outside every one of them, because the structure sheltering it was never given a Building task. The first is why the fog cut out and the rain stopped in the middle of an open yard; the second is why puddles formed on warehouse floors.

What it is instead. A raster, one cell every of world XY, holding the height of the highest solid surface standing over that square — solid meaning the collision geometry the level's placed objects carry, which is the same thing a bullet stops against and therefore the same thing rain does. Sheltered is then a comparison rather than a classification: the roof over this point is above it, and not so far above that it belongs to a different part of the map.

Why the highest surface and not the lowest one above the query. Because a single number per cell is what can be handed to a shader as one texel and read with a single fetch, and because IGI's compounds are single-storey: the ground under a roof and the roof itself are the only two surfaces a column usually holds. Storing the top means a roof does not shelter itself — its own upper face is the height stored, so it fails the comparison and goes on collecting rain like any other open ground, which is exactly what should happen.

Vertical faces cost nothing. A triangle is written into the cells whose centres fall inside its XY projection, and a wall projects to a line, so walls and fences claim at most the thin strip they actually stand on. No normal test is needed to keep them from roofing the yard beside them.

member.remarks: Half a metre: fine enough that the edge of the shelter follows a wall rather than staircasing around it, coarse enough that a level's built-up area is a couple of megabytes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.ShelterHeightField.MaxOverheadMetres

member.remarks: Generous — a hangar's ceiling is tens of metres up and is still the ceiling — but not unbounded, because a level's XY footprint can hold two areas at wildly different altitudes (mission one has a compound three kilometres of height below another) and a single top-down raster cannot tell them apart. A hundred metres separates "the roof over me" from "a different part of the map".

Three quarters of a metre clears that and clears a kerb, and is below any roof a person walks under.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe
member.summary: How much of the open sky reaches a point, and from which directions: the geometry behind hearing the weather from indoors.

remarks.para: What it answers. answers one bit — is there a roof over this point — and that bit is all the picture needs, because rain either falls on you or does not. The ear needs more than that. Standing in a warehouse with the loading door open, the roof is overhead in every direction and the rain is nonetheless plainly audible, plainly to the left, and plainly brighter than the same rain through the wall behind you. A single bit cannot say any of that. This says all three.

How. A fixed set of directions is cast from the ear, and each one is asked a single question: is the far end of what this ray travelled through out in the open. A ray that meets nothing is judged where it gave up; a ray that meets a surface is judged a step back from it, in the last of the air it crossed. So a ray out of a door and onto the yard beyond has escaped, and a ray into an interior wall, a floor under a roof, or a ceiling has not. Looking at the wet ground outside counts, which is as it should be — most of the rain heard outdoors is rain striking the ground, not rain passing through the air beside you.

Why a surface, not just the sky. Casting only upwards would make an open field score a half — half a sphere of directions ends in the ground — and would make a doorway score nothing at all, because a doorway is level with the ear and what you see through it is the yard, not the sky. Both answers would be wrong in the direction that matters.

The directions are the six world axes. Every ray's result is spread across them by the square of its cosine, which for an axis-aligned set sums to exactly one per ray — the components of a unit vector squared — so the spreading neither creates nor destroys energy. Six numbers then carry the whole directional picture: all six high is standing in a field, one high and five low is standing beside an open door, all six low is standing in a cellar. A listener that puts one emitter on each axis reproduces the field it came from, and a source between two axes lands between the two emitters where it belongs.

Cost. The rays are spread over consecutive calls — of them each time — so the per-frame cost is a fixed handful of casts against the same collision the grenades use, and the full set is never more than a few frames stale. The spreading weights are constant and computed once, so everything after the casts is adding sixty-odd floats.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe.DefaultReachMetres
member.summary: How far a ray travels before it is judged on where it ended, in metres.
member.remarks: Far enough to leave any room and cross any yard, short enough that a ray down a long corridor gives up rather than escaping through a door at the far end of the building and reporting the weather as though it were next to you.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe.RoofFadeMetres
member.summary: How far above the ear a roof stops being heard as a roof, in metres.
member.remarks: A hangar ceiling is still a ceiling, and it does still drum — less than a shed roof two metres over your head, but it is the loudest thing in a warehouse in a storm. Fifteen metres was too mean: it cut the drumming to nothing in exactly the large interiors that have no other way to sound wet, leaving them on the through-the-wall level alone and shut in like a cellar.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe.RoofNearMetres

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe.PullbackMetres
member.summary: How far back along a ray from what it struck the escape test is taken, in metres.

remarks.para: The test is taken beside the surface, not on it. Asking whether the struck point itself is under a roof cannot tell a ceiling from the ground: this game's roofs are frequently single planes with no thickness at all, so the underside of a roof and the top of a roof are the same height, and any test at that height says the same thing about both. A step back along the ray moves the question to the space the sound would have travelled through, which is the room for a ceiling and the open air for the ground outside, and those two are never confusable.

Half a metre — one raster cell — is far enough to clear the surface and its quantisation, and near enough that it cannot step through a wall into a different room. It must stay comfortably larger than , or a ceiling stops reading as a ceiling.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SkyExposureProbe.SurfaceEpsilonMetres
member.summary: How far above the sampled point a roof must stand for it to be out of the rain.
member.remarks: A tenth of a metre: enough to absorb the raster's quantisation, and far below so that the space just under a roof still reads as roofed. The field's own is three quarters of a metre and is sized for a different question — whether a surface collects rain — where a kerb must not shelter the road it stands on.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.SurfaceCacheLayout
member.summary: Where every card's page sits in the surface cache atlas.

remarks.para: A card is an orthographic view of part of a model; its page is the rectangle of atlas the capture of that view lands in. Everything downstream addresses surfaces through these pages — a trace that hits a model finds the card facing it, reads its page, and gets the albedo and normal there. Lighting later writes into pages of the same shape.

Shelf packing, not a perfect one. Pages are sorted tallest first and laid in rows, each row as tall as its first page. That wastes the difference between a row's tallest page and its shortest — a few per cent here, because card resolutions come from a small set of sizes and sort into rows of near-equal height. A tight packer would recover that and cost a search per page; the atlas is allocated once at load and never repacked, so the saving buys nothing.
What did matter was how the atlas GROWS. Doubling a square one quadruples its area, so a packing that only just failed landed near a quarter occupied — measured at 34%. The width is now chosen once and the height grows to suit, which costs nothing because shelves run horizontally.

Pages are padded apart. The capture is sampled with a linear filter, so a fetch at a page's edge blends in whatever was packed beside it — a different model's surface entirely. The same hazard the distance field atlas has, and the same answer, except that here the pages are written by a render pass rather than copied, so the padding is a gutter rather than an inset.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.SurfaceCacheLayout.Gutter
member.summary: How many texels are left between one page and the next.
member.remarks: One would do for a bilinear fetch, which reaches half a texel. Two leaves room for the capture's own edge to be slightly wrong — an orthographic render of a card catches geometry right at the boundary — without spending real space: at the resolutions cards use, this is under a per cent of the atlas.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainDiscardRegion
member.summary: One DiscardTerrain task resolved to the octree cube whose terrain the original suppresses.

remarks.para: Retail sub_52C290 snaps each task position down to a cube of twice 0x40000000 >> Level. During sub_4D14E0, the task's message-15 handler (sub_52C0B0) sets 0xB12BB8; the descent then clears that cube's terrain-child mask. Its DiscardTerrainArea proxy keeps the descent resolving until this level, so a coarse parent cannot cover the hole from a distance.
The bounds are three-dimensional. That matters where a level stacks discard cubes vertically around a building: a cube only removes the terrain node occupying the same X, Y, and Z octant.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainHeightBindings
member.summary: The heightmap bindings a level's HeightMap tasks publish: which terrain.hmp grid displaces the fine terrain inside which octree cube, and at what origin and scale.

remarks.para: This is the 48-byte table at 0xBA2030, indexed by heightmap id, that sub_507410 fills when a HeightMap task is parsed — and it is not in any terrain file. The task's position is snapped to the octree node of its Level, the node's minimum corner becomes the grid's origin, and the sample scale is 1 / 2^(31 - Level - log2(Size)), so the grid's cells tile the node exactly. The id is the task's texture-modifier slot plus one, which is why id zero means "none".

Which binding a chunk gets is decided by the descent, not by the chunk: the task registers itself in that node, the descent's enter hook (sub_506F00) pushes the id when it enters the node and the leave hook (sub_506F60) pops it, so a chunk takes the innermost task whose cube contains it — the same rule for the renderer (sub_4D14E0 copies the id into every descriptor), the ground query (sub_4CA010) and the ray test (sub_4C9020), all three of which sample the same table. is that rule without the stack.

Divergence, recorded. The original drops a ray from the task's position to find the ground before snapping its Z to the node; the port snaps the authored Z. Both land in the same cube unless the authored point is more than a node's height off the ground, which no retail level does.

Without these bindings the fine levels of detail are drawn as terrain.cmd stores them, and that is not the ground: the fine blocks are authored as the surface minus the heightmap, so a level that ships a heightmap shows its bumps inverted as sharp pits and ridges until the grid is added back. Measured over level 1: 1324 fine edges steeper than 45° without the heightmap, 60 with it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainHeightQuery
member.summary: Height-at-a-point: the query the player's feet stand on and the one nothing in the port could do before.

remarks.para: The whole chain in one call — descend the octree (), reach the leaf (), and interpolate the triangle () — which together are the terrain half of 0x4CBE40.
Terrain only. The original's downward cast also sweeps placed models (0x4CDB20), so a point standing on a crate reads the ground beneath the crate here. That branch is still unread.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainHeightQuery.SearchDepthUnits
member.summary: How far below a query point the ground is looked for, in world units.

remarks.para: 16385 — the offset 0x4CB050 puts the far end of its segment at. That is just over four metres, which is short: this is a query for a body already near the ground, not a probe from arbitrary height. The human's own step-down budgets are 0, 2048 and 8192 units, all well inside it.
Not to be confused with the 16387 the batched cast pads its bounding box by when choosing a descent depth; that is a different number for a different purpose.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainHeightQuery.AboveRecoveryUnits
member.summary: How far above a query point a surface is still accepted, in world units.
member.remarks: 65536 — sixteen metres. The near-ground query's four-metre reach below the body is the right window for a body already supported from underneath, but it goes permanently blind the moment a fast-moving body crosses below the surface: the surface is then above it, and a downward-only search can never see it again. The helicopter and plane anti-sink clamp widens its search upward by this much so a body that dips under a ridge or a valley slope still finds the surface it just crossed and rides it back up instead of diving to the bottom of the level.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainHeightRaster
member.summary: A top-down raster of the terrain's height, for the passes that march without tracing it.

remarks.para: The level's distance field is built from its placements, and the terrain is not one of them; a ray marched through it towards the ground goes straight through the ground and out of the field. Without an acceleration structure to trace, that ray could only be answered with a guess at what open ground gives back, which knows nothing of the pool a lamp throws on the pavement in front of a wall, and the wall's foot took none of that pool's bounce where the traced gather showed it.
Held as a because it is the same thing -- a height per square of ground, packed the same way, read by the same shader code -- with the terrain in place of the roofs.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainLightBindings
member.summary: The terrain lightmap bindings a level's TerrainLightMap tasks publish: which terrain.lmp page lights the ground inside which octree cell, and the colour ramp its 8-bit texels are read through.

remarks.para: The ground's light. The original draws every chunk's material passes and then this page over them as a last pass that multiplies the frame (ZERO, SRCCOLOR, sub_5144E0 mode 2); a chunk with no binding is drawn unlit, its tiles at their own colour. Without it the vanilla ground is exactly that: the tile pictures with no sun on them, a cool grey where the original shows warm sunlit dirt.

Binding. sub_4F8780 activates each task once at load: the cell is the octree node of its Level, 2^(31 - Level) units across, the position snapped down to it; the page is TextureIndex into terrain.lmp; Size must be 8 to 256. sub_4F8EF0 publishes a 48-byte entry at 0xBA80A0 (the cell's minimum X and Y, 2^(L - 23) and 128 / Size), and the descent pushes its slot on entering the cell's node (class slot 15, sub_4F82B0) and pops it on leaving (slot 16), so a chunk takes the innermost cell enclosing its own node (0x4D2226). A chunk coarser than every cell over it is not enclosed by any, and stays unlit.
Coordinates. sub_510010, per vertex (0x510200): u = (X - minX) / cell + 0.5 / Size and the same in Y, so texel (c, r) is centred on min + (c, r) * cell / Size, row-major, unflipped.

Colour. The texels are indices into a ramp sub_50FAE0 rebuilds from the level's light whenever it changes: min(255, sun * i + ambient * 255) per channel, the sun the first Dirlight's keyframe colour and the ambient the GlobalLight's terrain band; alpha 255 but for index zero (sub_517FD0). A level with no Dirlight keeps the load-time placeholder, i << 16: red alone.

Divergence, recorded. The original drops each task onto the ground by ray before snapping its height, and adds proxy copies one cell above or below where the ground spans more than one; a chunk is therefore covered at whatever height it stands. The port matches the cell in X and Y alone, which is the same answer for every retail level: no two tasks share a column of cells at one level.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainLoader
member.summary: Loads a level's terrain: Terrain_Load (0x4C6240), plus the terrain.lmp that Terrain_LoadTextures (0x4C5F00) reads just before it.

remarks.para: The loader is given an extensionless base path and appends each extension itself, in the original's order: .bit, .hmp if the file exists, .cmd, .ctr, then the terrain script. The script comes last because it is what declares the materials and tile maps, and it can only call the two natives while they are registered — the original registers them immediately before the run and unregisters them immediately after, so nothing else can reach them.

The last step of the original is to relocate every octree node's .cmd offset into a pointer. That is not done here: offsets are kept as offsets and resolved through , which turns level 14's 14400 impossible offsets into a terrain that reports itself unusable instead of 14400 wild pointers.
