member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainPointDescent
member.summary: Descends the octree to the deepest node containing a point — the walk every collision query starts with.

remarks.para: This is 0x4C9A30, and it is the shared front half of the whole collision module: the downward cast (0x4CBE40), the ray cast the bullets use (0x4CC2A0) and the area query the grenade uses (0x4CABF0) all reach the world through it.

It is the same octree M6 already reads. The descent indexes — the table at 0x548060 — and folds orientations with the same composition the terrain traversal uses, which was verified branch by branch rather than assumed. The world cube is the same 0x40000000. So the collision query and the renderer walk one structure, which is why a collision hit and a drawn triangle cannot disagree.

One detail the original writes confusingly and this does not: the X and Y octant bits are taken through the orientation table while the Z bit is OR-ed in afterwards. That is equivalent to looking the full three-bit octant up directly, because bit 2 of every row of the table is fixed — the group acts on X and Y only. Both forms are exercised by the tests.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainPointDescent.DepthForBounds(OpenIGI.Game.World.Vector3i,OpenIGI.Game.World.Vector3i)
member.summary: How deep a query over a box may usefully descend before the box straddles a boundary.
member.param: The box's low corner, already biased.
The box's high corner, already biased.
member.returns: The depth, clamped to .

remarks.para: 0x4CBE40 computes this once for a whole batch of query points: it ORs the three axes' corner differences together, takes the highest set bit, and subtracts it from . That is the length of the common prefix the whole box shares, and so the last level at which one node still contains all of it.

A box that collapses to a point shares every bit. The original's BitScanReverse leaves its output untouched on a zero input, so it would carry whatever the register held; this returns the full depth, which is what the descent would reach anyway.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainRayTrace
member.summary: Segment traversal through the terrain octree's authored triangle leaves.
member.remarks: Unlike TerrainSightBlock, this does not sample a heightfield. It walks every depth-16 octree cell crossed by the segment and intersects the segment with the exact packed triangles in that leaf. That preserves cliffs, thin ridges and underside geometry which a fixed-distance height sample can miss.

member.summary: The game material row a hit on this terrain reports.
member.param: The level's terrain.
member.returns: The row to look up in the game material table.

remarks.para: 0x4CB050 fills the trace's entry and exit material at 0x4CB7C3 from scene[0xD3C + 4·index] — the same per-level array 0x4C1840 indexes for a mesh face. The index comes from 0x4CB810: the low byte of the CreateTerrainMaterial record's first field (C28FE0, argument 1, stored by 0x4C6670) for the texture modifier that covers the point, or for terrain material 0 when none does.

So the answer is the level's own, not a constant: Ground in most of the campaign and Snow in the four Arctic missions. See for why one row answers for the whole map. A terrain that declares no material takes row 1, the entry 0x4C1840 falls back to (scene+3392).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainSightBlock
member.summary: Whether the terrain stands between two points — the ground's part of a sight or bullet ray.

remarks.para: The original's ray cast (0x4CDB20) tests the terrain octree whenever the category mask's sign bit is set, and both of the sight ray's passes send −1 — so in retail a hill hides you and takes the rounds fired at you. The port's collision index covers placed objects only, which let guards see and shoot straight through terrain.

Divergence, recorded. This is a sampled stand-in, not a transcription: the ray is walked in fixed steps and each column's ground height () is compared against the ray's own height there. The original walks the octree's leaves exactly. A sampled test can miss a blade of terrain thinner than the step and treats the ground as a heightfield (an overhang blocks as if solid below), but it blocks and un-blocks in the same places the real test does on open ground, which is where the divergence was visible. Replace it when 0x4CDB20's terrain arm is transcribed.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainSurface
member.summary: What decides which ground material covers a point and which authored terrain cubes do not exist: the level's TextureModifier and DiscardTerrain tasks, plus the tile maps and materials the terrain script declared.

remarks.para: The original keeps the active layers on a four-byte stack (0xBA5060) that its octree descent pushes and pops as it enters and leaves each modifier's region — most recently entered in the low byte, and tested first. A modifier entered deeper in the tree is the smaller and more specific one, so the ordering here is by descending, which is the same ordering by construction.

A point no layer covers takes . That is not a fallback invented here: with no layer bound the original's per-vertex material is zero, which is the branch it takes on every level before any modifier is entered.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainSurfaceTest
member.summary: The surface test — 0x4CA010. Turns a leaf's triangles into a height.

remarks.para: This is the end of the chain the whole collision module exists to run: descend (), reach a leaf (), and here find where the ground actually is.

The test is not a general ray-triangle intersection. It exploits the query being vertical: for each triangle it finds the two points where the horizontal line y = queryY crosses the triangle's edges, checks the query's X lies between them, and interpolates the height along that span. Two rejections come first, on the triangle's X and Y bounds.

The "global patch" the original folds into its vertex heights — a bilinear sample biased by 64 and scaled by 256 — is the level's heightmap, the same one the renderer adds to the fine chunks; an earlier reading took it for a level-of-detail morph and left it out. It comes in through , which resolves from the the level published.

member.remarks: 0.0099999998 — a hundredth of a unit, written as a and widened. It is applied on both sides of every test, so a query exactly on an edge hits rather than falling between two triangles.

member.remarks: The vertices are sorted by Y into low, middle and high. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainTileLayer
member.summary: One TextureModifier from a level's script, resolved into the record the terrain renderer reads: a square of the world, a bit mask over it, and the ground material the set bits select.

remarks.para: This is the run-time table at 0xBA5050, which sub_5062A0 fills from a TextureModifier task. The task's five parameters map onto it directly:

item.description: snapped down to its octree node, the square the mask covers.
an octree level, so the square is 2^30 >> Level either side of the centre.
that record's cells per edge; the two agree in all nine of level 1's modifiers.
the terrain material a set bit selects.

remarks.para: The mask covers the snapped square, not one centred on the raw position. sub_5062A0 floors the position to a multiple of the node's size — twice the extent — to build the activation region, and sub_4C6E70 writes that snapped centre back into the task at +32; the record the renderer samples takes its origin from the snapped centre minus the extent, which is the snapped minimum itself. Mask and activation box are the same square, so a sample can only leave the mask by leaving the region.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainTraversal
member.summary: The terrain octree descent: sub_4D14E0. Walks terrain.ctr from the camera, culls what the frustum misses, applies the level's DiscardTerrain cubes, and emits one per node that is the coarsest detail good enough at its distance.

remarks.para: A node's position is accumulated during the descent — the octant offset halves at every level — so nothing in any terrain file holds a coordinate. The descent carries two of these accumulators at once, one in world space for the distance and floor tests and one in view space for the frustum, both as integers relative to the camera. That is the original's arrangement and it is reproduced here including the arithmetic shifts, because culling decisions have to match at the boundary.

The original's descent also drives the object and sector lists that share the tree. Most of that half is not reproduced here, but DiscardTerrain is: its area proxy forces descent to the authored level, then its handler clears the matching node's terrain mask. Ignoring that interaction draws a coarse terrain sheet over intentionally exposed model geometry such as mission 3's ammunition ramp.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainTraversal.MaximumChunks
member.summary: How many chunks the original's descriptor buffer holds.
member.remarks: It is retail's bound and it belongs with retail's view distance, which is at most . The remaster's detail settings resolve the ground two and three times further out, where one frame's descent can ask for several times as many chunks — measured at up to 4062 across the campaign at the ultra distance on a 16:9 frustum, and straight through this bound on a wider one. Everything past the bound is dropped, which is a hole in the ground, so takes the bound as an argument and the renderer raises it with the detail setting.

member.remarks: The graphics detail setting chooses this, not the 0x54844C initializer. At startup sub_406390 writes the base from the terrain-detail flags: (96) when the low bit is set, (129) for medium, and otherwise (163) — the default with neither bit set, which is what the retail game runs at. member.summary: Lays every SplineObj chain: one bent segment per consecutive waypoint pair.

remarks.para: A segment spans from the previous waypoint to the waypoint that names its model, which is sub_500EF0's arrangement — a chain of N waypoints lays N−1 segments and the first waypoint's own Segment Model goes unused. The curve is the one sub_4E4530 builds: a Hermite cubic between the two waypoint positions whose tangents are the waypoints' local X axes scaled by the chord length, evaluated here per vertex rather than at the original's NumAreas sampled matrices — the same curve, continuously.

A vertex's local X picks its place along the curve (the original measures the model's X extent the same way, sub_4E4530's tail); its local Y and Z ride the curve's zero-roll frame. Divergence: the original also interpolates a twist angle between the endpoint orientations; every level-1 waypoint is authored yaw-only, so the twist is dropped until a level needs it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.VehicleDeathZone
member.summary: The volume a vehicle kills a human in by driving over them, in the vehicle's frame.

remarks.para: Every vehicle model carries a TASKTYPE_DEATHZONE attachment (the T80's 614_07_1, the APC's 601_07_1, the truck's 610_04_1). The class (0x465BC0) registers the zone's model into the collision world and re-seats it on its vehicle every tick (0x465F50). A human it touches runs 0x45FA80: once inside the zone's bounding sphere, a segment from the human to the zone's centre is cast against the zone's own model, and a human with no zone surface in between -- one inside the zone -- takes 10000 damage to zone 13 if the vehicle is moving at 50 units a tick or more. Probed in Mission 7: APC 352 killed a player standing in its road on contact.
The port takes the zone's volume as the bounds of its model's collision mesh, placed at the attachment's offset.

member.param: The volume's lower corner in the vehicle's frame, in world units.
The volume's upper corner in the vehicle's frame, in world units.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldInteraction.WeaponHit
member.summary: A round strikes the task: its WeaponHit handler.
member.returns: Whether the round broke it.

remarks.para: A switch's handler (0x445840, I.G.I. 2's Switch_WeaponHitHandler the same) breaks it when it is Destructable; nothing ever mends it. Its update then wears its fifth model, and it is never offered again. Mission 8's three breakable switches name one model for every state, so they look the same broken.
A cabinet's handler is the engine's empty one: the round stops on it and nothing happens.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldInteraction.MarkerPoint(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Single)
member.summary: Where a marker for this task belongs, in world units.
member.param: The human's view position, for the tasks whose answer depends on it.
How far the frame stands between the last two simulation states.
member.returns: A point on the thing itself.

remarks.para: The middle of the model, not the task's own origin and not . An origin is wherever the author put it — the hinge edge of a door, the floor under a terminal — and the activation point moves with the player by design, which is exactly what a marker must not do: it belongs to the object, and an object does not move when you take a step sideways.

A door is the exception that proves it. Its marker rides the leaf's live swing and slide, so it stays on the door as the door moves — and only then, because the door has moved. It rides the presented pose, not the tick's: everything moves on the thirty-hertz tick and is drawn far more often than that, so a mark that reads the tick state judders along beside a door that glides.
A fence and a wire are the other exception: they are longer than a player can use at once, so the part of them being offered is the part being marked, which is what already answers.

member.summary: Gets the exact root placement and gamma of a retail self-driving interaction state.
member.remarks: These are the constants in the state initializers at 0x40BED0, 0x40C2F0, 0x40C670, 0x40C970 and 0x40CF70. The interaction animations were authored against these roots; playing them at the player's arbitrary standing point leaves the hands visibly detached from the lock, cabinet, keyboard or gun.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldInteraction.PlantPose(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldTraceCast)
member.summary: State 36's entry (0x40D180): the body pose and the point the charge goes, from the eye.
member.param: The human's view position (HumanView+224), in world units.
The world cast 0x4CC2A0 makes, or to cast nothing.
member.returns: The pose before the ground snap.
member.remarks: The entry casts from the eye to the target (the task plus its model's magic vertex 1, ). On a hit the charge goes to the contact and the body faces the struck surface's normal; on a miss the "contact" is the eye and the direction is eye-to-target. Either way gamma is atan2(d.y, d.x) + π/2 (0x4B2D00) and the body stands 2048 units back from the contact along the normalised eye-to-target line (0x4B3100). Measured in Mission 6 with the probe: planting tank 1601 from the south-west put the body at contact − 2048·d̂ and gamma at −0.981745, the facet normal's, not eye-to-target's −0.927.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldInteraction.Run(System.Int32)
member.summary: The task's update, where its pulses clear on their stamps and its expressions are read.
member.param: The level's tick.

remarks.para: Each type's own update, as retail runs it: a switch (0x4450F0) reads its On expression, then, two ticks past its press, shifts isPressed into isLastPressed and clears it, so isLastPressed holds for the one update that clears it; a terminal (0x4438E0) and a GenericTBA (0x4480B0) read their On expression, are off while exploded, and clear isInUse and the finished-this-tick byte two ticks past their stamps; a cabinet (0x444590) clears isInUse likewise; a fence (0x43FC30) is electrified as its expression says, or not at all. Every isLast* takes its value in the same update, after the clear.
An expression slot that is empty or did not compile leaves its byte as it was, so a script's write to it stands; a door's expressions are its own update's ().

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldObject
member.summary: One node of the object tree a placement expands into: a LOD chain, where it sits, and the children its model attaches.

remarks.para: The original calls these sector objects. A placement supplies the root; every further node comes from an on the node above it, resolved through the (0x4DFA50). Attachments are read from the most detailed model only — the original passes *model, which is level 0.

is why the tree is built at all: the baked lightmaps of a whole placement are numbered by walking this tree depth first and counting one per level of detail, so a node's index cannot be known without every node before it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement.RenderGroup
member.summary: Gets which of the frame's sixteen queues this placement is drawn in.

remarks.para: The engine draws nothing directly. World_Draw (igi2ed 0x417F50) walks the world cube tree and lets the traversal enqueue each visible object into one of sixteen call queues; QCube_CallHandlers (0x4171B0) then empties them 0 to 15 with a shadow-volume flush after each. So the group is the object's place in the frame, and objects in different groups are separated by everything the groups between them draw.

Mostly the engine's, not the level's. An author can set it — I.G.I. 2 registers RenderGroup as a level parameter on its rigid objects and all 24 levels use it — but the values a level ships are largely the ones the engine would have chosen anyway. Read out of the create handlers: the sky takes 0, the sector object the camera is standing inside is forced to 1, terrain takes 2, a sector object 3, everything else 5, a vehicle 7, a human or the first-person view 9, a sector — and anything registered as interior to one — 12, and water 14.

Project I.G.I. authors none, so every placement of that game keeps and the sixteen queues collapse to one — which is why a fixed pass order is not a shortcut that happens to work there, but the same behaviour.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement.LightmapEntry
member.summary: Gets the archive entry name when the title knows it outright, rather than by formula.
member.remarks: The two games name the entries of the same archive differently. Project I.G.I. writes <set>_<%05d>.olm, which can compute from and ; I.G.I. 2 writes %04d_%04d_%1d.olm over a task id, a model index and a level of detail, and it reads the name out of the archive rather than rebuilding it — one of its levels registers full paths where the other 23 register bare names, so rebuilding would work on 23 levels and fail on the 24th. A title that has the name simply supplies it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldRayHit
member.summary: Where a ray met a surface.
member.param: The point of contact, in world units.
The surface's outward normal, unit length.
How far along the ray the contact sits, in world units.
Which material the struck face is made of — the fourth field of its , and a row of the game material table.

remarks.para: The material is what decides what a hit looks like. The original never lets a bullet choose its own mark: 0x4083C0 packages the impact and dispatches it to the material's own task class, so a round through glass and into brick leaves two different marks without the shot knowing about either. Carrying the index here is what makes that lookup possible at all.

Which side was crossed is carried for the same reason. The original's surface test (0x4CD300) reports an entry row and an exit row as two complementary flags — *a7 = c0; *a8 = !c0, so exactly one is ever set — and the shot resolution branches on which: an entry crossing sounds and marks the surface, an exit crossing leaves only the exit decal and no sound at all. The test itself is the face's own facing against the ray, which is computed here anyway in order to turn the normal towards the ray.

member.param: Whether the ray crossed the surface's BACK face — leaving solid rather than entering it.
Whether the surface is the level's terrain, which is no object: nothing on it takes a decal message, so a blood droplet that lands there (0x4640B0) draws nothing and marks nothing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.RayTriangle
member.summary: Ray against a triangle.

remarks.para: The Möller–Trumbore test. This is geometry, not transcription — unlike everything around it, it was not read out of the executable. A ray-triangle intersection has one answer, and the original's own test (reached through 0x4CDB20's shape dispatch) has not been read. What was read, and is what actually decides how the player moves, is which surfaces count as walls and what happens when one is met — see .
Both faces are hit. A collision mesh's winding is not established, and treating one side as invisible would let the player walk out through a wall they had somehow got behind.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.RayTriangle.Intersect(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Double@)
member.summary: Intersects a ray with a triangle.
member.param: The ray's start.
Its direction; need not be unit length.
The first vertex.
The second.
The third.
Receives the hit's distance as a fraction of , so a value in [0, 1) lies within the segment.
member.remarks: The far end is exclusive, and that matters more than it looks. After a slide the body rests exactly one skin width off the wall, so the next tick's ray — which reaches a skin further than the move — ends precisely on that same surface. Counting it would make the sweep slide to the same point ten times over and then revert the move entirely, so walking into any wall would stop you dead instead of letting you slide along it.
member.returns: when the ray misses.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene
member.summary: The drawable contents of a loaded mission: every task that places a model, joined to the pack instance that supplies its geometry and textures.

remarks.para: Level 1 places 501 of these, and all 501 resolve — the task's Model string is exactly a pack instance name. They are mostly EditRigidObj (380) and Building (26), with doors, trains and soldiers making up the rest.

Positions arrive in the engine's own units and are converted to metres here, once, so that everything downstream — camera, near and far planes, movement speed — is in one unit. The original works in engine units throughout and only divides for display; the reason to differ is depth precision, since a level spans millions of units and a near plane a fraction of one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.UnitsPerMetre
member.summary: Engine units per metre, the original's WORLD_METER script constant.
member.remarks: Registered as a double at 0x539558. Model vertices use the same units as world positions: the level-1 water tower measures 95005 units tall, which is 23 metres.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.ToMetres(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Converts a position or an offset from engine units into metres.
member.param: The value in engine units.
member.returns: The same value in metres.
member.remarks:
Beside the constant that defines it, because every title's scene walk needs it and the arithmetic is the kind that goes wrong by being retyped: a walk that forgets it renders a level four thousand times too large, which looks like an empty world rather than like a scale error.
Both games agree on the divisor. Game_Open registers WORLD_METER as a double (IGI.exe 0x539558, igi2.exe 0x640B80) and both hold 4096.

member.summary: Converts a position or an offset from metres into engine units.
member.param: The value in metres.
member.returns: The same value in engine units.
member.remarks: The inverse of , and it exists because both games' terrain needs it: the level-of-detail thresholds are authored in engine units, so the eye is converted into that space rather than the height field out of it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.FromPlacements(OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedMission,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldPlacement})
member.summary: Builds a scene from placements a title has already resolved.
member.param: The mission the placements belong to, which is what locates the lightmap archive.
Everything to draw, in the order the level placed it.
member.returns: The scene.

remarks.para: walks a task tree and knows a great deal about which types Project I.G.I. places and what their parameters are called — down to naming the security-camera models. That walk is not shared, and neither is it needed: a title that has already worked out what it places has nothing left to discover, and only needs somewhere to put the answer.
So this is the seam that lets one renderer draw both games. The scene, the placement and the renderer are shared; how a level is read into placements is the title's own business.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.GroundHeight
member.summary: Gets the level's ground height, in metres, as an absolute world Z.

remarks.para: A level's coordinates carry a large absolute offset — mission 1's ground sits some 42 km from the world origin — so a height authored as "four metres up", like the sky plane's or the fog base's, is nowhere near a world Z of four. It is an offset, and it has to be anchored to something before it means anything. This is that anchor.

It is the median placement height rather than the middle of the bounding box, because most of what a level places sits on the ground: the median lands on it, while a box is dragged upwards by a single radio mast and downwards by a basement.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.TrainCouplingDistance(OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel)
member.summary: Gets the coupling distance the retail Train solver reads from a car model.
member.param: The car model.
member.returns: The distance between its two couplers, or nought when it has no coupler vertices.
member.remarks: Train initialization (0x42A150) asks the model for magic vertices 0 and 1 through 0x414ED0, stores abs(v0.x - v1.x) at Train+1868, and passes one such value per car to the railroad evaluator. Mesh bounds include overhangs and are not the consist spacing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene.WheelRadius(OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel)
member.summary: Gets the rolling radius of a wheel model, in world units.
member.param: The wheel model.
member.returns: Half its largest extent, or nought when it has no geometry.
member.remarks: A wheel is a disc: its two largest extents are both the diameter and the smallest is the tread width, so half the largest is the radius. Retail keeps a radius on each wheel task's own record, which the port has no reader for; measuring the drawn model gets within a tenth of it. The Mission 1 truck's wheel measures 0.46 m here, against the 0.50 m its spin rate on a straight implies in a capture of the running game -- where the suspension travel that stood in for it before was 0.3 m, forty per cent out.

member.summary: Builds an orientation from the three Euler angles level data stores.
member.param: The alpha, beta and gamma angles in radians.
member.returns: The rotation.
member.remarks: A Real32x9 parameter is three angles on the wire, not nine components, and the original concatenates three axis rotations in 0x4B38E0.
